When you are trading straddles, strangles, or other multi-leg option strategies, it becomes difficult to see how the entire strategy is performing if you plot each leg separately.
For example, in a straddle, the call premium might go down while the put premium goes up. If you look at each of them individually, you will see what happened to each option, but you won’t at once know how the total premium has changed.
The Multi Straddle-Strangle Charts on Sensibull let you plot the total price of the legs on a single chart.
You can find this under Analyse > Multi Straddle-Strangle Charts on the Sensibull website or app.
You can track:
For straddles, you can select a fixed strike, a strike in relation to the at-the-money level, or Auto ATM, which mirrors the at-the-money straddle as the underlying asset moves.
For strangles, choose the call and put strike prices that you want to track together.
For custom strategies: you can add your own option legs, decide whether to buy or sell, and set the quantity for each leg.
You can also include several strategies on the same chart, such as comparing two straddles, a straddle with a strangle, or different custom strategies over the same period.
After you have added them, you will be able to see the details of each strategy, hide the individual charts, change the timeframe, and zoom in on a specific period.
This makes it easier to track how a strategy’s combined premium changes, rather than keeping multiple option charts open and adding up the legs yourself.

We do a lot at Zerodha, but most of it never reaches your inbox, thanks to our strict no-spam policy. This is our monthly roundup of product updates, new features, and everything else happening across Zerodha.
Here’s what happened in September 2026.
Trade From Charts is now on the Kite app
We’ve brought Trade From Charts (TFC) to TradingView charts on the Kite app. You can now place and manage orders directly from charts without switching between screens.
You can place orders using the Buy and Sell buttons, long-press a price level to place limit or stop-loss orders, and drag and drop existing orders to modify their prices.
You can also enable Instant Order Placement for one-tap orders, view open positions with live P&L, and exit or reverse positions directly from the chart. TFC also supports multi-chart layouts, with the option to save up to 10 custom layouts.
Read more .
Stock SIPs on Kite web have been revamped
We’ve revamped Stock SIPs on Kite web to make it easier to invest regularly in stocks, ETFs, and bonds.
You can now create SIPs directly from Marketwatch, Holdings, or the Orders tab. SIPs can be scheduled daily, weekly, or monthly, based on either a fixed quantity or investment amount.
With amount-based SIPs, you can set how much you want to invest, and Kite calculates the quantity automatically. You can also set custom allocations for multiple securities and link UPI Autopay to debit funds from your bank account before the scheduled investment.
The revamped experience is coming to the Kite app soon.
Read more .
Option Chain for NSE Commodities
Kite’s Option Chain now supports NSE Commodity derivatives (NCO), including bullion, energy, base metals, and electricity.
You can view Calls and Puts across strike prices, track open interest, and place orders directly from the option chain, without adding individual contracts to your watchlist.
To find these contracts, search for NCO followed by the commodity name on Kite.
Read more .
Bids is now IPO & Bids
We’ve renamed the Bids section on Kite web to IPO & Bids for better discovery.
You can use this section to apply for IPOs, Sovereign Gold Bonds, Government Securities, and company buybacks. The updated navigation is coming to the Kite app soon.
A faster account opening process
We’ve simplified the Zerodha account opening process by making income proof optional during signup and moving its collection to after eSign.
You can now complete your trading and demat account opening for equities and mutual funds without submitting income proof. If you want to trade F&O or commodities, you can submit income proof during signup or activate these segments later from your Profile.
This also prevents delays in bank verification or Account Aggregator services from holding up registration.
New pre-open session rules and ETF price bands
Stock exchanges have revised the pre-open session rules and ETF price bands.
Under the new rules, market orders can only be placed, modified, or cancelled between 9:00 AM and 9:05 AM. After that, until order entry closes randomly between 9:08 AM and 9:10 AM, only limit orders are allowed.
Gold and Silver ETFs are now included in the pre-open session, helping them discover opening prices before regular trading begins at 9:15 AM.
The exchanges have also changed how ETF price bands are calculated. Instead of using an older NAV, the reference price is now based on the volume-weighted average price (VWAP) during the final 30 minutes of the previous trading session. The permitted price bands also differ across ETF categories.
Read more .
Zerodha Life Cycle Fund 2031
Zerodha Fund House has launched the Zerodha Life Cycle Fund 2031, designed for financial goals roughly five years away, such as buying a car or saving for a house down payment.
The fund automatically adjusts its asset allocation as 2031 approaches. It starts with a higher allocation to equities and gradually shifts towards more conservative assets, including government bonds and arbitrage.
Zerodha Fund House also offers the 2036 and 2041 Life Cycle Funds for longer-term goals.
Mutual fund sessions on Varsity Live
Varsity Live now hosts regular, free interactive sessions on mutual funds.
The sessions cover topics such as Direct versus Regular plans, active versus passive funds, reading mutual fund factsheets, index funds, and portfolio construction.
You can register for upcoming sessions on Varsity Live .
Fourth Cross: Zerodha’s open-source collective
Zerodha has relied on Free and Open Source Software since the beginning. We’ve now formalised our open-source work under Fourth Cross, an independent collective dedicated to building and maintaining open-source software for the public good.
Based in JP Nagar, Bengaluru, the collective brings together our engineering team of around 35 people, who work on tools used by developers and organisations around the world.
Explore more at: https://fourthcross.tech/

Karthik talks about his 18-year journey with Nithin, building Varsity over more than a decade, why Zerodha doesn’t track business metrics for its educational initiatives, his financial struggles in 2008, and the story behind Zerodha Capital.

In our latest episode of I n The Money by Zerodha , we start with how covered calls are pitched to investors, as a way to earn "free money" on stocks you already own, and why even Fischer Black, co-creator of the Black-Scholes formula, was skeptical of the idea.
We then look at the history of the strategy, how it was sold by brokers over the decades, and what a behavioral study on Dutch investors revealed about why people find it attractive in theory but less so when they actually see the payoff.
The episode breaks down the mechanics of a covered call with real numbers, what happens when the stock falls, stays flat, or rallies, and why the strategy has a capped upside but nearly full downside.
Finally, we run a backtest on 10 of the most liquid large-cap Indian stocks from January 2022 onward, selling a 5% out-of-the-money call every month, and compare the results stock by stock to see whether covered calls actually add value to a buy-and-hold portfolio in India.
Check out In The Money

What followed weeks like this one?
This week’s market condition: the Nifty sits 7.3% below its 40-week average, while India VIX is higher than 70% of days over the past year. In historical records back to 1 April 2022, 36 weeks had a comparable combination of trend distance and volatility rank (within 5 percentage points on trend and 25 points on VIX).
The chart below shows how often each return range occurred: the bar height represents the number of historical weeks (observations), not the return percentage. For example, after a negative week with elevated volatility, on 15 occasions the Nifty went on to gain between 0% and 2% the following week (the tallest bar in the chart), while on 9 occasions it fell between -2% and 0%.

Over four weeks, the median return was +1.05%, positive in 60% of instances.
Historical base rates describe how markets behaved after similar technical setups in the past; they do not forecast or guarantee future returns.

Welcome to The Climate Brief’s newsletter, where we break down India’s BIGGEST climate stories in a way that feels personal and relatable.
Dear Readers,
Hasn’t this September felt SO HOT? Usually, by this time of the year, we’re stepping out with an umbrella because it’s raining. But this year, the respite from heat hasn’t come, and across parts of India, we are still using ACs.
In fact, India witnessed an unusual surge in electricity demand this September, with power demand reaching levels of what it was in summer months.
What’s The Unusual Thing that Happened?
On September 10, India’s peak electricity demand touched 269 gigawatts – the HIGHEST recorded in any September. This is also just a whisker away from the year’s all-time high of 270.82 GW on May 21 .
During the first 9 days of Sept, India’s peak demand averaged at 254.63 GW , similar to what we generally see in summer, not in the middle of monsoon.
What is peak power demand, though? It’s the highest average amount of power drawn from the grid at an interval of 15 to 30 minutes.
Think of it as rush hour traffic - though vehicles are on the road throughout the day, there’s ONE period when traffic is the highest. Just like that, throughout the day, homes, offices, factories and businesses are using electricity. But when all of them start using a LOT of electricity at once, the demand on the power grid shoots up and THIS high point is the peak power demand.
Normally, electricity demand peaks during the summer months between April and July. And of course, that’s because extreme heat and rising temperature pushes up the usage of ACs and coolers.
But over the last few years, another trend has emerged
In fact between 2019 to 2026, September peak demand has risen by 56%! And in just one year, the demand has increased by 17.5%.
What’s Driving This Unusual Surge?
There are 2 big reasons:
#1 More Heat = More Electricity
It’s STILL very hot in several parts of India. This is because 2026 is a Super El Nino year! The last time there was an all-time peak it was in September 2023 - which was ALSO an El Nino year. In August, the IMD forecast that average maximum temperatures in September remained above normal . And when temperatures stay high, we use more ACs, coolers and fans.
You can see this happening in Kerala, for instance - The state experiences unusually high Sept temperatures and power demand is up by about 15% higher than the same period last year.
But quick pause to acknowledge - Even without El Niño, let’s not forget the other problem: Global warming. We are seeing more frequent and intense heatwaves that keep increasing cooling demand. It just gets worse in El Nino years, but the overall trend is that it’s getting hotter every year.
#2 Rainfall Deficit: Now, this is something we’ve spoken about in our previous videos. Between June 1 and September 9, India faced a 15% seasonal deficit. Not only does lack of rain retain heat, but leads to farmers being forced to depend on other sources of water like irrigation that needs more electricity.
Like in Karnataka which has an 81% rainfall deficit this monsoon . More than 200 of the 239 taluks are facing drought and the state govt has warned of possible water and power shortages. At the same time, peak power demand crossed 19,000 MW, with high consumption during the night.
While heat and reduced rain are pushing electricity demand up on one side, the same deficit is cutting supply on the other. That’s because many states depend on hydropower electricity.
Less rains means low reservoir levels which means less energy generated. And this year, El Nino has squeezed India’s hydropower generation. Between April and September 2026, India’s hydropower generation fell by almost 11% as compared to the same period in 2025. Out of 30 major hydropower reservoirs, 23 had lower water levels than during the same period last year.
Once again, let’s go back to Kerala which had a 26% rainfall deficit till September 11, while rainfall in Idukki (which has Kerala’s largest hydropower reservoir) was 47% below normal. And with less monsoon rains, the state is now exploring other floating solar projects and pumped- storage to meet long-term electricity demand.
Here’s what you should take away from this video:
The surge in electricity demand is another SIGN that El Nino is HERE! We’ve been talking about EL Nino for months and this rising electricity demand is another sign of just how big its effects are
El Nino is also a reminder that the weather patterns we’ve relied on to plan for electricity demand are becoming harder to predict. So it’s now more important than ever to plan ahead and find solutions that mitigate negative impacts.
Here’s why this matters: The only way to fix it is by first identifying it so solutions can be sought and a crisis in the future can be prevented.
Until next time,
Team Climate Brief

Welcome to The Climate Brief’s newsletter, where we break down India’s BIGGEST climate stories in a way that feels personal and relatable.
When you think of floods, you probably imagine heavy rainfall, raging rivers or a glacier collapse, don’t you? But what if floods can occur without rains?
Yes, we’re not kidding. Tidal flooding, which is the inundation of low-lying areas for a brief period due to high tides, is a real problem in coastal areas. In this week’s newsletter, we will explain what tidal flooding is, why it’s getting worse, and how Kerala became the first STATE in India to declare it a disaster.
What is tidal flooding?
Let’s start with a science lesson. How do tides occur? It actually starts 384,000 kms away, with the Moon. The moon’s gravity pulls water from the Ocean , creating bulges called high tides. As the Earth spins, coastlines pass through these bulges creating TWO high tides and TWO low tides everyday.
And every 15 days, we see either a full or a new moon. During these periods, the SUN and Moon align resulting in a stronger gravitational pull and higher tides than usual.
When the level of the high tide crosses a certain threshold, it can overflow and temporarily flood low-lying coastal areas - This is called TIDAL FLOODING .
Coastal communities in Kerala have faced this problem for years, with locals calling it nuisance flooding. Usually, Tidal Flooding is more noticeable between November and January, due to the Perigean Spring Tide season (called ‘Vrishchikam’ in Malayalam). This is when the Sun, Moon, and Earth align at their closest possible distances, leading to extra gravitation pull, forcing water much higher than usual.
But, note that water doesn’t come gushing in like you see in rain or cyclone induced floods. What makes this worse is that the frequency of these floods are increasing at an alarming rate. From 2011 to 2022, there were only 11 days when the tide rose above 1.5 meters. However, In January 2025 alone, the tide rose above 1.5 meters on 15 occasions.
And it’s not just homes on the coast that are at risk - Even villages as far as 10KM away are affected.
Image courtesy: EQUINOCT Community Sourced Modelling Solutions
What makes this difficult is that tidal flooding can happen when people least expect it. Water enters homes and stays there for hours till the tide retreats. At least 10% of Kerala’s population which means 20,000 people across 23 gram panchayats are affected by Tidal Flooding in nine coastal areas around Ernakulam.
When saltwater regularly floods these localities, homes and infrastructure gets permanently damaged with rusted household appliances and walls that are eroding. Tidal water also carries pollutants contaminating drinking water .
But why is Kerala particularly at risk?
#1: Kerala (unlike any other state) has perennial monsoon-fed rivers that form estuaries, an extensive backwater systems and a dense network of canals.
#2: Most coastal villages are situated on the floodplains or along these estuaries, canals and backwaters.
#3: During high tides, seawater rises, through these backwater canals and adjoining rivermouths and travels as far as 10 km inland entering into houses in these villages.
Why Tidal Flooding Is Becoming Severe
Tidal flooding is not a new concept for Kerala but the impacts have been much more severe:
Tidal flooding, which was traditionally an issue between November and December, is now dragging on from October all the way to May .
Flooding is increasingly being reported well beyond the traditional hotspots. In fact, many HOUSES along the banks of Vembanad Lake have stagnant saline water for prolonged periods!
Areas like these and other relatively high-value , urbanised parts of Kochi are now experiencing water-logging associated with high tides. These places never reported flooding before 2018!
In fact, Kerala’s 2026 government notification itself recognises that tidal flooding is now occurring in ways “not previously experienced”
So why is this happening?
#1 Rising Sea Levels: As the planet warms, oceans absorb more heat and EXPAND, while melting ice adds more water to the sea. This means the baseline level of the sea keeps rising and when that is already high, it takes much less for a routine high tide to spill into low-lying areas.
Think of a bucket that’s already filled to the brim, it only needs a slight push (high tides) to overflow.
In fact, between January and March 2025, Equinoct - an organisation working with communities in Ernakulam - said that tidal water levels reached 1.6 m which is associated with unprecedented flooding across Kochi!
But this isn’t just happening in Kerala. Reports suggest that sea levels along the Indian coast have been rising at around 4.9 mm a year between 1999 and 2025 . In fact, studies have warned that rising sea levels could put parts of Mumbai, Goa, Chennai and Kerala at risk of inundation in the coming decades.
#2 Rapid Development - The other side of the story is of course damages due to human activities. Remember we said seawater travels inland through rivers and backwaters? Well, over the years, we’ve changed these pathways by building OVER them, especially in low-lying areas.
Experts have linked increased tidal flooding to unregulated sand mining in Kerala, which has caused riverbeds to fall below sea-level. In the Vembanad catchment, studies found that riverbeds had been falling around 7-15 cm every year.
A river with a deeper channel gives tidal water more room to travel upstream. And this is one reason we’re now seeing tidal waters travel as far as 10 km.
Image courtesy: EQUINOCT Community Sourced Modelling Solutions
Around the Vembanad region, changes in river channels, wetlands and sediment movement intensified tidal flooding along the coast. Add to this the loss of wetlands and mangroves, which would otherwise act as natural sponges, and we have a serious problem at hand.
What Can Be Done?
The good news: Kerala has made great progress in terms of addressing the issue, a big milestone being declaring it a state-wide disaster earlier this year!
After years of communities and panchayats raising the issue, Kerala, in January 2026, declared tidal flooding a state-specific disaster, with families entitled for financial relief .
This has come after years of efforts by communities and organizations like Equinoct. They have designed a calendar that the people living in affected areas are using to record flooding days, measuring water levels of tides and the time at which the tide came in. This helps in documentation and creating warning systems for when to expect tides.
They are also working on the ground to map affected homes and villages - so you know what parts are likely to flood. Real-time systems are being developed to warn communities when tidal flooding may occur, so as to give them more time to move their belongings.
But here’s the bad news: A lot more needs to be done. There is NO single solution for every coastal community - While some places may need stronger embankments or better drainage, others may need to protect natural waterways and wetlands.
And while Kerala has become one of the most visible examples of tidal flooding in India, this ISN’T a Kerala problem alone. India has a coastline stretching over 7,500 km and roughly 171 million people living along the coast. Across our coastline, experts believe that tidal flooding is happening, but neither is there enough research nor documentation - primarily because it’s a SILENT problem, one that does not make headlines.
Until next week,

Household debt in India has climbed to roughly 48% of GDP while net household savings have plummeted to an all-time low of 5%. From financing the latest smartphone on Buy-Now-Pay-Later (BNPL) to taking personal loans for vacations and whey protein, Indian borrowing has undergone a massive cultural shift. In Episode 8 of Cash & Copium , Abid, Bhuvan, and Aakanksha dive deep into India’s expanding credit ecosystem, the myth of “no-cost” EMIs, and why borrowing for lifestyle consumption in a high-interest country is a recipe for distress.
Watch the full episode here:
If you’d rather skip to the arguments:
India’s credit expansion isn’t inherently a crisis, but stress is real. The influx of New-To-Credit (NTC) borrowers represents formalization away from loan sharks, but default rates are rising in loans under ₹1 lakh.
“No-Cost” EMIs are a marketing illusion. Between processing fees, GST on interest, lost cash discounts, and merchant markups, lenders ensure someone always pays.
Comparing Indian household debt to the US is a dangerous fallacy. America’s debt is anchored by low, fixed-rate mortgages, whereas Indian retail borrowing is dominated by high-interest unsecured credit.
The real estate loan trap has shifted from land to speculative flats. Previous generations borrowed to buy appreciating land parcels, while today’s buyers take 30-year loans for apartments 25 kilometers away from major city centers.
Gen Z is borrowing without the income base to support it. Over 40% of smartphones sold in India are now bought on credit, with frictionless digital lending targeting younger, lower-income demographics.
Mindless consumerism & the “No-Cost” EMI myth Social media feeds have transformed local peer pressure into global comparison. As Abid puts it, Instagram allows people to look at the entire world’s possessions and vacations and feel “sad, sorry, jealous, and miserable” . He notes: “In this game of trying to ca- keep up with everybody else, I think a lot of people are ending up owning, buying, experiencing things which they think they need, which they might not even actually need... Yeah, I think it’s a genuine problem of mindless consumerism enabled by credit on steroids.”
The flagship lure for this consumerism is the “no-cost” EMI. Whether buying electronics online or stepping into a store, buyers are told that interest is zero. Bhuvan dismantles this assumption: “XYZ financier is not a philanthropist to give people interest-free loans. Nobody is that good in this country. You actually have to read the terms and conditions.”
Even if a retailer absorbs part of the fee to drive store footfall, hidden costs persist. You pay GST on the interest component, pay convenience or processing fees, and forfeit the 5% to 10% cash discount you could have negotiated by paying upfront in cash. More importantly, lender business models depend on delinquency penalties.
Abid explains the underlying business model: “I don’t think there is any such thing called a no-cost EMI. I think all of credit card or credit or any kind of BNPL or anything, their business model is actually not built on everybody repaying on time. Their business model is inevitably built on, uh, somebody...” He adds his friend Balaji’s famous takeaway: “Every Indian fintech company... is a loan shark hiding behind an app.”
Why India isn’t America when it comes to leverage Defenders of rising household debt frequently point to the United States, arguing that mature economies thrive on leverage. However, using the US as a benchmark ignores stark structural differences in interest rates and purchasing power.
First, America’s household debt is largely built on 30-year fixed-rate mortgages that historically sat at low interest rates. India’s debt expansion, by contrast, is fueled by floating-rate personal loans and credit cards carrying interest rates anywhere from 12% to 40%+.
Second, debt in the US has not eliminated financial vulnerability. Abid notes: “Federal Reserve survey found that roughly a third of American adults could not cover a $400 emergency expense with cash.” When leverage is used for non-productive consumption rather than asset creation, even minor economic shocks leave borrowers stranded.
Abid emphasizes: “America is not the proof that household debt is a good idea. America is actually the single biggest proof that if you let household debt go into frenzies fueled by speculation, it can take down not just that country, but the entire bloody world with it.”
From land parcels to 3-crore flats hanging in the air A subtle generational shift has occurred in how Indians approach property loans. When previous generations took home loans, the money was spent primarily on buying land in accessible areas, with a small portion spent on construction. The underlying asset was a finite, appreciating resource.
Today, young professionals in major metros take on massive 30-year EMIs for high-density apartments built far on the city outskirts. Abid highlights the absurdity of current real estate marketing: “I found an ad recently, ‘Residences for Bangalore’s most sophisticated elites, 25 kilometers off Sharjapur.’ I’m like, ‘Bro, Bangalore elite live in Sadashiv Nagar, okay? They don’t even come towards Sharjapur because it is below their status.’”
Committing 60% to 70% of a young salary to service an EMI on a speculative flat destroys your financial flexibility. It strips away the optionality to switch careers, start a business, or relocate for better opportunities.
Gen Z, frivolous loans, and bad personal bets The data on digital lending shows where credit is flowing. Half of new-to-credit card customers are Gen Z (under 30), and nearly 60% of digital personal loans go to borrowers under 35—with 40% of those loans originating in tier-3 cities. In fact, 42% of all smartphones sold in India are now financed through loans.
To determine whether a purchase justifies a loan, Abid offers a simple filter: “Would you still enjoy whatever you purchased while you’re still paying back the loan?” This eliminates ephemeral purchases like vacation BNPLs or short-lived gadget upgrades.
The hosts also shared their worst personal loan experiences. Bhuvan admitted to getting accidentally opted into a BNPL scheme for whey protein, while Abid shared his own trading disaster from 2011: “I borrowed a personal loan to buy Nifty 4800 put option in 2011... And blew all of it up.”
While Bhuvan notes that overall system-wide stress is currently concentrated in the under-₹1 lakh loan bucket, the risk for younger borrowers remains acute.
Abid sums up the core mismatch in India’s credit boom: “All the money, all the AUM with this is with uncles, okay? These midlife uncles. Like everybody saying, ‘Oh, Gen Z rising,’ they are all on acid because Gen Z genuinely doesn’t have money on an average... So basically, you are saying that people who don’t have much money are in a structurally high interest rate country, spending on consumption at a very high interest rate when their affordability is low”.

Hi folks. I’m Pranav, and I’ve been fascinated by the economics of innovation for quite a while now.
The pioneer in this field is Joseph Schumpeter, who analyzed the relationship between market turbulence and innovation that characterizes modern capitalism. He had many other things to say about human society — some of them downright depressing — but it was because of him that our understanding of companies living and dying came to be. Last year’s Nobel Prize in Economics was awarded partly to two economists who formalized Schumpeter’s work mathematically.
Interestingly, though, Schumpeter wasn’t the first one to identify this. That credit goes to an economist (some may say social scientist) whose name splits audiences completely down the middle. I am, of course, referring to Karl Marx.
Now, many economists today work in the tradition of Schumpeter. They usually mix it with other sub-fields of economics (like Post-Keynesian, classical, institutional, even mainstream), but largely, their work gets categorized under the term evolutionary economics . Their work spans how industries perish, re-generate, how new ones spawn, how knowledge works on the factory floor, how do you transfer such knowledge across companies with different incentives, what is the role of public and private actors in all of this, and how the innovation trajectory of developing countries differs from that of developed ones.
Some names that I’m also a huge fan of who do incredible work in this are: Carlota Perez, Mariana Mazzucato (who’s very famous in her own right today), Richard Nelson, Giovanni Dosi and Steven Klepper.
But when I read their work, I’d be constantly nagged by one question: who’s doing this kind of scholarship in India?
For all our shortcomings, we genuinely do have stories of innovation (and I don’t mean jugaad ). Not necessarily that of new products altogether, but I’d argue that the way we took over global pharma is nothing short of mind-blowing. Similarly, India has one of the largest auto ancillary industries in the world. And, of course, there’s the IT industry. Why they look the way they do today was a long, often-unpredictable march. But I could never see anyone in the mainstream of Indian economics with such work, even if they had done it.
Until one day, I did a little bit more digging, and realized that India does have its own, small set of economists who have studied how innovation in an emerging market like ours works. And they’ve been doing this for a long, long time, so it was really on me to not have known that they did. This Subtext interviews one of them.
Prof. Rakesh Basant is the ex-JSW Chair Professor of Innovation and Public Policy in IIM-Ahmedabad, where he’s spent more than 30 years teaching economics in various forms. His focus is understanding what India’s national innovation system could be. That involves connecting the macro picture to firm strategy, trade policy with joint ventures, and understanding how academia-industry linkages work in India.
You’d argue that, hey, innovation is not best taught in theory at all, and there’s no better way than to actually be on the ground. Well, Prof. Basant is one of the rare academics that actually put theory to what I’d call ground-breaking practice . He was one of the founding members — and later Chairperson — of the CIIE, which is now better-known as IIM-A Ventures. CIIE is one of India’s first-ever incubators. And in this episode, he tells me what it’s like to have set up an incubator when there were hardly any proper Indian VC funds, let alone Indian incubators. By virtue of his time at IIM-A, Prof. Basant has not just educated, but also advised some of India’s most famous investors and entrepreneurs.
This is quite a technical conversation that needed a lot of preparation on my part. Prof weaves in a lot of theory with a lot of actual industrial application of that theory, particularly in Indian pharma.
But what I think was most alarming in this conversation is the sorry state of academic research in India.
The core of any innovation system in any country is research output and how quickly and effortlessly it’s commercialized. So that means that if you’re a scientist in a public research lab, how quickly can you get your scientific invention to the market? Before that, can it be scaled on a factory floor? How mobile is such a researcher to start their own company to realize this, and how do companies collaborate with research labs, which often have different incentives? All the successful economic development stories, like China and the US, have cracked this very specifically.
Except in India, those linkages are sadly very broken.
I will stop here and let you seep in the conversation for yourself. Here are some of the most interesting quotes from the conversation that I think were worth highlighting:
On why process and product innovation are two different beasts
Most Indian innovation stories (pharma and IT services most notably) are, so far, process stories: take something that already exists and make it dramatically cheaper. That’s not a bad thing, either: every developing country goes down this path before making it’s own pathbreaking products. Plus, process innovation doesn’t stop when you become a developed country, either.
Even then, I wanted to know whether moving from that to inventing genuinely new products is a natural next step. Prof’s answer was that it isn’t an upgrade as much as it’s a different game, with a different internal structure with a heavier load of risk.
“Process changes usually have an internal focus as firms try to optimize or modify processes to reduce costs. These have much lower market risks as compared to product changes, which have an external focus and where revenue generation is dependent on consumer adoption. Therefore, firms generally face much larger market risks when they undertake product changes, and this change can also disrupt their supply chains if new materials and new components are required for this new product. And this is over and above the technological uncertainty the firms face while developing a new product. So broadly, process to product transition is hard, as firms have to deal with both new internal and external challenges and face a higher level of both technological and market uncertainty. And therefore, many companies or firms or nations, when they move from process to product, they find it quite hard.”
On why Indian pharma hasn’t yet made the leap to new drugs
On that note, I wanted to ask him how he views the trajectory of Indian pharma. We became the pharmacy of the world on the back of weak patent laws and brilliant process engineering — and then the jump to discovering original molecules never came. Prof’s explanation isn’t that our scientists aren’t good enough. It’s that nobody de-risked the bet, and that the way the Indian state funds research is structurally unlike every country that has pulled this off.
“But when you’re trying to develop new drugs, it requires taking much higher technological and market risks. The uncertainties are much higher, both on the market and the technology side, and the investments required are also significantly higher. Apart from that, the time horizon when returns are likely to kick in — if at all — is much longer. Not many Indian firms are ready to participate in this kind of innovation activity where technological and market uncertainties are extremely high. And they don’t have those capabilities, because for several years the focus was on building new processes and selling drugs cheap in Western and domestic markets. One can call it a kind of lock-in into technological capabilities that are process-driven rather than product-driven.”
On the role of public R&D
One of the key complementary policies that Prof advocates for to boost our product innovation in industries like pharma is public R&D spend.
“In Western economies — the US and many other developed nations — de-risking of R&D happens through really large research grants to the private sector and to universities. The NIH and the NSF in the US are prime examples. As compared to that, the share of industry in Indian R&D is only about 37%, and the government contributes about 54%. The rest is contributed by higher education institutions, which is quite small. In developed countries, and even countries like South Korea or Brazil, the share of industry is much higher.”
Moreover, to my mind, one of the most critical differences between India and developed countries is that while in other countries the state funds R&D, it is undertaken by private industry and higher education institutions. In India, the state both funds and undertakes R&D through public sector labs and other departmental undertakings. De-risking R&D undertaking by the private sector is critical for India at this stage, particularly in industries where technological uncertainty is extremely high.”
At the same time, Prof is particularly brutal about the prospects of increased private-sector R&D spend.
“I don’t think we can expect the private sector, which has been spending 0.6 or 0.7% of its sales on R&D, to suddenly respond to the policymakers’ call to start spending more than 1%. That expectation is, to my mind, quite foolish.”
But he also goes on to point out bright spots:
“The expectation that public sector research organizations will be able to develop new technologies — we have done extremely well in space, we did quite well in drugs earlier, but in general our experience with public sector research outputs has not been very great. So it has to be a public-private partnership where the public funds are primarily used by private sector establishments, of course with the right governance structures.”
On catch-up and protectionism
Prof’s case for temporary protection is not a case for permanent walls. It’s that a protected firm has to use the breathing room to actually build capability, so that when the foreign competitor arrives the gap is small enough to learn from. And if the gap is too wide, he says, you can’t even copy. He uses a funny Hindi phrase to illustrate his point.
“When the foreign firm comes in, the domestic firm might find it difficult to compete, but the gap is not so high in order to completely kill it. So over time, they try and bridge that gap. And when that gap gets bridged, the multinational brings in new knowledge and the domestic firm copies it again. And so you get into a virtuous cycle. There is this phrase — nakal ke liye akal chahiye [you need intelligence to imitate]. And so if the gap is too high, it’s not possible for you to learn from them. So spillovers and externalities only work when the gap is not very high.”
On the knowledge that can’t be written down
An idea Prof kept circling back to is tacit knowledge: the kind that lives in people and routines rather than in patents or manuals, and that you can only really pick up by doing.
“Tacit knowledge is embedded in individuals and in the systems, routines, and practices used in an organization. And since they are embedded in these practices, transferring such knowledge is difficult, because often it’s difficult to codify. And if you can’t codify, transferring becomes tricky. So the human interaction and exposure to the contexts in which such knowledge is developed or utilized is probably the only way to transfer such knowledge. So training and interaction with persons who have this knowledge becomes extremely critical. If a firm is buying complex knowledge from outside, training and hand-holding is important as firms utilize this new knowledge, because otherwise they will not be able to understand the nuances.”
When I brought up Foxconn recalling its Chinese engineers from Indian factories last year, he nodded — that was exactly this story, told in reverse. Knowledge that refused to move, because it couldn’t be put on paper. In fact, tacit knowledge is considered as, or sometimes more important than intellectual property in manufacturing.
“Absolutely. The Chinese didn’t want to pass on the tacit knowledge to the Indian workers. And I think eventually we got some Taiwanese engineers, right?”
Are patents effective tools for pharma innovation?
One of the questions I had was around how to figure out which kind of knowledge tool is right for which kind of industry. To that extent, there’s a debate about whether patents really boost pharma innovation. For instance, this paper by Giovanni Dosi, who Prof Basant has actually referenced in his own work, argues that their role is overrated. Dosi uses the example of penicillin, which he argues actually came about because of the suppression of patents. One other reason given in favor of this argument is that patents seemingly do not address the real bottleneck in new drug development: clinical trials .
Here’s what Prof says:
“We have not come up with an alternative to IPRs, in some sense. The penicillin example — penicillin development was happening during the war period, and IPR protection was given up because the need was quite critical. But there are very few cases like penicillin where IP was set aside for the widespread use of a drug. It was a wartime effort where public and private entities collaborated across countries — some European countries also participated, if I remember right.”
“I’m not sure whether manufacturers or firms would invest in all the downstream complementary assets — clinical trials, manufacturing, and so on — if they are not sure of the core molecule having some protection. Because there’s no incentive for them to do so, as it’ll get copied quite easily. So some protection is certainly required. What the extent of IP protection for drugs should be remains an open question, as IP can potentially be used for monopolistic practices. But I have not come across any coherent non-IP way of protecting knowledge that creates incentives for firms to invest so heavily in drug development and do all the downstream investments. If one wants to use the penicillin model for all types of drugs, that would require significant state capacity and effort, and might actually result in a kind of regulatory failure.”
On the split between teaching and research in India
The part of the conversation that stayed with me longest was about a decision taken in the 1950s and ‘60s: concentrate research in specialised labs like CSIR, and leave universities to only teach. Decades on, Prof argues, it has become a vicious cycle that has hollowed out both the teaching and the research — and it’s clearly something he grieves.
“The teachers who were teaching did not have access to new research. The kind of teaching that happened in universities was not research-intensive, and therefore the quality of output that we have from our universities is fairly poor. And since we have no long tradition of research in universities, they are not appropriate for tying up with the private sector or industries to develop new products. They simply don’t have the capability. So it has become kind of a vicious cycle. I feel quite sad about it at times, because there’s hardly any large universities which are doing good research as well as teaching.”
On the broken handoff between labs and firms
If there’s one thread running through Prof’s entire career, it’s the broken handoff between what Indian research institutions discover and what Indian firms actually build. I asked him what a working link between a lab and a business really requires. He laid out four conditions — clear industry demand, genuine research capability, the right incentives, and workable contracts — and then told me, bluntly, how few of them we meet.
“For certain kinds of institutions, all of them to some extent. But for a large number of higher education institutions, and even for a large number of businesses, none of them. I have come across firms which say that we want to do some work with education institutions in this space. When you ask them to articulate the needs clearly, they are not able to do that. Of course, I still think that the higher education institutions are the weakest link in this whole thing, because of the capability deficit that we spoke about. And the contractual structures, the regulatory mechanisms — whether a university or a department can sign up with a firm for a certain kind of project — all that is quite cumbersome even today.”
On why a college couldn’t own a stake in the companies it built
It’s often discussed that Ather, the electric-scooter company, is partly owned by IIT Madras’s incubation cell, and IIM-A Ventures holds stakes in the likes of Razorpay and Agnikul.
But for a long time, public institutions weren’t allowed to hold equity in the startups they incubated at all. Similarly, IIM-A Ventures is also an entity distinct from IIM-A that can’t exactly transfer their stakes in startups to the institution whose name it takes.
The reason, Prof explained, was almost theological: a not-for-profit that owns equity is making a profit, and that can’t be allowed.
“The idea was fairly simple. Educational institutions were seen as not-for-profit entities. So as soon as you have equity, you are making profits. It’s as simple — or as foolish — as that, as you pick. That was the reason entities like IITs and IIMs were not allowed to take equity, because they were not businesses. Even today, some people think IIMs and IITs can actually hold equity in these companies. In reality, that’s not the case. What happens is you create a separate legal entity which holds equity on the institution’s behalf. So the IIM is not holding equity. They can only support the institution if some profits are made by this legal entity. It’s not that profit-sharing is happening, because as soon as you use the word ‘profit-sharing,’ you say you’ve become a business and should be paying taxes and all that rigmarole.
On building an incubator before the ecosystem existed
Prof Basant helped set up CIIE — now IIMA Ventures — when India had almost no domestic VC funds or incubators to imitate. I wanted to know what that felt like. His answer is a gentle rebuke to the idea that practice simply follows theory: they had no framework, they learned on the job, and they deliberately ran at the hardest problems, because that was where the market had failed.
“I wish I had such a clear theoretical understanding of this kind while we were setting up CIIE. Whatever I’m sharing with you is something which we have learned on the job, experimented, made mistakes, and slowly built things that helped us mature and grow. So nothing was done with a pre-known framework. The frameworks evolved, got adapted, got modified as we did learning by doing. The key guiding principle for us was that our activities should focus on areas where the market has failed. We should not enter those areas where the market is well functioning. We said we should not focus on easier tasks, and more difficult tasks require more learning, and that’s what we did.”

Hi folks, I’m Pranav , and I love The Matrix.
So does our latest guest, Sidu Ponnappa .
In fact, when we shot this podcast live at our office, for a moment, it seemed like Sidu was seated the same way Morpheus was when he gave his infamous “red-pill” speech to a naive Neo about how AI has become sentient. You’ll see the moment on YouTube.
Sidu may not be fighting the agents like Morpheus does, but rather embraces them — in all fairness, the agents of today are not sentient like in the movie. But he shares many of the same traits. He’s unafraid of strong beliefs as much as he’s unafraid of changing them. He’s argumentative, contrarian, philosophical, and an extremely clear thinker who always seems to know what needs to be done, all at the same time.
Perhaps, the resemblance goes too uncanny. It wasn’t long ago that on Twitter, Sidu wrote a fantastic essay called “ There is no product ” . For fans of the movie, the inspiration behind the title shouldn’t be a surprise. But for those who don’t, I’d like you to just watch the “There is no spoon” scene.
A veteran in the Bangalore tech ecosystem, Sidu started at ThoughtWorks in the mid-2000s, in what he describes as the last era when a consultant was expected to learn a new industry and a new tech stack inside four weeks and nobody thought that was unreasonable. He co-founded a boutique IT services company called C42 Engineering with Aakash Dharmadhikari, which he sold to Gojek in 2015, Indonesia’s largest internet commerce company. Then, he led all of Gojek’s core engineering efforts, helping them turn into a giant in their native country.
Sidu and Aakash are now building realfast , an AI-native IT services firm that went from a hundred thousand dollars of revenue in a year to seven figures in the two months. By the way, this was after he threw out the thesis he had been building on for two and a half years.
He also writes at his personal website and on X, in a register that is unusually willing to be wrong in public. Even at The Daily Brief , we used some of his commentary on a podcast with The Ken to help us base our understanding of what AI could be potentially doing to the IT services industry.
Sidu is perfectly placed to tell us how AI changes organizations. In manufacturing, for instance, you have the “ Toyota Way ”, which had certain key pillars that drove an efficient factory floor (just-in-time was among them). Japan’s management principles became so ubiquitously known that you were likely to find books on them in every other middle manager’s office 10 years ago. Similarly, you had the Ford assembly line before the Toyota Way.
What does AI do to such management principles? What are the key tenets that organizations across industries have to live by now, especially if they’re tech or software-adjacent?
The conversation starts with a question he likes to put to VCs: what is an agent? His answer turns out to be the spine of everything else. An agent, he says, is not a junior colleague you delegate to. It is an extension of your own subconscious, and it magnifies whatever is already in there, including the parts you cannot see.
From that one claim he gets to why systems built with agents rot into slop after about two weeks, why a competent person armed with an agent often produces worse work than before, why the enterprise AI pilots everyone is quietly writing off failed for reasons that have nothing to do with the models, and why the only business he can see worth building is an unfashionable one made of people (yes, he means good old IT services, the one sector that’s been in a downfall if the NIFTY is concerned).
He is also, by his own admission somewhere 20 minutes into the episode, possibly wrong about all of it. And of course, that makes arguing with him all the more interesting.
“I could be horrendously wrong about the stuff that I’m saying, but I believe it”.
His ability to say this while making every other highly-logical claim rooted purely in rational economic incentives is what made this conversation so fun for me and my boss Bhuvan , who host him.
Every 2 mins in this episode, Sidu rapid-fires one bomb after another. I am sharing some of them below, but be assured that they’re not enough.
On what an agent actually is
The popular definition of an agent is something that iteratively pursues a goal using tools. Sidu accepts that one, then says it is the less interesting of the two available, and the one that gets people into trouble. The trouble starts with the word itself: agent implies agency, agency implies a person, and once you are picturing a person you start handing it work the way you would hand work to a person.
His alternative is stranger and more useful. This is also the belief he says he has most completely reversed in the past year.
“When a human uses an agent to solve this problem, the human doesn’t use the agent as an externally anthropomorphised entity that is running by itself. You actually use it as an extension of your own subconscious. You have magnified your system one. I want to build a sub-module here that achieves sub-objective X. System two, system one delegation works this way — that I’ve thought of an objective and system one executes it for me. This is the actual mode in which real agent usage operates today. Everything else now is trivial use cases.”
On learning to use AI
A large industry has grown up in India around teaching people AI: certifications, cohorts, weekend bootcamps, ads everywhere. Sidu is at pains to say this is not the old scam — nobody is promising crypto riches or a guaranteed job, and the people selling these courses are being entirely honest about what they are selling.
His objection is that the format is obsolete rather than dishonest. He makes it very clear to us that he does not refer to scammy courses. Rather, it would be completely normal to assume that taking a course to learn a subject is the correct instinct for every subject.
Except this one. The best way to learn about AI is, well, by asking AI.
“There is this idea of learning AI by taking an AI course. Which actually, if you stop and think about it, is the old motion. Perfectly sensible: I wanna learn something, I will take a course. Perfectly sensible, but absolutely illogical if you’re using it to learn about AI, because AI knows about AI. The AI course you want is to use an AI and ask it: “How do I use you? Help me learn. Construct a pedagogy for me. Construct a curriculum to my taste. What is the first stage? No, I find this boring. Can we start with the second one? Rework the thing. Okay, great. Second one. Now teach me, how do I do this better?” It is to use this thing to teach you, because that’s what it is if you want it to be a teacher. And it’ll be better than any course anyone’s constructed, because you would use it completely personalised. But the challenge is that cognitive jump. It seems so simple, but it’s so hard. Yet most people will still go out there and pay lakhs of rupees for an AI course.”
On pivoting as the sane thing to do
Startup orthodoxy treats the pivot as a thing to be forgiven. Sidu, who’s lived most of his life as an entrepreneur, points out that we only had to normalise it because it was understood as a failure, and that the shame attached to it is now actively dangerous: it makes founders absorb a step change in the models six months late, reactively, after the evidence has piled up high enough to overcome their commitment to a thesis.
He takes a page from the early days of realfast itself. They had closed a hundred thousand dollars of revenue across an entire year. Then a model release turned a set of deals they had been refusing as off-thesis into exactly the deals they should have been taking.
“There were deals in the pipeline that we had been ignoring and saying no to because they were off thesis. We made the change, revisited the thesis, validated that these deals are no longer off thesis — in fact, arguably are now on thesis. And by January 20th, we had seven-figure revenue. We 10x’d in two months because we pivoted. And I think this is something that businesses, especially startups that don’t have debt, that don’t have a history they have to support, but are starting clean — it is so crucial now to ask, is this a step change that is relevant to my business? And if it is a step change and it is relevant — some of them are directly relevant — I need to pivot. I have to throw away everything that I was building towards and just pivot. And this is the sane thing to do. It is not the insane thing to do anymore.”
On building a business that gets better when the models do
One of Sidu’s essays argues that when the models improve, your addressable market should go up — that a well-built AI business should treat every frontier release as free expansion rather than a threat to be absorbed. We put it to him that this seems far easier to write than to build, given that releases now land every few weeks.
He agreed it was hard, and then reframed what kind of hard it is. The useful distinction, he says, is between a problem that is merely difficult to operate and one that is difficult economically — and he thinks the second kind is now the only sort worth picking.
“Which is why, at the end of the day, every time you build a startup, the startup exists to solve a hard problem. People usually make the mistake of thinking the hard problem is something which is difficult to solve for operational reasons. What you wanna pick is the hard problem that is operationally challenging, yes, but is foundationally an economically hard problem to solve. And this is that. Look, we have to accept that now, moving forward, your alpha as a business comes from your ability to extract alpha from the improvements in the underlying. It’s always been true. New regulations come in, figure out how to extract alpha. Political situation changes, extract new alpha. New special economic zone.
Businesses naturally do this. It’s just that they’ve never done it on a three-month horizon.”
On product firms and services firms
Indian IT has spent two decades being told, and half-believing, that services work is the lesser thing — that the real prize is owning a product. We asked whether AI has blurred that line. He said it hasn’t, and then went after the premise from the other direction. The claim is that the distinction was always partly a story companies tell about themselves, and that it dissolves the moment you look at how the operations are actually staffed.
“People don’t like to admit this, but all product companies are a business team and a services backend. You don’t like to think about it that way. But unless, bro, you are going out and closing that deal yourself, there’s somebody between you and the customer. That person understands the business better than you, because they’re the ones moving the things that matter in the business. So now look, all product companies are a business team with a services company bolted on. No one likes to admit this. It’s cooler to think of yourself the other way, but structurally, if you break down the operations over time, you will start to see that segregation form. And then you will start asking like, “Where do I staff my people? Which parts of the product are important?” And so very clearly, the only thing left is to do hourly billing. That last logical step, no one will take.”
On why enterprise AI has terrible UX
Most explanations for the failure of enterprise AI pilots blame procurement, or data, or the models. Sidu’s explanation is older and duller than any of those, and borrowed from consumer product: every additional decision you ask a user to make costs you conversion. An agent is a machine for generating decisions.
He distinguishes between the small minority who find that energising — the people who will not open Codex at 11pm because they know they will still be there at 3 — and everyone else, for whom the experience is simply dread.
This, he points out, is a very big reason as to why the average user hasn’t moved away from chatbots to more complex platforms like Claude Code.
“You introduce AI into a workflow, you’re increasing the rate of decisions that the human makes, which means that by definition, most kinds of AI being deployed have terrible UX. If I deploy a high-end agent for a normal user, the cognitive load imposed on them is tantamount to making them use a really shitty app. In fact, it’s probably 100x worse. You give a powerful agent or an AI system to a user, you have given them horrendous UX. The vast majority of people in the workforce, across industries, if given the same experience, are not energised. They have anxiety. It is the same anxiety that a user has when they log into a horrendous enterprise app. “Dude, I don’t wanna do this.” That’s the reaction.”
On acceleration as an organising principle
Underneath the AI question, Sidu says, is a much older split that has nothing to do with models. Some companies decided a long time ago that moving faster than everyone else was the whole point, accepted that this would cost them enormously in org structure and talent costs, and built around it anyway. Everyone else treats speed as a thing you apply where it helps.
That split, not technical sophistication, is what he thinks determines who can absorb AI now. The examples he reaches for are not AI companies at all.
One strategy is to become a tech company. You build the whole company around acceleration as a core value proposition. Always has been, pre-AI also. It’s what you call a tech company. Like, what is the difference between your regular large scaled-up taxi company and Uber? Or your brick-and-mortar large scaled-up retailer and Amazon? One has said that acceleration is core. It is part of our strategy forever. It is going to have an enormous cost in terms of managerial structure, org structure, talent, talent cost — but the alpha is worth it, because we will drive the business through this.
And there are companies that say, “No. Acceleration is not the key value proposition. We have other key strategies that we deploy. Acceleration is situational, it’s not universal, and we will not rebuild the business around this.”
”Now, you’re an oil and gas company. Is acceleration a core alpha? That has always been questionable. But the moment the acceleration stems from turning individual humans into super intelligences — forget about your physical operations being gated. You’re an oil and gas company, you are gating on physical operations first. So now, how much software can you build? It’s irrelevant. Maybe not irrelevant, there are operational accelerations. But at the end of the day, the drill bit will drill at — no software is going to speed up the drill bit. You have a fundamental physics. Fundamentally, you’re on atoms.”
On the middle disappearing
This is the part of the conversation that should worry anyone who runs, staffs or trains an Indian services business. The economy of good-enough work rests on a quiet agreement: for most problems, average talent producing average results is acceptable, and the education system is tuned to supply exactly that in volume.
Agents, he argues, break the agreement — not by replacing the average worker, but by making their output bimodal. The thirty-dollar hour was the price of predictable adequacy. Predictable adequacy is what has gone.
“You had a certain expectation when you go and hire a median developer out of India, outsourced at the median price point, which is roughly $30 an hour. $30 an hour will require a certain amount of management and will produce an adequate outcome. What has happened now because of agents is that the $30-an-hour good-enough band has suddenly dropped down here. There is no $30-an-hour band anymore. There is no middle. There are only people who perform exceptionally well and people who perform exceptionally badly with an agent. There are no people who produce okay, okay results with an agent. Think about it. Have you seen anyone produce adequate results with an agent? Either they’re producing slop or they’re producing bangers.”
On what Indian IT has to do
If the good-enough middle has gone, the question that follows is what happens to the companies built on selling it. Sidu is careful not to treat this as a story about incompetence — he has said repeatedly through the conversation that the Indian IT majors made perfectly rational choices, and that Infosys’s Mysore campus represents an enormous amount of serious thought about how to manufacture talent at scale.
The problem is that none of that can be retuned at the edges. He walks through what an actual retooling would require, and the list is a description of breaking the company on purpose.
“And now all of that is gonna get disrupted, and you cannot really deliver value to the customer until you disrupt it. It’s not like you can say, “Hey, in this management hierarchy, on these comp bands, with this performance review, I will make this team AI-native.” You have to 4x comp bands. You have to drop review cycles to one quarter. You have to move this out into a new management structure. That new management structure has to directly report to the board, not even the CEO necessarily — or if it’s a certain type of CEO, yes, maybe. Then you have to now figure out how to scale this out while cannibalising this in a way that doesn’t spook investors. And Indian investors are easily spooked.”
On what India should be competing for
Sidu lies on the pessimistic side of things when it comes to India’s sovereign AI ambitions. He wanted to sharpen that: he is not pessimistic about the ambition, he is pessimistic about the target. The US and China are not peers to be caught; at fifteen, twenty, thirty trillion dollars of GDP they are a category with two members, and their advantages are as much political and cultural as economic.
Which leaves, in his reading, a position that is both available and worth having — and that nobody in India is explicitly playing for.
“What is meaningful for us is to build a strategy to crush France, Germany and Japan, to make sure that we are number three. Clean. No one else can come and touch us on number three. We are not doing that, no? We are either coming up with these weird, infeasible plans to mimic China or the US, or just giving up, like “oh, there’s no point”. I mean, what is number three? Why does France have Mistral? If France has Mistral, we should be able to do something. Why are we not financing Sarvam properly here? Why aren’t there more Sarvams? The gaps are obvious, because what we are trying to do is either compete with the US or China, or give up. That’s not the game. The game is we have to be number three.”
