Sidu Ponnappa: True, true, true. The reason I love it so much is there’s so many parts of it which are so conveniently referenceable for so many real-life things, right?
Bhuvan: It’s a movie that spawned many memes.
Pranav Manie: He’s seated right now like he’s Morpheus in that chair.
Sidu Ponnappa: No, my wife is also amused because I actually find it comfortable to walk with my hands behind like this, and sometimes I’m reminded it’ll actually go up into that pose and my wife will be like, “Hey.”
Pranav Manie: So, first things first. I wanna start out with — and obviously we’ll make a lot of reference to your tweets — one tweet of yours that I saw was really funny, where you said something on the lines of, you know, so many VC dollars get exchanged in the name of vague AI terms, like agent, harness, XYZ. Which is where I also asked a bunch of my teammates, and we all like to think we use AI, but we asked ourselves the question that you had also posed in the tweet: what’s an AI agent? How do you define an agent? How is an agent different from a workflow? When do you decide an AI agent is something that you can sell to anybody?
Sidu Ponnappa: I think there are two modes in which this actually exists, and the answer is different depending on which. I think the more traditional, popular one is an agent that has agency, hence agent. I think the crude definition is very simple: it can iteratively pursue a goal using tools. This is very straightforward.
I think the more interesting one is the other definition. Everyone looks only at the first because agents are anthropomorphised. You wanna reason about this, so you think of it as another person. And I think that is dangerously flawed for the current crop of models, because what I have realised with each step forward — from 3 to 3.5 to 4.0 to, you know, Sonnet, Opus, now to Astra — there is agency, but that agency seems to have serious limitations. And those serious limitations operate in very subtle ways.
For example, I was just talking to a friend this morning, and I was pointing out that if you remember when 4.0 dropped, making your own website became hot —
Pranav Manie: Yeah.
Sidu Ponnappa: — because it was so easy. And it’s great. You can hammer out a website in no time. But the moment you say that I now want to build a website with a very clear intent, I have these three core brand pillars, this is my design language, this is my communication strategy, these are my key talking points — suddenly, you can no longer build that website with AI. Now you will find yourself constantly in the loop fixing drift from the anchors you have set.
There’s a senior of mine from ThoughtWorks who moved to Google. When I was talking to him, he once told me this. He said, “When you’re designing any system, as the architect, you can hammer down three pegs, no more.”
Pranav Manie: You pick pillars.
Sidu Ponnappa: Yeah. These are largely invariant, or the barrier to changing them is very high, and then you rotate the architecture around them. The subtle distinction I’m making today is that with agents, you can’t hammer down those three pillars and expect the agent to adhere to them.
Which means that non-trivial systems — whether it is a communication system or a software system or a sales system or a recruitment system, whatever, because we now run everything on top of this — you cannot hammer down architectural pillars and have an agent follow them unguided. There is a human in the loop always, and that human in the loop is the one who’s protecting the architectural pillars, the integrity of the system.
And this leads to an interesting question. Ultimately, we still do not have an agent with agency. At the end of the day today, practically, inductively, without that human in the loop, the system turns to slop.
Again, this is one of those reductionist terms where people think of slop as bad copy, but bad copy is just the most trivial example. The more insidious, important example is: you’re designing and building a system. You’ve nailed down your architectural pillars. You’re working with an agent, so you’re making dozens, hundreds of decisions a day revolving around those pillars. You miss one. Something slips in that breaks the integrity of the system. You don’t notice. And this is gonna happen at a certain error rate even if you’re incredibly disciplined, highly attentive — some of those decisions will slip through. This compounds the next day and it compounds the day after.
And unfortunately, the best term for this that I’ve seen comes from engineering, though now it is a universal problem. We call it technical debt. But it is not technical anymore, it is just debt. It is the compounding violation of the integrity of the system in a way that undermines the ability of that system to achieve its objectives.
And what I realised is, if you really look at how humans use agents now to mitigate this — because this is where the game is now — the game is not, can I one-shot something? The game is not even now, can I sustainably build a system for two weeks? The threshold has reached two weeks. Beyond that, it turns to slop, and it turns to slop at an architectural level.
When a human uses an agent to solve this problem, the human doesn’t use the agent as an externally anthropomorphised entity that is running by itself. You actually use it as an extension of your own subconscious. You have magnified your system one. I want to build a sub-module here that achieves sub-objective X. System two, system one delegation works this way — that I’ve thought of an objective and system one executes it for me. This is the actual mode in which real agent usage operates today. Everything else now is trivial use cases.
Bhuvan: A lot of people make this argument saying that, one, of course, you need to have a human in the loop, but with each model upgrade, there seems to be a point in the distance where the human in the loop will become a liability. How do you reason around that? Because right now, the image I had in my mind when you were talking about this variation in models is trying to put a leash around a wild beast, and the human in the loop is trying to hold down the beast today. Is there a flip side to that, where that becomes counterproductive considering how fast these things are?
Sidu Ponnappa: I think with the current — I don’t know if it is an architectural aspect of today’s generation of models —
Bhuvan: Right.
Sidu Ponnappa: — and the way the agents are built, but I don’t see that going away for the current crop. Hypothetically, in the near future, do we see it going away? Yes. And when that happens, the economic basis of everything changes. Arguably one of the inflection points of the singularity. There’s no point looking beyond that, because what will happen beyond that is by definition unpredictable.
But before that, I think the more useful way to approach the problem is to ask: what are the invariants? If you say that at some point humans will no longer be required in the loop, and we put that as the boundary, because beyond that there’s no point looking at it unless you’re a frontier lab — the question to ask is what are the invariants before it? Because we know everything will change.
The one invariant is a human will be required. It’s what we’ve built realfast around. And we are always searching for invariants. Obviously, I think the longest invariant is a human will be required until they are not, and then everything changes. But within that you find situational invariants. They’re always moving, but they are not going to evaporate in two weeks or in three months. Right now, the operating horizon for these strategies, I believe, is around three months, give or take. So you want invariants that allow you to build a strategy that is longer than three months, otherwise you have a problem.
And the second invariant is what I was just talking about, which is that when you want to build any non-trivial system, there are architectural pegs you nail down. Today, the models do not respect those. And if you look at how we operate, you will see that we have those two invariants at the core of our business. But any business that is sitting on top of using AI has to operate on identifying invariants that they are playing into, not asking the question what will change, because the answer is most of it.
Bhuvan: Just to set the baseline, so that it becomes a starting point for us to take the discussion further — where do you lie on the spectrum of “I have full-on AI psychosis, I am AI-pilled”, to “I think this is a tool, I am the God-level programmer and this is still beneath me, so it’s a junior intern that I am corralling”? On the spectrum of different types of feelings about AI, where do you lie?
Sidu Ponnappa: I think that entire scale that is so popular is wrong. Connecting it back to my previous argument — if it is an extension of your subconscious, then that entire maturity model, that scale, it doesn’t work that way. The question is: how deluded are you by your own subconscious? The more deluded you are by your own subconscious, the more you are going to be bamboozled by your agent, because the agent is an extension of your subconscious.
Bhuvan: You versus you.
Sidu Ponnappa: It’s you versus you, fundamentally. It is reflecting back to you. Your obvious biases, at least you can see. But what is reflecting back to you is your subconscious biases, that it magnifies through the interaction as it tries to please you.
And if you are not constantly, aggressively accepting that you have AI psychosis because of this, and you’re not constantly running defence against it, the quality of your output will be bad. But more fundamentally, especially if you are in a fragile mental state, you are prone to full-blown psychological breakdown.
So you have this spectrum driven by self-awareness and mental integrity, starting from “my work degrades” to “I will internally implode”. And I do not even say this lightly. I’m talking about full-blown schizophrenic breakdown, hallucinations. It does happen. So I don’t think it’s a question of like, this is an intern I’m corralling. This is a question of: how self-aware am I, and how aggressively am I chasing down the artifacts of my lack of self-awareness as it surfaces through this interaction, and corralling that to ensure that, A, I’m not losing my mental integrity. You are extremely vulnerable when you use an agent. This is not a joke. You have to treat it as an info hazard of the highest order.
Bhuvan: It’s a weird kind of high.
Sidu Ponnappa: Yeah, absolutely. And take that all the way out to saying: now that this is so, what is it then when we all try to do good work, we all pursue our craft? This is how I think of it, and I think it’s widely framed. It doesn’t matter what it is we pursue — doing something like this is a craft. And you folks are improving at your craft. It is apparent, and therefore the output of it becomes better.
The ability to pursue the improvement of your craft while you are now not using an agent as an externality — but you’re accepting that what you are is a superhuman cyborg. You have already started crossing the threshold into transhumanism. You are more than human when you use an agent.
I used to joke about this before AI also. People just dismiss these things, but six million intraocular lenses have been implanted every year for decades now. That is —
Bhuvan: That is —
Sidu Ponnappa: Cyborgs have been around for decades. It is superhuman for someone at that age with that medical condition to have those physical capabilities. It has happened already, decades ago.
What is happening now with agents is super intelligence. And what matters over here is that super intelligence is two-sided, just like our own subconscious is two-sided. What is your ability to navigate this in pursuit of your craft when you yourself now are super intelligent? It’s not that that is super intelligent and you are something separate. When you work with it, you are super intelligent. How do you use that super intelligence in pursuit of your craft is now the whole game.
Bhuvan: So one question I try to ask people who are really close to this is — we started at, let’s say, GPT, November ‘22, if I remember correctly. “Oh, this is a dumb thing. It can’t do one plus one.” Then we went through the whole process of, it can’t count the number of R’s in strawberry.
Sidu Ponnappa: Yes.
Bhuvan: Then as soon as Claude Code came, suddenly you could see the shift in vibes. Then it just took off after Opus 4.5, or whenever you wanna mark that point. In all of these things, a lot of people went through a typical template of, let’s say, hope: “Oh, this is dumb. Eh, not so dumb, not so dumb, not so dumb. Dude, this is good. I’m toast.” How did your own journey — rather, how did you go about making sense of navigating this technological shift? Because it’s that Stalin quote, like, “Weeks happen in” —
Sidu Ponnappa: Lenin.
Bhuvan: But yes. Sorry. Did you find it hard to build a mental model where you said the last thing which you said — which is, having a craft as a North Star probably will help you anchor your tendencies towards psychosis, or basically just sycophancy, or whatever, outright break? How did that process happen?
Sidu Ponnappa: I think a lot of that discussion assumes the “I am toast” at the end as the problem you’re solving. So, yeah. I have been pursuing transhumanism since I was in ninth standard. I read — there is this famous Asimov, I think they made a movie out of it, which is not that great — The Bicentennial Man.
Bhuvan: Certainly, yeah.
Sidu Ponnappa: It’s a very famous Asimov short story, and it is the story of a robot bound by the three laws of robotics seeking to be human and looking for the most fundamental invariant of humanism, which is dying. And I read that story and I’m like, “Well, obviously, all of us are on the opposite trajectory.”
I obviously, deep down, instinctively crave immortality. It’s a different thing that you should have the wisdom to let that craving go, and I think we have one of the most ancient traditions in the understanding of the flaw in that desire — but the desire is there. And ever since then, I’m like, “Well, I’m walking the other road.”
And then as I got older, I realised that it’s not just me. The entire human race is walking that road — through better hygiene, better medication, intraocular lenses, computers. We are all in pursuit of godhood. We are hardwired to play God. To seek that. It’s not just to play it, but to seek that state. Whether we can play it or not, I think is an open question, but the craving is there. For me, it has just been an amazing ride.
Pranav Manie: I think Westworld, the TV show, had the tagline for every season: “Play God, pay the price.” And you clearly see a lot of that in what you speak.
Sidu Ponnappa: I don’t take that perspective very seriously, and I know it’s odd for me to say it. You know, the uncles say that is a Western concept, and they mean something without understanding what it means. And what they’re saying is a Western concept is usually a British one — it’s a contradiction to a Western concept they believe. They’re like, “That’s a Western concept. My Western concept has been here for 100 years, therefore so.”
But I think the core premise holds. Play God, pay the price is a Western concept. You pay the price of being alive. We understand this at a deep cultural level, that you are paying the price the moment you’re born. None of this changes that for us.
In some ways, I like to joke that the deep multivariate Indian cultural history is actually the best suited to navigate the singularity. They will break because they don’t know how to bend. They’re not water. They’re the rock. We are water. The singularity will shatter all rocks.
And so even that framing of Westworld is rock thinking. Play God, pay the price is rock thinking. Water thinking is: you were born paying the price. You’re just riding on the balance. Existence has a price, and it is baked deep into everything. We understand this even though we have now 100, 200 years of uncle thinking borrowed from the West, masquerading as Indian thinking. The reality is, in our bones, we understand this. We understand the Tandava.
Pranav Manie: I wanna circle back to you talking about the architecture. You have a very solid essay called When The Models Improve, Your TAM Should Go Up — your addressable market should go up. But again, we look at model developments that happen at this point, I don’t know, every three weeks, every month —
Sidu Ponnappa: Overnight.
Pranav Manie: Overnight, sometimes. How hard is it to build an architecture and an operating system that sustains the principle behind that essay — that with every model improvement, you should only see your potential business increase? Because from where we sit, it seems like it’s much harder. Easier said than done.
Sidu Ponnappa: It is. It is. Which is why, at the end of the day, every time you build a startup, the startup exists to solve a hard problem. People usually make the mistake of thinking the hard problem is something which is difficult to solve for operational reasons. What you wanna pick is the hard problem that is operationally challenging, yes, but is foundationally an economically hard problem to solve. And this is that.
Look, we have to accept that now, moving forward, your alpha as a business comes from your ability to extract alpha from the improvements in the underlying. It’s always been true. New regulations come in, figure out how to extract alpha. Political situation changes, extract new alpha. New special economic zone.
Bhuvan: But these things operated on a much slower timeframe. They’re fleeting also.
Sidu Ponnappa: Yeah, they’re fleeting. I mean, these are fleeting too, to be fair. But my point is the dynamic has always existed. Businesses naturally do this. It’s just that they’ve never done it on a three-month horizon.
Now, if you wanna build a business in the foothills of the singularity, one of the core premises of any business started in this era is that we are now capturing the alpha that grows every three months.
For example, for a startup to pivot — we’ve tried to normalise it in the startup ecosystem for well over a decade now that it’s okay to pivot. But we don’t look to the question of why did we have to normalise it? We had to normalise it because it is a bad thing.
Bhuvan: It’s still very dirty, yeah. It is perceived as a failure.
Sidu Ponnappa: Hence, we have to normalise it. And there is a normalisation up to a degree. Even until 2022, a startup that pivoted every quarter was sketch.
What we realised through the first two years of our journey — that was there subconsciously — we were also inheriting dangerously obsolete premises from the previous cycle of startups, like build to a thesis. You try to identify a thesis and you build into it, and you don’t think about that thesis too much in terms of invariants. Remember what I mentioned earlier. Now, given the circumstances, you focus on invariants.

Hello there, hope you’ve had a great couple of weeks!
We at Markets like to read widely, and weirdly, and then eat people’s heads about our newest preoccupations. Some people seem to like the links we send them (even though more people let our recommendations sit, unread, in their Whatsapp chats). And so, we thought we’d start sharing them with the wider world.
If this is the sort of stuff you like chatting about, come catch us at our weekly book club. More on that at the end!
We’re always hungry for more links by the way. If there’s anything that you want the world to read, drop a link in the comments.
Max Read, How Everything Became Gambling ( link 🔒): Consider the sheer number of things the world gambles on today, through easily accessible apps. Sports. Elections. What the Fed might do. Whether a celebrity couple will break up. Whether Donald Trump will threaten to nuke Iran in his next speech. What does this say about the world? Has Silicon Valley’s penchant for probabilistic thinking infected our culture to a point where everything has become the butt of a bet? Max Read is one of the best writers I’ve come across on the internet, and this piece is as good as any he’s written.
Leila Aboud and others, France: between the bond market and the barricades ( link 🔒): France is stuck in its difficult place. Its youth think its government is miserly. The bond markets think it spends way beyond its means. Between these diametrically opposed groups, the country has no room to maneuver. The country runs a generous welfare state. It can’t pull back from it without the ire of its public. It can’t fund it either, because it has a debt burden of over €3.5 trillion, all vulnerable to bearish bets. How does it dig itself out of this hole?
John Harriss, Peasants to Programmers: Continuity and Change in a Tamil Village Over 50 Years ( link ): In April 1973, a young English researcher, while trying to understand the green revolution, found himself in the Tamil village of Nesal. It was a little settlement, with roughly 1,500 people, delighted to find a foreigner from across the world enmeshing himself in their social world. Then, a small lifetime came and went by, before the researcher returned in 2025. It was a very different place now. Its mud huts had been replaced by pucca buildings. Young men from the village worked as software engineers in nearby cities. How did those years change the village? What happened to its old hierarchies? How did its ways of being transform? A poignant little history.
Lars Doucet, Does Georgism Work? Five Years Later ( link ): Progress, the economist Henry George once argued, creates poverty. The more an economy grows, the more valuable it turns certain locations — certain parcels of land — giving its owners inordinate and perhaps undeserved power. George had an elegant solution: tax land, by its value, instead of what people build on it, capturing some of that wealth, while pushing people to use that prized land as efficiently as they could. Only, the idea has almost never seen traction in the real world. Doucet has spent the last five years trying to bring the idea to life. This is the story of the odd journey an academic idea takes into practice.
Josh Hendrickson, Price is Opportunity Cost ( link ): Even if you’re an econ nerd, you’ve probably only encountered prices in the tame, domesticated realm of markets . The idea, though, is broader than that. It explains, for instance, why bombing an enemy into smithereens makes it harder to end a war. Or why parents that get a baby-sitter might go to a more expensive restaurant. Every choice is a price, whether or not there’s any money involved. Price, in this telling, is opportunity cost — what you must forgo when you decide to do something. Once you see that, so much of the world suddenly falls in place.
Ben Thompson, Nvidia’s Risky Business ( link ): Nvidia built its empire, as the adage goes, selling shovels during the AI gold rush. Its customers, happily, were at the heart of the highest concentration of wealth in history, and could afford to pay obscene amounts of money for its innovation-on-steroids. But hockey stick graphs tend to infinity, and soon, these behemoths too had little cash to finance their ambitions. So, Nvidia got into a new business — of arranging capital for its customers. Instead of selling shovels, it seems to be taking a bet on the gold trade itself. Will it survive the risk?
Damien Ma and Binyi Yang, Who’s Ahead in the Global AI Talent Race? ( link ): Something unusual is happening. The United States, for so long at the heart of all modern technology, is having to share its pedestal. China now employs two-fifths of the world’s AI talent — above the one-third the United States can draw. Somewhat uncomfortably, India seems to have bowed out of yet another technological race, contributing a negligible portion of the world’s AI talent, and none of its world-class institutions. Check out this fascinating, somewhat sobering Carnegie piece for more.
Marcus Olang, I’m Kenyan. I Don’t Write Like ChatGPT. ChatGPT Writes Like Me. ( link ): Why does AI write in that specific, slightly over-considered manner? It’s trying to imitate human writing, of course, but who does it imitate the most closely? Writer Marcus Olang thinks the answer is Kenyans . The English taught to Kenyan school-children has that peculiar lilt of someone extremely proficient in a second language: an elaborate vocabulary, a slight penchant for grandeur, paragraphs structured almost mathematically, and littered with odd turns of phrase. That is, now, how AI writes. To want to write in our era is a tragedy in itself; to be a Kenyan writer, it seems, is worse still.
Rahul Sanghi, Scimplify: Material Ambitions ( link ): India has factories that manufacture chemicals. India has scientists that can make specialty chemicals. But somehow, India can’t seem to put the two together into a globally relevant specialty chemicals industry. The world, despite much chatter about de-coupling, still relies on China. Can one company change that? That’s the story Rahul Sanghi explores with his wide-ranging heavily-annotated interview of Sachin Santhosh, the founder of the Bengaluru based chemicals start-up, Scimplify.
Samuel Hughes, Why were Victorian elites so effective? ( link ): Victorian Britain, if you don’t know better, sounds aggressively colourless: a world made of the prissy, the austere and the prudish, with wrinkled noses turned up at the world. Hughes, however, shows you a different side. His Victorians ran an empire while staying up late, drinking copiously, and attending an endless succession of parties. In fact, this may have given the empire its lifeblood, stitching its elite together with strong bonds, and building habits that forged future leaders.

HCL Technologies Limited | Large Cap | Software Services
HCL Technologies is one of India’s largest IT services companies and the third-largest India-headquartered listed IT-services company by FY26 consolidated revenue, offering software services, infrastructure management, and engineering and R&D services to global enterprises. It also develops and sells enterprise software through HCLSoftware.
[ Concall ]
HCLTech’s advanced AI business is now large enough to show up in the overall numbers, with an annualised run rate of $876 million, closing in on $900 million. Management says this is how the company plans to grow despite AI shrinking the value of traditional IT contracts.
“Advanced AI revenue reached $219 million this quarter, up 28.4% sequentially and 78% year-on-year, and annualised advanced AI revenue is now $876 million. This quarter’s performance validates our strategy and advances our ambition to become the leading AI solutions company for global enterprises. You can also see that we are able to offset AI-driven deflation by gaining market share in our core services and through our advanced AI offerings, which is helping us capture a share of the rapidly expanding AI spend across the technology ecosystem. This is the growth template we aim to consistently replicate going forward.”
— C Vijayakumar, CEO & Managing Director
New deal wins were the second-highest in the company’s history, and management said AI was central to every large deal it won. Management also reiterated that the previously announced mega deal will start contributing only from Q1 FY28, not in the second half of FY27.
“New deal bookings reached $3.3 billion, up 27% year-on-year and 35% sequentially. This is the second-highest bookings quarter we have ever recorded and gives us our strongest first-half booking performance. Clients are working with us on more strategic programs and are choosing us to shape their technology agenda. AI was a central theme in every large deal we won.”
— C Vijayakumar, CEO & Managing Director
Operating margin rose to 19% once one-time restructuring costs were excluded, up from 17.5% in the previous quarter. Most of the gain came from internal cost programmes (Project Ascent), operating leverage from faster growth and higher-margin AI work; foreign exchange contributed a smaller 23 basis points.
“Our EBIT was $377 million, representing 18.2% of revenue. Adjusting for restructuring expenses of 84 basis points during the quarter, our Q2 EBIT margin was 19%, compared with 17.5% in the previous quarter. The margin bridge is as follows: Project Ascent, including AI-driven efficiencies, gave us 73 basis points; superior margin of services offerings under our advanced AI revenue gave us 32 basis points; operating leverage at the SG&A level due to growth acceleration gave us 50 basis points; and foreign exchange gave us 23 basis points. On the headwinds, there was a 22-basis-point impact on account of higher restructuring costs in this quarter compared to the previous quarter, and a 25-basis-point impact due to the HPE Telco Solutions acquisition.”
— Shiv Walia, Chief Financial Officer
Management says advanced AI offerings currently achieve better margins than traditional services, with particularly high gross margins in IP and platforms. A growing contribution from these offerings could support overall margins, although HCLTech intends to reinvest operational gains in capabilities, IP and talent.
“There are two components to this. One is the services component, and the second is the IP and platform component. For the IP and platform component, the margins will be very high, very similar to a software business. The gross margins will be upwards of 70%. For the services component, I think the margins will be at least 7% to 10% higher than traditional services. At least so far, in all the deals we have been able to secure, we have generally achieved better realisation and margins.”
— C Vijayakumar, CEO & Managing Director
HCLTech announced a global premier partnership with Anthropic on the day of the call, adding to its existing tie-up with OpenAI. Management said some of its products, such as AI Force, already have native integrations with OpenAI, and it now plans to build similar integrations with Anthropic, with pricing that includes token costs.
“Today, we announced a global premier partnership with Anthropic to accelerate enterprise adoption of agentic AI, with a focus on safety, cybersecurity, and governance. We will establish a dedicated Anthropic business unit and a centre of excellence to accelerate deployments of Claude in enterprise environments. HCLSoftware will become an Anthropic ISV partner, embedding Claude and Claude Code into select enterprise products with frontier safety guardrails. … With Anthropic … it is largely a services model. But I think the biggest non-linearity is coming from the fact that some of our products, such as AI Force, are being integrated, and a number of software products are having native integrations into OpenAI. We now propose to build them with Anthropic as well. There, I think, we have pricing that includes the token costs as well. So, there, I think the equation will be a little less people-centric and will be non-linear.”
— C Vijayakumar, CEO & Managing Director
Software revenue fell 11.2% year-on-year. Management attributed the decline largely to fewer multi-year licence renewals falling due this year, since a large share of a multi-year licence’s revenue is recognised upfront. Annual recurring revenue (ARR) grew 7.6%, though excluding the JasperSoft acquisition it grew only 2.6%.
“This year, and particularly in Q2, we had fewer multi-year licenses that were due for renewal compared to last year. You would notice that the revenue recognised from multi-year subscription licenses has gone down from $81 million in Q2 FY26 to $39 million in Q2 FY27. Revenue recognition for an on-premises term license varies based on the term of the license. Typically, upfront revenue recognition is as much as 60% to 70% of the entire term for a two- to three-year license, with the balance recognised over the contract term. The reported revenue decline does not accurately reflect the underlying health of the software business. The same is evident in the healthy ARR growth that we have witnessed even in this quarter.”
— Shiv Walia, Chief Financial Officer
Despite a strong quarter, management trimmed the top end of its FY27 revenue growth guidance from 4.5% to 4%, setting the range at 2.5%–4%, and declined to raise it, citing geopolitical volatility. The guidance now also includes about 87 basis points of contribution from acquisitions.
“We had a strong quarter on multiple fronts, and obviously Q3 will be a strong quarter due to the software step-up. However, the environment remains fluid. — C Vijayakumar, CEO & Managing Director
Management retained FY27 EBIT margin guidance at 17.5%–18.5% and reiterated an 18%–19% desired band. The company’s priority remains investing in AI capabilities and differentiation rather than maximising margins during the transition.
“Our earlier aspiration was 18% to 19%. Last year, and specifically this year, we called out the restructuring charges, and then we reduced the guidance to 17.5% to 18.5%. However, 18% to 19% is our desired band. — C Vijayakumar, CEO & Managing Director
IBM India MD | $4.5 billion AI impact | Productivity gains | Next big shift
IBM India provides high-value IT services including AI-driven automation, hybrid cloud infrastructure, and enterprise consulting. The company is currently scaling its Sovereign AI initiatives in India to help regulated industries manage data security and operational control.
[ Interview ]
IBM exceeded its cost-saving targets by focusing on process redesign rather than just basic automation. This suggests that the company’s AI strategy is delivering much higher financial returns than initially projected.
“I do not think that is a valid argument; in fact, I do not think we can build fast enough. What matters is whether we are building the right capabilities around the right use cases, and doing so to genuinely move the needle on business outcomes. As with any technology throughout history, the critical question is how you put it to work and develop it to drive true business value. When adopting AI, enterprises must evaluate whether they are picking the right use cases, executing with sound economics, and fundamentally reimagining core business processes before automating or infusing AI into them. To illustrate this with real-world examples: IBM recently conducted a State of AI Adoption survey, which revealed that roughly 58% of surveyed companies are actively deploying AI solutions, while others are still testing the waters or evaluating adoption timelines. AI technology today is fully ready to scale, and organisations should be far more deliberate in building with it. Within IBM, we embarked on an internal transformation journey three years ago to apply AI to our own core operations. Our initial objective was to take $2 billion out of our bottom line over a three-year period through process automation and AI infusion. We exited that three-year cycle having delivered $4.5 billion in bottom-line value. Achieving that required redesigning core workflows, automating where appropriate, and embedding AI to drive higher productivity.”
— Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia
The company developed an internal AI tool that significantly improves the speed and efficiency of its software engineers. This tool is now being sold to external clients, creating a new potential revenue stream from internal innovations.
“Another internal initiative is an internal software engineering tool we developed called “IBM Bob”. Beyond basic code completion, we used AI to enable the entire software development lifecycle. Today, over 80,000 IBM engineers use IBM Bob, delivering productivity gains of up to 45% in development functions, allowing us to build better software faster. Furthermore, external clients like ISG (Inspirage Solutions Group) in India have implemented IBM Bob across their developer teams, achieving similar productivity gains and changing how they solve client problems. The core question is not whether the industry is building too fast, but whether we are building the right tools to drive tangible business value for enterprises.”
— Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia
Many businesses are finding that their AI projects fail because their internal data is messy and unorganised. Investors should realise that spending on data infrastructure must happen before AI can generate any real value.
“Our research indicates four primary reasons why organisations hesitate to move beyond pilot stages. First is information architecture and data readiness, as organisations have historically hoarded data in disconnected silos. Today, data types are shifting—such as sensor data or real-time data in motion—which requires immediate availability at the point of decision-making. We often say there is no AI without Information Architecture, because if an enterprise has not invested in structuring its data for readability and usability, AI initiatives stall.”
— Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia
The industry is moving away from massive, expensive AI models toward smaller, specialised models that are cheaper to operate. This shift helps enterprises control costs while still getting high-quality results for specific business needs.
“Second is AI economics and ROI, where enterprises must architect solutions that deliver sustainable return on investment rather than spending immense capital running massive frontier language models. While large frontier models serve specific purposes, enterprise adoption favours targeted, domain-specific small language models that are agile, faster, use significantly less compute, and cost less to run. IBM actively open-sources small language models to foster developer innovation.”
— Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia
Successful AI adoption requires senior leaders to understand where the technology can actually help their specific business. A lack of executive training is currently a major bottleneck for scaling AI across large organisations.
“Third is executive and organisational skilling, where beyond developer capabilities, C-suite leaders require the education and domain context to identify high-value AI use cases across their business operations.”
— Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia
Concerns about AI mistakes and data privacy are preventing many companies from fully launching AI products. Establishing clear rules for how AI makes decisions is necessary to reduce legal risks and build user trust.
“Fourth is trust, governance, and risk, where concerns surrounding hallucinations, data privacy, and legal liabilities make executives cautious. Overcoming this requires robust governance frameworks built on four structural pillars: data provenance, explainability of AI outputs, operational transparency, and continuous model governance.”
— Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia
The software services business is changing as AI speeds up development and shifts how contracts are written. This evolution allows companies to deliver advanced solutions faster, potentially leading to more frequent, high-value projects.
“The software services industry operates in a hybrid environment across on-premises infrastructure, SaaS models, and cloud-delivered services. As AI-driven productivity tools expand across the software development lifecycle, software services will naturally evolve. While contract structures adapt to shorter integration projects alongside large transformational deals, AI enables faster development of new capabilities, providing enterprises with access to advanced software solutions.”
— Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia
Governments and highly regulated industries are demanding more control over where their data is stored and how it is managed. This trend toward technological sovereignty is creating a massive demand for localised and private AI infrastructure.
“Sovereignty has become a central conversation across global jurisdictions, driven by geopolitical shifts and a growing emphasis on technological independence—or what can be described as digital swaraj. Organisations are re-evaluating what infrastructure they control versus what they outsource. Sovereignty encompasses two primary dimensions: infrastructure data residency and technological operational control. Beyond basic data residency, regulated industries demand assurances that external parties cannot access sensitive data through foreign legislation or third-party platforms, while requiring direct operational control over their operating environments so they are not held hostage to external jurisdictions.”
— Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia
IBM is working with telecom providers like Airtel to build secure cloud environments specifically for Indian industries with strict data rules. This partnership expands IBM’s reach into sensitive sectors like banking and government services.
“To address these requirements in India, IBM partnered with Airtel to combine their data centres and network infrastructure with IBM’s software stack, delivering a secure, private cloud-like environment for regulated industries.”
— Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia
New software tools are being launched to allow Indian companies to manage their cloud operations entirely within their own borders. This helps clients meet local compliance laws while still using modern AI and automation features.
“We also introduced Sovereign Core, a software stack that enables client and partner data centre environments to run cloud capabilities—including FinOps, automated provisioning, continuous compliance, and an agentic control plane—entirely within their local jurisdiction, which we are deploying in India in partnership with Yotta and NextGen.”
— Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia
IBM has created a blueprint for government AI systems that can be reused across different states and countries. This standardised approach makes it easier and cheaper for public sector clients to adopt advanced technology securely.
“Furthermore, IBM collaborated with the Government of Andhra Pradesh, NextGen, and BharatGen to create SWAM, a reference architecture for a fully sovereign AI stack designed for government entities and scalable across global jurisdictions. Replicability and fungibility are essential so solutions can be built once and deployed securely across diverse regulatory environments.”
— Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia

RBL Bank Limited | Mid Cap | Financial Services
RBL Bank is a Mumbai-headquartered private sector bank offering corporate, commercial, retail and rural banking services. In June 2026, Emirates NBD completed a roughly $2.75 billion investment for a 60% stake, making the Dubai-based lender RBL’s majority owner.
[ Concall ]
The capital raise and the special foreign-currency (FCNR) deposit scheme together brought in funds equal to 35% of RBL’s balance sheet as of 31 May 2026. The bank is using the money first to repay costlier borrowings and bulk deposits, then to lend to highly rated corporates and in secured retail, with the rest parked in short-term investments and loans.
“We have generated a large amount of liquidity on our balance sheet between the capital raise and the deposits raised during the FCNR(B) scheme. For context, between the two, we have added 35% of our balance sheet as of 31 May 2026. This liquidity is deployed as follows. First, we prepaid or chose not to renew borrowings and bulk term deposits that were at a higher cost. Second, we are growing our business across both wholesale and secured retail, where we have seen demand and business conditions continue to remain fairly stable. Wholesale lending is to highly rated corporates where we want to start or deepen the relationship. The balance liquidity is tactically deployed in a combination of short-term investments and short-term loans given to our wholesale customers.”
— R. Subramaniakumar, MD & CEO
The bank crossed several size milestones this quarter, and its cost-to-income ratio fell sharply. A lower cost-to-income ratio means more of each rupee earned is left over as operating profit.
“The balance sheet crossed 2 lakh crore to end the quarter at 2,22,344 crore, more than doubling from financial year 2022. Term deposits crossed 1 lakh crore to reach 1,15,746 crore. Operating profit crossed the 1,000 crore mark to reach 1,396 crore for Q2 FY27. The cost-to-income ratio for the quarter was 56.5% versus 70.7% in Q2 FY26.”
— R. Subramaniakumar, MD & CEO
With better credit ratings and the Emirates NBD network behind it, RBL says it is going after large corporate relationships that were out of reach earlier, as well as trade flows in the corridors where Emirates NBD operates. It also says it will keep building granular, stable liabilities to narrow its cost-of-deposit gap with larger banks.
“We are working on putting together building blocks, which we will articulate in greater detail over the coming months. Briefly, these would focus on deepening and starting new relationships with large corporates that were not accessible earlier, either due to constraints related to credit rating, capital position, or our cost of funds. We are also working to target trade flows in the corridors where Emirates NBD is present, where we believe we have a competitive advantage because of the Emirates NBD network. We will continue to build granular and stable liabilities to progressively narrow the cost-of-deposit gap vis-à-vis the larger banks.”
— R. Subramaniakumar, MD & CEO
Credit card stress, one of RBL’s biggest pain points in recent years, appears to be easing. Card slippages for the quarter were still 600-plus, but September alone was 125–135, and management expects card credit costs to fall from the low double digits to about 6%.
“Card slippages are in line with expectations. While the quarter still had a 600-plus number, if I take the last month’s number of the quarter, we are already in the 125-135 zone. … We are quite happy to report that, while it took us a little more time to get this in order, we are now actually seeing it on the ground. Hopefully, we would expect card slippages to come down to a 400-plus-or-minus number for Q3 and Q4. Therefore, credit cost on cards should come down from the low double digits that we have seen to the 6% zone. The rest of the businesses will hold where they are, give or take, unless we see some very material deterioration in any of the rural businesses, which so far we have not seen at all.”
— Bhavin, Chief Financial Officer
Management expects margins to dip slightly next quarter. Much of the new money still sits in lower-yielding investments, and the full-quarter cost of the FCNR leverage will come through, partly offset by the repo rate hike. Margins should improve as the money moves into wholesale and then blended loans, but management says that will take more than a couple of quarters.
“The liquidity generated is currently sitting in investments, in non-SLR investments, which still yield less than the blended advances yield. Going forward, the first stage will be moving from the investment yield to the wholesale yield, and then from the wholesale yield to the blended advances yield. That is a journey, but it is not a one-quarter or two-quarter journey; it is going to take a little longer. The flip side is that you will see the full-quarter impact of the FCNR leverage given this year, because you see only a month and a half, or just a little more than a month, in this quarter. The insurance regulator’s (IRDAI) draft circular could cut deep into RBL’s bancassurance fees. The CFO put the business at about ₹300 crore of income a year and said a 50–60% hit is the minimum to pencil in if the draft is implemented as proposed.
“We have approximately 300 crores, plus or minus, of income per annum. Based on a plain reading of this, I would imagine that it will be substantially impacted. I would imagine that a 50-60% impact should be the minimum to pencil in. … However, you would expect a substantial drop in fee income if nothing changes and the draft circular is implemented in the manner proposed.”
— Bhavin, Chief Financial Officer
Management says the new money is effectively fixed-rate funding in a higher-rate environment, which it expects to support both margins and growth. It declined to give a specific return-on-assets (ROA) target for FY28, saying it would come back with fuller details over the coming months.
“It is very interesting to have a situation where there is a significant amount of liquidity between FCNR and equity that is effectively fixed-rate in a high-interest-rate environment. There will therefore be a tailwind to margins and a tailwind to growth. Clearly, I think there is going to be material improvement. Our BAU business, excluding all this noise, is obviously trending much better in terms of growth, with cards and MFIs pretty much normalised. I think margins should also see significant tailwinds, but I do not think we should comment on a specific point at this stage.”

RBL is keeping its unsecured lending on a tighter leash. Microfinance will grow only as much as needed to meet priority-sector lending (PSL) targets. Card balances are still shrinking, but management expects the decline to stop within a quarter and then sees high single-digit to low double-digit growth, with a shift toward better-quality customers.
“For cards, we expect to stop the decline within a quarter. Hopefully, the coming quarter is the festive season, so we will see some balance build-up there. Rising interest rates in the bond market have caused paper losses on the bank’s investment holdings, which weighed on operating profits this quarter. Every small move in market yields has a significant financial impact, though the bank is using specific trading strategies to reduce these losses.

New rules limiting the commissions banks can earn from selling insurance and mutual funds will reduce annual fee income by roughly 200 crore rupees. Additionally, stricter cash reserve requirements are creating a small but steady monthly drag on profit margins.

Strong growth in core lending profits has been enough to offset the financial pressure from lower fee income and treasury losses. This suggests the bank’s primary business model is resilient enough to handle external regulatory and market shocks.
“These fee and treasury impacts remain small relative to our core business earnings, where net interest income grew 20.39% year-on-year and 7.73% sequentially to reach record highs, easily absorbing non-interest income pressures.”

Management says it targets a pre-tax profit above 40% and a post-tax margin above 30%, and treats this as an unbreakable rule. If margins climb well above that, it would rather reinvest in the business than show higher efficiency to shareholders.

The firm has received approval to operate in GIFT City but will use it only to bring foreign money into India, not to invest Indian money abroad. Management describes this as choosing focus over new opportunities.
“In the short term and in the long term, our current thought process is to look only at inward flows. India itself currently requires a great deal of research. We were conducting a study on 213 derivative stocks, and there is still so much to understand. Without beating around the bush, it will be inward, and even in the long term it will be inward. We want to miss some opportunities in order to maintain focus. Focus is underrated, and opportunities are overrated—that is our belief. We want to master India as much as possible, and I think we have only scratched the surface.”
— Feroze Azeez, Joint CEO
The firm is about to apply for a mutual fund licence, which would let it make its own products instead of only distributing other fund houses’ schemes. Management says it will not launch plain long-only funds that copy what others already sell.
“We will submit the mutual fund license application by the end of this month. We are already prepared, or nearly prepared. We should be able to file it by around October 20.”

Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India | Insurance Decommissioned
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India is the statutory body tasked with regulating and licensing the insurance and reinsurance industries in India. It focuses on protecting policyholder rights and maintaining the financial stability of the insurance sector through comprehensive policy frameworks.
[ Interview ]
The regulator is framing new rules not just to cut costs, but to overhaul the entire efficiency of the Indian insurance ecosystem. Investors should view this as a structural shift that will force all industry participants to justify their cost structures.
“To clarify a key point: this consultation paper is not merely about distribution costs. It lays the foundation for a far more efficient insurance sector positioned to support India’s Viksit Bharat journey. Every stakeholder across the value chain—insurers, distributors, and the regulator—must become more productive and cost-efficient.”
— Ajay Seth, Chairman, IRDAI
Management is highlighting a significant spike in operating costs across both life and general insurance sectors over the last few years. The regulator expects companies to slash these expenses back to historical norms, which could pressure short-term earnings for high-cost insurers.
“To look at the numbers: Life Insurance: In FY21, the industry’s cost of doing business was around 16.5%. Today, it has escalated to 22%. We are asking the industry to return to the 15% efficiency levels achieved five to six years ago. General Insurance: Operating costs were historically 30% plus, declined to around 26% between FY17 and FY19, but have now spiked back to 32%. Our expectation is simple: regain the efficiency levels achieved seven to eight years ago, and then build further productivity milestones from there.”
— Ajay Seth, Chairman, IRDAI
The Chairman expressed concern that mature insurance companies have allowed their expense ratios to balloon rather than achieving scale benefits. This indicates that established players will no longer be given leeway for high costs and must transition to leaner, tech-driven operations.
“However, we observe companies that have been operating for 15 to 25 years with cost-of-doing-business metrics as high as 25% to 30% or more. They are no longer startups; they have relied on market information asymmetry to sustain high-cost operating models. For example, one major private life insurer previously operated at an expense ratio below 12%, but that metric has escalated to 18% today. Insurers must cut operational flab and focus on digital efficiency and technology adoption.”
— Ajay Seth, Chairman, IRDAI
The regulator is favouring an ‘open architecture’ model where distributors offer products from multiple companies rather than just one. This shift will likely increase competition and could impact the high-margin ‘tied-agent’ networks that many traditional insurers rely on.
“It comes down to open versus closed architecture rather than IDE versus IDP. IDEs operate on an open architecture, offering competing products across multiple insurers or bank partners. IDPs—specifically tied agents—can only sell the products of the single insurer with whom they are affiliated. In a closed architecture, an agent presents a single choice that may or may not fit the customer’s specific financial needs. In an open architecture, an intermediary offers a range of options across multiple entities, making product suitability easier for the customer to evaluate.”
— Ajay Seth, Chairman, IRDAI
The regulator is allowing individual distributors to sell a wider range of financial products, including complex insurance and mutual funds, to boost their total income. This change aims to expand insurance reach into rural India while making the distributor role more financially viable through volume rather than high commissions.
“First, the framework provides additional commission incentives for smaller towns (defined liberally as towns with a population below 50,000) and smaller cities (population below 10 lakh). This covers underserved geographies. Second, we are significantly expanding the operational scope for POSPs. Previously, POSPs were restricted to selling simple, low-ticket products like basic motor or term insurance. Under the proposed framework, POSPs who complete online training and pass an on-demand test can sell the full suite of insurance products, including ULIPs and complex policies, without ticket-size limits. Third, we are enabling distribution cross-selling. Insurance intermediaries and POSPs will be permitted to sell non-insurance financial products (such as pension products and mutual funds) as well as non-financial products. Furthermore, over five lakh Common Service Centres (CSCs) and Banking Correspondents (BCs) in rural areas are being integrated into the insurance distribution ecosystem. By enabling individual distributors to earn across multiple financial products, volume expansion and higher overall productivity will offset lower per-product percentage margins.”
— Ajay Seth, Chairman, IRDAI
IRDAI has identified excessive profit margins and commission rates among top distributors that it believes should instead be returned to customers. This signals an impending squeeze on the margins of large, listed insurance distribution platforms and bank-led distributors.
“To provide a concrete data point: one major insurance distributor currently generates a post-tax profit margin of 44% on its top-line commission income. Another major distributor saw its effective commission rate rise from 6%–7% a few years ago to 38% today. When distribution margins reach these levels, value is being diverted away from policyholders. The savings achieved through commission caps and EOM rationalisation must be passed directly to policyholders through better pricing and improved product value.”
— Ajay Seth, Chairman, IRDAI
New rules will force brokers to disclose their commissions on large corporate deals worth over ₹50 crore to ensure transparency. This is likely to push the corporate insurance market toward a fee-based model, potentially reducing commission income for brokers in the high-ticket commercial segment.
“The mandatory disclosure requirement applies specifically to large commercial policies where the sum insured exceeds ₹50 crore (representing medium-to-large corporate risks) and large corporate group health policies. It does not apply to retail policies or small enterprise policies below ₹50 crore. Corporate buyers purchasing large-scale commercial covers have the sophistication to evaluate risk-advisory fee structures versus commission payouts. In group health insurance, we observed counterintuitive data where commission percentages on large corporate group policies were sometimes higher than on retail policies. Mandating transparency for large commercial covers encourages a shift toward fee-based risk advisory and allows corporate buyers to evaluate whether distribution costs are justified.”
— Ajay Seth, Chairman, IRDAI
The regulator is banning digital platforms from collecting customer data before showing product quotes, viewing this as a ‘dark pattern’. This will force digital aggregators to change their lead-generation tactics and could affect their customer conversion rates.
“Under Central Consumer Protection Authority guidelines and general market principles, dark patterns—including forcing consumers to surrender personal data before displaying product pricing—are prohibited. In a competitive market, consumers have an absolute right to view product features, coverage details, and pricing upfront before deciding whether to share personal information for KYC and underwriting purposes. Restricting price transparency behind a paywall or data-collection wall violates basic market principles.”
— Ajay Seth, Chairman, IRDAI
IRDAI plans to lower renewal commissions for health insurance because renewals require less work than new sales. This change is intended to stop agents from unnecessarily moving customers between companies just to earn higher commissions.
“Health Insurance Renewals: Data shows that policyholders naturally persist with health insurance due to cumulative benefits like No-Claim Bonuses. Selling a health policy for the first time requires substantial advisory effort, whereas servicing a renewal requires a reminder prompt. First-year commissions reflect that initial acquisition effort, whereas lower renewal commissions align with actual servicing costs and discourage commission-driven churning or forced portability.”
— Ajay Seth, Chairman, IRDAI
The regulator is unbundling motor insurance costs and setting very low commissions for mandatory third-party covers on new cars. Investors should note that this will improve pricing for consumers but may lower the revenue profile of motor insurance for many distributors.
“Motor Insurance: Motor Third-Party (TP) cover is mandatory by law. First-year TP insurance on new vehicles involves zero selling effort, so commission limits are set at minimal levels. Subsequent renewals after the initial multi-year policy period require active agent outreach, which is why higher commission allowances apply to renewal servicing. Furthermore, line items across Third-Party cover, Own Damage (OD), legal liability, and personal accident cover must be unbundled and clearly itemised.”
— Ajay Seth, Chairman, IRDAI
The regulator is moving toward a Risk-Based Capital model by April 2025 and is incentivising ‘term’ insurance over investment-linked products (ULIPs). This strategic shift will favour companies with strong protection portfolios and could require capital adjustments across the industry.
“We are actively working toward implementing the Risk-Based Capital (RBC) framework, targeting a rollout timeline around April 1st. The consultation paper deliberately allows higher commission flexibilities for pure protection (term) products, which require greater distribution effort to sell, compared to market-linked investment products like ULIPs where lower commission structures preserve underlying policyholder yields. Expanding pure protection coverage is vital for national financial resilience, and our capital and distribution frameworks are being calibrated to support that objective.”
— Ajay Seth, Chairman, IRDAI
Automobiles
Bajaj Auto | Large Cap
Bajaj Auto is a leading global manufacturer of two-wheelers and three-wheelers, renowned for brands like Pulsar and the Chetak electric scooter. The company maintains a strong export presence in over 70 countries and is a significant player in the transition to electric mobility.
[ Interview ]
Management clarified that the recent sales miss was due to specific supply chain issues rather than a drop in buyer interest. This helps investors understand that the volume drop is a temporary logistics hurdle rather than a long-term demand problem.
“While we delivered a strong quarter overall, our internal monthly target was approximately 570,000 units. Breaking down that 40,000-unit shortfall: 1. Chetak EV (20,000 units): Inbound shipment delays for critical components prevented us from maxing out production. Instead of hitting over 60,000 units, we completed only 42,000 units. Channel inventory remains extremely low, and we are working to convert existing bookings into retail sales. 2. Exports (15,000 units): Outbound logistics constraints impacted shipments. Operating at our scale—where a container leaves our plants every 10 minutes, 24/7—any shipping availability disruption causes severe deferrals. 3. New Launches & Component Bottlenecks (5,000–7,000 units): Market reception for our 10 new Q2 launches across Pulsar, Triumph, and KTM ranges exceeded expectations. Channel stock for these models sits at only 9–10 days, particularly for sporty 150cc+ models like the Pulsar N160. Rapid volume growth led to shortages of key electronic components like Electronic Fuel Injections (EFIs). Without these supply disruptions, total monthly volume would have reached 570,000 units, representing around 13% growth.”
— Rakesh Sharma, Joint Managing Director
Component issues for the electric scooter segment have been fixed, and production is now ramping up to meet strong demand. Investors should watch for a significant volume jump in the coming month as backlogged orders are fulfilled.
“The primary bottleneck on Chetak was resolved over the last few days of the month. Our total Chetak production capacity ranges between 60,000 and 65,000 units, while underlying demand exceeds 65,000 units. We expect Chetak volumes to climb from 42,000 units in September to over 62,000 units in October.”
— Rakesh Sharma, Joint Managing Director
The company expects a strong recovery in total sales for October, supported by record-breaking performance in the three-wheeler segment. This signal suggests that the infrastructure for both electric and traditional engines is operating at high utilisation.
“Overall, October sales should comfortably exceed 5.7 lakh units. There is no underlying demand weakness. The recent shortfall was entirely driven by supply chain constraints and component shortages. In fact, three-wheeler volumes hit an all-time high of 90,000 units in a single month, with strong demand across electric and ICE autos challenging our production capacity.”
— Rakesh Sharma, Joint Managing Director
Global container shortages are currently making it difficult to ship products to international markets despite healthy demand. The company is actively diversifying its port usage to bypass these bottlenecks and protect its export revenues.
“The export shortfall was not geography-led or demand-driven; it was purely caused by container availability and shipping line constraints. Global shipping lines have diverted container capacity toward China-Europe and China-US trade routes. To mitigate this, we scrambled logistics across JNPT, South Indian, and Gujarat ports.”
— Rakesh Sharma, Joint Managing Director
Sales in Nigeria, a critical export market for the company, are showing signs of stabilisation and recovery. This growth reduces a major risk factor that has historically impacted the company’s international earnings.
“Regarding Nigeria: demand is recovering well. September sales in Nigeria crossed 35,000 units, landing between 35,000 and 37,000 units.”
— Rakesh Sharma, Joint Managing Director
Management expects a predictable 40% surge in volumes during the festive period based on historical seasonal trends. This transparency allows investors to benchmark the company’s performance against historical peaks during the high-stakes holiday season.
“Festive demand remains structurally healthy. Looking at seasonal trends over a 3-to-4-year window, Q3 volumes typically expand to 1.4 times pre-festive run rates. Year-to-date total volume growth stands at 13%, while our premium 150cc+ motorcycle segment grew at 28% from April to August. We see no underlying weakness in consumer demand heading into the festive season.”
— Rakesh Sharma, Joint Managing Director
The premium motorcycle category is growing twice as fast as the overall business, driven by strong interest in high-end models. This shift toward a more expensive product mix generally supports better profit margins for the company.
“Year-to-date total volume growth stands at 13%, while our premium 150cc+ motorcycle segment grew at 28% from April to August. We see no underlying weakness in consumer demand heading into the festive season.”
— Rakesh Sharma, Joint Managing Director
While markets like the Philippines are doing well, economic or regulatory issues in neighbouring countries are weighing on the Asian export numbers. Investors can see that the company’s geographic diversification helps offset localised regional slowdowns.
“Asia remains a mixed bag and our most underperforming export region. We are witnessing rapid growth across Latin America and Africa, while the Middle East and North Africa remain soft due to geopolitical factors. Within Asia, markets like the Philippines and Sri Lanka are performing well, whereas Nepal and Bangladesh continue to underperform.”
— Rakesh Sharma, Joint Managing Director

State Bank of India | Large Cap
State Bank of India is the country’s largest public sector lender, commanding a dominant market share in domestic remittances and digital payments. The bank provides a comprehensive suite of financial services through its extensive branch network and digital platforms like YONO.
[ Interview ]
SBI has confirmed it is technically ready to implement the new merchant discount charges on UPI transactions starting October 15. This indicates that the bank’s core systems can already handle the complex task of split-fee distribution across the payment network.
“From an operational and technical preparedness standpoint, collecting and distributing MDR across payment ecosystem participants is a well-established process within banks. When the framework kicks off on October 15th, SBI will have the full technical capability to operationalise it in close coordination with the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI).”
— Rama Mohan Rao Amara, Managing Director
Management is focusing on educating the public to prevent concerns that small transactions or consumers will be taxed. This clarity is important because it protects high-volume, low-value digital payment habits while targeting a specific merchant segment for revenue.
“Right now, the primary focus across banks and regulators is creating stakeholder awareness—among consumers, merchants, and technology providers—to dispel misconceptions: 1. Consumer Protection: P2M transactions under ₹2,000—which account for 96% of total UPI transaction volumes—remain completely exempt. Furthermore, retail consumers incur zero charges regardless of transaction size; the cost is strictly a merchant-side discount rate. 2. Targeted Merchant Application: The charge applies to a small subset of large merchants handling transactions above ₹2,000. 3. Caps and Exemptions: Critical and essential utility payments (such as fuel and railway ticketing) carry a flat ₹5 MDR rather than a percentage fee. Across all applicable P2M transactions, MDR is capped at a maximum of ₹300 per transaction.”
— Rama Mohan Rao Amara, Managing Director
The bank believes that introducing these fees is necessary to fund the expensive technology and security upgrades required to keep the payments system safe. Investors should see this as a move toward making digital banking infrastructure a self-sustaining business rather than a sunk cost.
“From an industry perspective, MDR revenues will partly offset the substantial, ongoing capital investments banks make in underlying payment infrastructure—specifically in upgrading cybersecurity, strengthening fraud risk management, and expanding server capacity. It creates a far more equitable and financially sustainable model for digital payments.”
— Rama Mohan Rao Amara, Managing Director
The management clarified that the vast majority of their transaction volume will not be affected by the new fee structure. This suggests that the immediate revenue impact will be limited to a small, high-value tier of their merchant network.
“While I cannot share specific internal merchant metrics, industry-wide data indicates that 96% of all UPI transactions are exempt. A similar ratio applies to our merchant base, meaning only around 4% of total transaction volume will be subject to MDR.”
— Rama Mohan Rao Amara, Managing Director
SBI plans to use the new revenue stream to expand its presence in merchant services, where it has traditionally been less active. This shift could diversify the bank’s digital income beyond its current dominance in processing payments for individual users.
“Historically, SBI’s primary strength has been on the remitter (payer) side, where we hold a dominant 27% market share. On the beneficiary and merchant acquisition side, our footprint is relatively smaller, managed partly through our joint venture, SBI Payments. However, introducing a modest MDR stream creates a clear financial incentive for SBI to play a far more active role across the merchant acquiring value chain. We will evaluate specific segments where SBI can deliver distinct value-added services to merchants rather than simply replicating existing market players.”
— Rama Mohan Rao Amara, Managing Director
The improved economics of digital payments are driving the bank to scale up its technical services for merchants and payment apps. This suggests that SBI is looking for profitable growth in the digital ecosystem rather than just chasing transaction volume.
“Definitely. Rebalancing the economics encourages us to expand beyond our traditional remitter dominance into merchant acquisition, PSP services, and our proprietary digital applications. However, revenue is only one element. We will expand into new segments of the payments value chain only where we can deliver tangible technology and operational value to merchants and ecosystem partners.”
— Rama Mohan Rao Amara, Managing Director
While the fees will help cover the massive costs of maintaining the UPI network, they are not expected to be a major profit centre for now. Investors should view this as a way to reduce the financial burden of digital operations rather than a massive boost to net interest margins.
“UPI infrastructure operates as a shared technology stack within the bank, supporting multiple digital banking services, so we do not isolate a standalone cost figure. However, broader industry estimates place the total annual system-wide infrastructure and maintenance cost between ₹15,000 crore and ₹20,000 crore. While actual MDR collections will depend on consumer and merchant transaction behaviour post-rollout, we expect the revenue to largely offset core infrastructure costs rather than act as a net profit driver. It provides the financial foundation to continue investing in digital innovation and value-added merchant features.”
— Rama Mohan Rao Amara, Managing Director
SBI chose not to partner with Apple Pay for its India launch after reviewing the business terms. This reflects a disciplined approach to partnerships where the bank prioritises its own strategic interests and commercial viability over simply joining global platforms.
“Apple Pay did approach SBI, and we had the opportunity to evaluate their commercial proposition and technical framework. After a thorough internal evaluation, SBI took a strategic decision not to participate in that specific ecosystem at this stage. We continually evaluate global payment partnerships, and our position may evolve as commercial and operational terms shift over time.”
— Rama Mohan Rao Amara, Managing Director

Emami Agrotech is a prominent Indian edible oil and food products manufacturer under the Emami Group. The company produces a variety of branded oils, spices, and snacks, leveraging an extensive national distribution network.
[ Interview ]
The government’s decision to lower import duties has helped stabilise domestic supply and cap international price increases during the peak festive season. This move has cleared distribution bottlenecks and restored consumer demand that was previously stalled by high costs.
“Following a significant multi-month rally driven by geopolitical tensions, elevated energy prices, rising input costs, and rupee depreciation, the government’s duty cut was timely and welcome. It arrived right as consumer festive demand builds up, balancing the needs of farmers alongside consumer affordability in conjunction with recent Minimum Support Price (MSP) increases. Demand is picking up now that duty certainty has returned. Products are moving steadily from ports into distribution pipelines that had run dry in anticipation of the announcement. Interestingly, following India’s duty cut, international edible oil prices actually moderated. The 10% duty reduction on sunflower oil created an artificial ceiling on price surges, keeping soybean oil and palm oil prices in check.”

Short-term supply growth in Southeast Asia is currently managing palm oil availability, but future markets are forecasting higher prices. Investors should note that increasing biofuel requirements and potential weather disruptions are expected to tighten supply in the first quarter of 2025.

— Sudhakar Desai, CEO
Recent price reductions are reaching institutional and bulk buyers quickly, though retail consumers will see the benefits after existing stocks clear. Rapid price adjustments in mass-market brands indicate high competitive intensity within the sector.
