In today’s edition of The Daily Brief:
1. The RBI’s 3-front war on inflation, explained
To tackle rising food prices and energy supply shocks pushing retail inflation to 5.54%, the Reserve Bank of India raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%. Beyond interest rates, the central bank is actively supporting the rupee by opening a direct dollar window for oil companies to curb spot currency demand, while tightening daily liquidity requirements to ensure rate hikes effectively transmit across the economy.
2. Will tougher pharma rules change who gets prescribed?
The Supreme Court directed the government to set up an expert committee to strengthen pharmaceutical marketing regulations under the Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices (UCPMP). With pharma companies spending 25–30% of revenue on sales and promotion, stricter legal enforcement on doctor inducements could reduce promotional expenses, drive prescription demand toward established brands and trade generics, and improve operating margins for major drugmakers.
The RBI’s 3-front war on inflation, explained
If you’ve been following the RBI over the last week or so, you’d have noticed it has been unusually busy. It raised interest rates. It rolled out measures to prop up the rupee. And it started pulling money out of the banking system.
On the surface, these look like three separate stories. But they’re tied together by one thing that affects all of us: inflation. Each of these moves, directly or indirectly, is part of the RBI’s effort to keep prices in check.
To see how they fit together, though, we first need to understand what’s pushing prices up in the first place.
What’s driving inflation?
India’s retail inflation rose to 5.54% in September, from 4.83% in August . That’s how much more a typical basket of goods and services, as tracked by the consumer price index, costs compared to a year ago. Food inflation jumped even more sharply, from 5.97% to 7.74%.
Source
Part of this story is painfully familiar. Food prices in India live and die by the weather, and the weather hasn’t been kind this year. We’ve written about this before on The Daily Brief, and its effects are now showing up clearly in the numbers.
India received about 13% less rainfall than normal this monsoon, partly because of El Niño, a warming of the tropical Pacific that tends to weaken India’s monsoon. A weak monsoon hurts twice. It damages the crops already in the ground, and it leaves less water stored up for the next season. You can already see this playing out. Rice prices are rising as acreage shrinks, and wheat acreage is expected to fall too. Edible oils are a separate headache. India relies heavily on imports for them, so their prices move with global markets.
CareEdge’s September inflation note flags these pressures, along with the risk a weak monsoon poses to farm output. On top of that, energy is getting expensive again, with crude climbing back up to $100 per barrel .
What really caught our eye, though, was how widely price rises are spreading.
CareEdge estimates that core inflation, which strips out food and certain energy items, edged up from 4.2% to 4.3%. Meanwhile, its diffusion index jumped from 72 to 82. Think of this index as a measure of breadth: it tells you how many categories are seeing prices rise faster than before.
By the same report’s count, inflation picked up in 11 of the CPI’s 12 major categories.
Source
It’s tempting to look at this and conclude that the economy is overheating, that people are simply buying more than the economy can produce. We’d be careful with that conclusion.
Prices can rise across the board even when demand is perfectly normal. If fuel gets expensive, almost every business feels it, whether or not its customers are buying more.
The RBI made this exact distinction in its press conference . Governor Sanjay Malhotra said there were very few signs of demand pushing prices up. In other words, this is supply-led inflation. The worry, instead, was that persistent supply shocks might start changing how businesses and people set prices.
Source
Here’s how that works. Imagine a transport company whose fuel bill goes up. It raises its freight charges. Now a manufacturer that uses that transporter faces a bigger delivery bill, and raises its own prices.
Now imagine people start expecting prices to keep rising. Workers ask for bigger raises. Businesses build larger price hikes into their plans. At this point, the original shock is shaping decisions far beyond the businesses it first hit.
That’s when inflation becomes really hard to shake off.
Why raise interest rates?
Which brings us to a tricky question for the RBI. If inflation is mostly coming from supply problems, what can an interest rate hike actually do? Higher rates don’t make it rain, after all.
Still, on October 7, the RBI raised the repo rate by 0.25 percentage points to 5.50% , its first hike since February 2023. It also shifted its stance to “calibrated tightening.”
The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks, and it ripples out into borrowing costs across the economy. When loans get pricier, households and businesses get more cautious about spending. And with buyers holding back, companies find it harder to keep raising prices.
But the bigger point is about expectations. Remember the spiral we just described, where people start treating inflation as permanent and bake it into wages and prices? A rate hike signals that the RBI won’t let that happen. It can cool expectations today, even if its effect on actual prices takes much longer to show up.
But there’s another reason the RBI can’t sit still, and it has to do with the rest of the world.
Why the rupee matters
In September, both the European Central Bank and the US Federal Reserve raised their rates by 0.25 percentage points.
Why does that matter for India? One reason is the India–US yield gap . Right now, India’s ten-year government bonds yield roughly 7.3%, against about 5.3% for US ones. So a foreign investor earns about two percentage points more by lending to India. But they weigh that extra return against the risk that the rupee falls, and against what it costs to protect themselves from that fall.
When US returns rise relative to Indian ones, that trade looks less attractive. Some investors may sell Indian assets and convert the proceeds into dollars. All that dollar buying puts pressure on the rupee.
By October 7, it had lost about 7.5% against the dollar during 2026 .
Here’s why that matters for inflation. If you’re an importer, a weaker rupee changes your bill even if your supplier hasn’t touched its price. A $100 purchase costs ₹9,000 when a dollar costs ₹90. At ₹97 to the dollar, the same purchase costs ₹9,700.
Imports get more expensive in rupee terms, and some of that eventually reaches consumers. Think about what this means for energy. Oil was already expensive because of global factors. A weaker rupee makes it more expensive still.
This is how the currency becomes part of the inflation problem.
Higher Indian interest rates help here, by making rupee assets more rewarding to hold. But rate hikes are only one part of how the RBI is defending the currency.
How the RBI is supporting the currency
Think of the rupee’s value as a tug of war between those who need dollars and those who bring them in. Importers need dollars to pay their foreign suppliers. Foreign investors need them when they take money out of India. On the other side, export earnings, remittances and investment inflows bring dollars in.
When demand for dollars outstrips supply, buyers have to offer more rupees for each dollar. That’s what a falling rupee is.
The RBI has been working on both sides of this equation.
First, the supply of dollars. Earlier this year, the RBI encouraged dollars to flow into India through special swap facilities. One of them was linked to FCNR(B) deposits, which are foreign-currency deposits that non-resident Indians hold with Indian banks.
Here’s how it worked. Banks collected these dollar deposits, handed the dollars to the RBI in exchange for rupees, and agreed to reverse the trade later. The RBI offered favourable terms, which made it worthwhile for banks to go out and gather these deposits. More dollars coming in meant more support for the rupee.
And it worked. Revised figures put FCNR(B) deposits at about $133 billion .
But there’s a catch. These swaps have to be reversed eventually, and when they are, the RBI has to hand those dollars back. The RBI’s future dollar obligations stand at around $200 billion . Set against that, its $734 billion war chest of foreign exchange reserves looks less comfortable than it first appears. A temporary inflow of dollars doesn’t make currency pressure go away for good.
So the latest measures go after the other side: the demand for dollars.
Oil companies are among the biggest and most regular buyers of dollars. Normally, they go to banks to buy the dollars they need to pay for crude, and those purchases add to demand in the currency market.
The RBI has now opened a special dollar window for Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum. From October 12, it can meet their daily dollar needs directly, through designated banks. That takes a big, steady source of demand out of the open market.
The next set of measures deals with currency contracts.
Say an importer has to pay a supplier in dollars three months from now. If the rupee weakens in the meantime, that payment gets more expensive. So the importer can lock in an exchange rate with a bank today. This is called hedging, and it serves a real business need.
But the same contracts can also be used to bet on where the rupee is headed. And when companies rush to buy dollars, or take positions bigger than their actual needs, they add to the pressure on the currency. The RBI wants these contracts to more closely reflect genuine business needs.
So it has lowered the threshold for establishing the exposure behind certain currency positions from $100 million to $5 million. In plain terms, companies taking currency positions above $5 million now have to show the business need behind them. Larger hedges are still allowed, but they have to be backed by real exposure. The RBI has also banned companies from rebooking contracts they’ve cancelled.
Together, these steps aim to curb excessive bets on the currency, although genuine importers may end up paying more too. If they help steady the rupee, they also limit how much inflation comes in through costlier imports.
There’s one more piece to this. When the RBI defends the rupee by selling dollars, it also changes how much money sits in the banking system. That brings us to liquidity.
Making the rate hike work
Liquidity, here, means the readily available cash banks use to settle payments and meet their short-term funding needs.
Banks lend this cash to each other, often overnight. When there’s plenty of it going around, nobody has to scramble for funds, and short-term borrowing rates stay low. That’s a problem for the RBI. It can raise the repo rate, but if market rates stay low, the hike doesn’t really bite.
And right now, the system is flush with cash, partly because of those currency swaps. When banks handed dollars to the RBI, they got rupees back, and those rupees landed in the banking system.
The RBI’s October policy statement shows that, since the August meeting, the banking system has had an average daily surplus of roughly ₹5.9 lakh crore. Banks with that much money on hand also have little reason to raise deposit rates to attract more.
So the RBI is mopping up some of that surplus, to make sure market rates actually reflect its tighter stance. It’s using a few tools to do this.
The first is open market operation (OMO) sales. The RBI sells government bonds it already holds. Banks pay for them, and that money moves out of the banking system and into the RBI. On October 13, it accepted bids for ₹25,000 crore in face value of government securities .
This pulls money out for longer, since it doesn’t automatically flow back the next day. Another is a tweak to cash reserve requirements, and it works a little differently.
Banks have to keep a certain share of their deposits as cash with the RBI. This is the cash reserve ratio, or CRR, and it stays at 3%. But from October 16, banks must maintain at least 99% of their required cash reserve each day, up from 90% . What they have to hold on average over a fortnight hasn’t changed.
Here’s what that means. Say a bank has to keep an average of ₹100 with the RBI. Earlier, it could dip to ₹90 on a given day and make up for it later. Now, it can’t go below ₹99.
That gives banks less wiggle room to use those balances elsewhere in the meantime. They may need to borrow more in the short term, which nudges market rates closer to the RBI’s policy rate. So this isn’t a conventional CRR hike. It’s a stricter rule on how banks maintain their reserves every single day.
Currency intervention adds to this. When the RBI sells dollars to defend the rupee, banks pay for them in rupees. Those rupees leave the banking system, unless the RBI puts money back some other way.
This is where all three policies meet. Selling dollars supports the rupee while draining liquidity. And tighter liquidity helps the rate hike actually reach the wider economy.
How much room does the RBI have?
All this tightening has a cost. Costlier credit can make families put off big purchases and businesses delay investments. And a poor harvest is already a hit to rural incomes. Tighter financial conditions would add to that strain.
That said, the RBI does have some room. It raised its growth forecast for FY2026–27 to 7.1% from 6.7% . The World Bank increased its forecast to 7.1% , from 6.6%, while the IMF now expects 7% , up from 6.4%.
These upgrades suggest the economy is more resilient than expected. But they’re no guarantee that growth can take more tightening without getting hurt.
Nor does inflation being below 6% mean the RBI can relax. Its target is 4%; 6% is just the upper limit of what it can tolerate. Its own October projections put inflation at 6% in October–December, 5.7% in January–March and 5.6% in April–June. That’s a long stretch above target.
So the RBI is trying to stop inflation from settling in, without choking growth. How much more it needs to do depends partly on things outside its control: the next harvests, water availability, global commodity prices, and the government’s decisions on releasing food stocks.
That’s the balance we’ll be watching: whether supply pressures ease on their own before the RBI has to slow the economy much more sharply to contain them.
Will tougher pharma rules change who gets prescribed?
You visit a doctor, get a prescription and buy the medicine. But why did the doctor choose that particular brand when several companies might sell essentially the same drug?
For Indian pharma companies, that decision is worth fighting for. Sometimes, the competition goes well beyond explaining why one medicine is better than another, even involving buttering up the doctors in other ways.
On October 8, 2026, the Supreme Court directed the government to set up an expert committee to examine whether pharmaceutical marketing needs stronger legal enforcement.
Oddly, though, India already has rules against these practices. They’re called the Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices, or UCPMP. India has spent more than a decade trying to stop drugmakers from offering doctors expensive gifts, sponsored holidays and other personal benefits.
The problem is that there are some misaligned incentives at the heart of how those rules are enforced.
What is UCPMP?
In an earlier edition , we covered in-depth how pharmaceutical companies use medical representatives, free samples and other promotional activities to influence doctors’ prescriptions. We also explained why drugmakers resisted restrictions on medical representatives visiting central government hospitals.
It’s the UCPMP that sets the rules for this marketing. When India introduced the code in 2015, it was voluntary, with little to compel drugmakers to follow it. The government finally made it mandatory in March 2024 . The code regulates how drugmakers promote medicines to doctors.
Companies cannot offer doctors cash, personal gifts or sponsored holidays. They can provide certain educational materials worth up to ₹1,000 each. They can also distribute free medicine samples, but within quantity limits. The total value of samples cannot exceed 2% of annual domestic sales.
Source
Medical conferences have their own rules. Companies cannot organise these events abroad. They can support educational programmes in India, but generally cannot pay for doctors’ travel and accommodation unless they’re speakers at eligible events. Companies must also maintain promotional records and disclose certain marketing expenses.
So UCPMP doesn’t stop drugmakers from promoting medicines. But what they cannot do is offer personal benefits to influence prescriptions.
What happens when the marketing machine slows?
Even without these restrictions, though, pharma marketing can be a bit capital-intensive.
A June 2024 report by Avendus Capital estimated that Indian pharmaceutical companies spend roughly 25-30% of their revenue on sales and marketing. About half goes towards employees, largely the salesforce visiting doctors. The rest covers other selling and promotional expenses. Most of this spending is allowed under UCPMP.
Source
But if companies cut back on improper promotional practices, could that affect their sales? We can’t answer that directly yet. But the COVID-19 lockdown gives us an interesting comparison.
From April to June 2020, medical representatives couldn’t visit doctors freely, and companies cut back sharply on promotional travel. Even today, there are restrictions on medical representatives visiting central government hospitals to limit the potential (mis)influence of pharma firms on doctors. During the lockdown, though, the disruption was much wider.
That year, on the Q1 earnings call of Alkem Laboratories, an analyst estimated that the company’s quarterly other expenses had fallen from the usual ₹500 crore to around ₹340 crore. But the company’s brands performed differently. For instance, Pan, which was one of Alkem’s biggest medicines, saw fewer new prescriptions written by doctors during the lockdown. Yet, its sales barely changed from the previous year. That being said, brands smaller than Pan weren’t nearly as fortunate.
A pharma company has two distribution channels: trade-generics and branded generics. The former refers to chemists and distributors, while the latter refers to doctor’s prescriptions. As a whole, Alkem’s trade-generics business grew during the pandemic. Trade generics’ share of Alkem’s domestic business rose from around 20% to nearly 28%, although partly because the branded business slowed down.
Of course, the lockdown affected patient visits, medicine demand and availability too. We can’t attribute everything to reduced marketing. But an established brand doesn’t need to win every sale from scratch. Doctors already know it, and chemists already stock it. A newer brand has to persuade doctors to try something unfamiliar, and doesn’t yet have the benefit of prescriptions.
A rulebook that struggles to enforce itself
Now, if you crack down harder on marketing, you might create conditions that may be similar, if not the exact same, to the lockdown. Which is where we come back to the enforcement problem UCPMP faces currently.
Consider what happened with AbbVie Healthcare. In May 2024, the Department of Pharmaceuticals received an anonymous complaint accusing the company of paying for travel and accommodation for 30 doctors attending medical conferences in Monaco and Paris. But the complaint never received a straightforward hearing on whether AbbVie had crossed that line.
The Department forwarded it to an ethics committee run by a pharmaceutical industry association. In September 2024, the committee rejected it because the complainant hadn’t revealed their identity. You see, under UCPMP, anonymous complaints aren’t allowed. They must also provide evidence and pay a ₹1,000 non-refundable fee. That protects companies against false accusations.
Source
But say you work at a pharmaceutical company and discover improper payments to doctors. Would you want to put your name on a complaint against your employer? No, you’d rather do it anonymously.
The case then went to the government’s Apex Committee, which looked into the complaint anyway because the allegations were too serious for the anonymity condition to hold. In December 2024, the committee reprimanded AbbVie and asked the National Medical Commission to take action against the doctors involved.
The doctors challenged that decision. They argued that the committee shouldn’t have considered an anonymous complaint. In August 2026, the Delhi High Court temporarily stopped action against the doctors who had challenged the decision. It didn’t decide whether they had done anything wrong.
Source
So instead of settling whether the payments broke the rules, the case ended up in court over whether an anonymous complaint could be investigated at all.
The wider enforcement system has a conflict-of-interest problem, too. Pharmaceutical industry associations run the committees investigating complaints, with their own executives in charge. These committees can warn companies, demand corrective action or suspend association membership. But they cannot directly impose penalties.
India has also used tax rules to discourage such spending. In 2022, the Supreme Court ruled that Apex Laboratories, the company behind Zincovit, couldn’t claim tax deductions for prohibited freebies given to doctors.
Meanwhile, in September 2025, after industry complaints about compliance burdens, the government relaxed some reporting requirements . Companies now submit standardised annual marketing disclosures through industry associations. Associations no longer have to upload those disclosures to the government’s portal.
The Supreme Court now wants the government to examine whether these rules need stronger legal backing. It has given the government two weeks to form a committee, which must submit its recommendations within two months. The government must then report its decision to the Court.
Nothing has changed for drugmakers yet. But if the government makes violations harder to get away with, companies may have to rethink how they spend money promoting their medicines.
Why the biggest brands might benefit
Stricter marketing rules could have an unexpected effect: they might improve profits for some of India’s largest drugmakers.
Avendus Capital estimates that lower doctor-related marketing expenses could potentially improve operating margins by 2-3 percentage points, with another 1-2 points possible from a more efficient salesforce. This is a way to protect profits as more medicine sales move towards trade generics and government-backed Jan Aushadhi stores.
Source
But large companies may have a second advantage. If improper incentives to doctors become riskier, companies could put more effort into trade generics, where chemists and distributors play a bigger role in driving sales. And the economics there are different.
Take a medicine with a printed price of ₹100. As per Avendus’ calculations, in branded generics, distributors and chemists together receive about ₹30. In trade generics, their combined share can reach a little more than double that. That money is shared across the distribution chain, but it gives sellers a stronger reason to stock and promote trade generics.
Naturally, chemists cannot simply replace every medicine a doctor prescribes. And patients may pay less for trade generics, depending on their selling price and how much of the distribution margin retailers pass on. This is yet another version of the tradeoff between margins and growth. And distribution , they say, always comes first.
Neither outcome of higher margin or higher growth is guaranteed. Smaller companies could also benefit if improper inducements become less influential. But established drugmakers would still have the advantage of brand recognition and distribution networks built over decades.
Conclusion
The Supreme Court’s intervention raises a bigger question: who should police pharmaceutical marketing? The AbbVie case shows the limits of leaving it largely to the industry. But tougher penalties may not solve everything if companies simply shift their spending from doctors to chemists. India needs a system that can hold drugmakers accountable, while recognising the moving targets at play.

In today’s edition of The Daily Brief:
1. The US is one step away from banning green cards
The US Department of Labour indefinitely suspended eight major tech firms—including Microsoft, TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and Cognizant—from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) program, freezing the primary pathway to green cards for foreign workers. However, top Indian IT firms have already dramatically reduced their reliance on US work visas and green cards over the past decade, shifting to high offshore delivery ratios (~77%) and local US hiring, while Big Tech firms like Microsoft bear the brunt of the freeze.
2. India’s housing boom has narrowed
Headline data shows major-city housing sales remaining flat at 2.58 lakh units between January and September 2026, but underlying segment trends reveal a stark divide. While the ₹1–5 crore mid-to-premium housing segment surged—now accounting for over half of all sales—the affordable market (<₹50 lakh) fell 12% due to soaring land costs, reduced developer launches, and buyer affordability constraints exacerbated by the RBI’s recent rate hike.
The US is one step away from banning green cards
Just a few days ago, US Vice President JD Vance and Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling held a press conference to announce one of the Trump administration’s most aggressive immigration enforcement actions yet. Eight major technology companies were being indefinitely suspended from the Permanent Labour Certification program, or PERM. No new applications would be accepted, nor would any pending applications be processed.
As per Sonderling , since 2009, these companies alone had received over 2.3 lakh H-1B approvals and obtained over 1 lakh PERM certifications. Vance singled out Microsoft for laying off 6,000 American workers while obtaining over 6,000 H-1B visas and ~3,000 green cards. He called the foreign workers these companies employed “ indentured servants ”.
However, four of those eight companies are TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and Cognizant, which have already reduced their green card applications significantly to a negligible scale. Their combined filings in FY26 were essentially zero. The company this freeze hits hardest is actually Microsoft, which is the single largest filer of PERM cases.
This is also hardly the administration’s first move against skilled immigration. Just last year, the US had steeply hiked the application fee for the H1B visa . But since then, it’s hardly made a dent to the Indian IT business, which has been preparing for long against this eventuality.
So, what really is the intention behind this PERM move? How does it measure up against the goals it has set out to achieve?
The H1B fee hike
Let’s start with last year’s H1B fee hike.
In September 2025, the Trump administration issued a proclamation slapping a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa applications on top of the previous cost of just $5,000. Indians account for ~70% of all H-1B beneficiaries, so this was, in effect, an India tax.
However, the fee barely survived contact with the courts. A Massachusetts judge vacated it in June 2026, calling it an unlawful tax. The First Circuit, which hears appeals from federal district cases in some states, declined to reinstate it in July. Between September 2025 and February 2026, the Department of Homeland Security actually collected the fee on just 85 applications. Fee-subject filings collapsed by 87%.
But perhaps, the fee was probably not needed at all. Indian IT firms have been reducing their reliance on H1B registrations for much of the last decade anyway.
As we’ve covered before, Indian IT chooses one of two ways to reduce their reliance on H1B. The primary move is to move as much of their work offshore as possible. When that isn’t possible, they pull the secondary lever: hiring Americans locally .
In fact, between 2015 and 2025, there has been a 70% drop in H1B registrations for initial employment from the top Indian companies. In FY24, these firms only filed nearly 4500 petitions, which represented 0.003% of America’s civilian workforce. The H1B fee only nudged these companies further in a direction they were already headed in.
The bridge between guest and resident
Now, an H-1B visa is a temporary work permit. It lets a skilled professional live and work in the US for up to six years. But it’s tied to a specific employer. If you lose your job, you have 60 days to find another sponsor or leave the country. You can’t freelance, you can’t start a company, and your bargaining power with your employer is limited, because there is no alternative to leaving your employer other than leaving the US altogether.
A green card, though, is permanent residency. It lets you live and work in the US indefinitely, for any employer, on your own terms.
PERM is the bridge between the two. Before an employer can sponsor a worker for a green card, it must first get the Department of Labour to certify that no qualified American worker is available and willing to take the job . The employer posts the position, runs a recruitment campaign, documents that no suitable American applicant turned up, and then files for PERM certification. Only after that can it petition for access to a green card.
Source
In other words, the PERM process is specifically designed to protect American workers.
So what does freezing PERM do? It doesn’t cancel anyone’s work visa, nor does it immediately deport anyone. What it does is freeze their path to permanence. Workers can keep working, but they can’t move toward a green card through these eight employers. The freezing of PERM, then, locks out many hopefuls from the ability to exit the trap Vance described.
Shooting moving targets
That being said, Indian companies have relied even less on the PERM as they have on the H1B.
The US Department of Labour publishes PERM disclosure data every year . In FY25, Microsoft had 3,161 PERM cases that were decided . This was more than the Indian outsourcers on the list combined . In FY26, the gap became even starker: Microsoft got 1,683 of those, while each of Infosys, Wipro, TCS and Cognizant had either a negligible number or flat zero.
As per HDFC Securities , only two Indian IT firms feature in the top 20 PERM users of FY25.
Source
That also tracks with the intentions that Indian IT firms have publicly announced. For instance, TCS CEO K Krithivasan said publicly that the company is not looking to hire any new H-1B applicants in the US at all.
TCS told the stock exchange that except for its backlog, its new PERM applications had been in “ single digits “ over the last two years. Cognizant went from over 1,200 PERM cases a year to zero. Even when certifications came through, many companies let them expire unused . They weren’t carrying workers with green cards.
Meanwhile, the companies hit hardest are American multinationals like Microsoft and Adobe, who often onboard Indian workers under both H1B visas and the green card.
For many Indian engineers, a job at a Big Tech company has long been the American Dream. But now, Trump’s policies are only making it harder to realise it. In fact, this is exactly what we discussed in a recent Subtext episode with serial entrepreneur Sidu Ponnappa .
Like we mentioned before, Indian IT firms have been pulling two levers to escape America’s anti-immigration measures.
The first is offshoring. It’s well-known that Indian IT has been increasing its offshore mix over the last 10-15 years. The share of work done at the client’s location in the US has been falling across companies, much of it directly in response to the risks posed by American policy measures.
Moreover, a paper in Management Science by economist Britta Glennon found that restricting H-1B supply doesn’t cause companies to hire Americans. It causes them to move work abroad. A one-percentage-point cut in H1B supply led to 12-16% growth in foreign affiliate employment. It just moves the work.
The second lever, though, might contrast with this paper’s findings, because starting around 2016, Indian IT firms actually began hiring locally . By 2017, Infosys had committed to hiring 10,000 Americans and opening innovation hubs across the US. Today, TCS has ~30,000 US employees , of whom a third are on the H1B visa.
Later, Trump instituted a “ Buy American, Hire American “ executive order, which only accelerated it. The localisation rate has climbed steadily since. Wipro went from about 50% local workforce in the US in 2017 to over 80% by late 2025. Meanwhile, HCL also has a ~80% localisation rate as of this year.
Now, you might think that both levers might be at odds with each other. But the nuance here is that the localisation rate has been rising, but the onsite footprint share has been shrinking. The US jobs Indian IT adds are dwarfed by the headcount it keeps adding offshore. The net flow of work is still moving to India, not away from it.
Additionally, offshore growth is also taking the form of GCCs in India, where companies like Microsoft, Amazon, and Google are building their own captive operations. These centres bypass both the visa system and the IT services vendor entirely.
Source
So Indian IT might be doing what Vance says he wants: hiring Americans, building local workforces, reducing visa dependence. But the ban may not be as effective, particularly on Indian IT that have more or less already abandoned the PERM program. And while it potentially hurts Big Tech firms more, their most rational response might be to move more of the work outside.
The AI invariant
However, there’s one variable we’re yet to account for that might intersect with this ban in unseen ways.
AI is, of course, rapidly forcing software product and services firms to upend their organisations and even shrink the base of the pyramid. The routine work that filled the offshore pyramid, like testing, code maintenance, and basic application development, is exactly the kind of work LLMs are getting good at.
In light of that, there could theoretically be a limit to how much offshoring you could do.
Meanwhile, as AI automates the commodity layer, the work that remains valuable is the exact opposite. It’s the work that requires being deeply embedded with the client, understanding their data, their systems, their specific problems. Sometimes, if not always, that might mean actually being physically present at a client site. This, in fact, was also alluded to in the same Subtext episode with Sidu Ponnappa .
This is the Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) model, where small teams of highly-skilled engineers sit wherever the client’s key workflows live. It is a heavily customer-facing role, much unlike most offshore work Indian IT has done this far. And while it’s hardly a new model, it was made popular by a very specific American company: Palantir.
Interestingly, some months ago, Alex Karp, the CEO of Palantir, said that AI makes large-scale skilled immigration hard to justify “ unless you have a very specialised skill “. In a sense, that is also the ideology behind the PERM restriction. Karp also has extremely close ties with the Trump administration.
Alex Karp
Indian IT firms are starting to build FDE-style capabilities. TCS, for instance, has already begun hiring FDEs . Plus, as we’ve covered before, some of the fast-growing mid-cap IT firms are following a model somewhat similar to that of Palantir, where teams are arranged in small “ pods ” of human FDEs and AI agents, dedicated wholly to certain clients. When the business grows, the size of the pods themselves doesn’t; only the number of pods does. But it’s still early days.
The real volume, meanwhile, is flowing toward India’s GCCs, with firms like Amazon and Microsoft committing billions of dollars to India. That does mean more jobs in India, but does it mean more decision-making power? Well, GCCs expected that Trump’s policies would give them that. But, as The Ken found out , many of the critical decisions continue to remain in American headquarters, while India does the execution.
Source
Fighting the last war
The PERM freeze is indefinite with no end date in sight yet. But, like the H-1B fee before it, is aimed at a model that’s already mostly gone. The Indian IT body-shop has been in retreat for a decade, while also diversifying away from the US. Most of the companies named in the suspension had already stopped using the programme.
The policy assumes a world where blocking a foreign worker creates a job for an American. While there are signs it does, much of the best available evidence says that the relationship is not 1-to-1. It may even be negative.
It also goes without saying that this is yet another measure from the Trump administration to de-globalise and insulate the US from the rest of the world. However, if there’s anything we’ve learned this year, it’s that trade always finds a way to move and skirt past barriers.
India’s housing boom has narrowed
If you only looked at the headline numbers, you’d think India’s big-city housing market has simply stopped moving. Knight Frank counted 2.58 lakh sales across eight major markets between January and September 2026 , almost exactly what it sold a year earlier. In July–September alone, sales slipped just 1%. Boring, right?
Not quite. A market can be flat in two ways. Either nothing moves, or some parts surge while others sink and the two cancel out. India’s housing market is the second kind. Cheaper homes are selling less, the ₹2–5 crore bracket is booming, and some corners of the luxury market are slowing hard. To see what’s really going on, you have to look underneath that total
Knight Frank, Q3 2026 report
Premium demand is real but uneven
In July–September, sales of homes priced between ₹1 crore and ₹2 crore rose 4% from a year earlier. The ₹2–5 crore segment grew 20%. Put together, these two brackets now make up just over half of all the homes sold across the eight markets.
And these are actual homes changing hands at those prices, not just developers announcing bigger booking numbers. Developers are seeing it too.
In an interview , Prestige Estates chairman said its luxury projects, like Prestige Nautilus and Prestige Ocean Towers in Mumbai, had seen a strong response. He admitted there’s a lot more luxury supply coming up, but his point was simple: get the location, design and price right, and buyers will show up.
Of course, that’s one developer talking about his own projects. Zoom out, and the picture gets messier.
In NCR, sales of ₹5–10 crore homes fell 63% in July–September, while unsold stock in that bracket rose 33% . That’s a staggering fall. Knight Frank’s read is that NCR’s top end had become an investor-heavy market, where prices ran ahead of what people who actually want to live there could pay. That’s the consultancy’s take, though. The sales numbers alone can’t tell us why buyers stayed away.
Even the booming ₹2–5 crore segment is piling up homes fast. Across the eight markets, its unsold inventory rose 37% from a year earlier . That sounds alarming, until you notice that it would take about 4.5 quarters to clear, quicker than the market-wide 6.1. So it’s something to keep an eye on, not a sign that demand has fallen off a cliff.
There’s one more catch here. Think of a flat that cost ₹85 lakh a few years ago and now costs ₹1.1 crore. It’s the same flat, but it has quietly moved into a higher price bracket. So part of this shift towards crore-plus homes is buyers genuinely upgrading, and part of it is just homes getting pricier. It doesn’t all mean Indians suddenly got richer.
The affordable end has two problems
Now go to the other end of the market. sales below ₹50 lakh fell 12% in July–September, while the ₹50 lakh–₹1 crore bracket fell 8% .
Part of the story is that builders simply aren’t making enough of them. Reporting on the first quarter of 2026 , Knight Frank blamed much of the fall in cheaper-home sales on fewer launches.And this isn’t a recent blip. It’s been building for years. In early 2022, about a quarter of all new homes launched across India’s top seven cities were priced under ₹40 lakh, according to Anarock. By April–June 2026, that share had shrunk to just 6%. Homes under ₹80 lakh, which made up 60% of launches back then, had fallen to a quarter.
There was a small bounce in July–September, when sub-₹40 lakh homes rose back to 14% of launches. But one good quarter doesn’t undo four years of drift.
Source
Builders, for their part, say costs, especially land, have made it hard to build homes at those prices and still make money. But that can’t be the whole story. If the only problem were a shortage of new homes, the ones already on the market should be flying off the shelves. Are they?
Here’s where it gets interesting. By September, there were nearly 1.7 lakh unsold homes below ₹50 lakh . That’s actually 5% fewer than a year ago, so cheap homes aren’t exactly piling up.
And yet, the time it would take to sell them all has stretched from roughly 26 months to 28 months . Think about that. The stock is shrinking, but it’s selling even more slowly. That only happens when buyers are pulling back too. In other words, the affordable end has a supply problem and a demand problem at the same time.
Knight Frank, Q3 2026 report
Why are buyers holding back?
So what’s keeping buyers away? The industry’s first answer is affordability. In April, Knight Frank’s Shishir Baijal pointed to rising prices alongside weakening sales as a sign of pressure on buyers’ ability to purchase . That makes sense, but it doesn’t explain every unsold home.
That said, it would be wrong to claim homes have become less affordable everywhere. Knight Frank’s separate first-half assessment found affordability broadly stable across most major markets, because earlier interest-rate cuts softened the blow of rising prices. But that cushion is now being taken away. On October 7 , the RBI raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5%, its first hike since February 2023. Higher rates mean higher EMIs, and that bites hardest for buyers already stretching to afford a cheaper home.
And these affordability figures are city-wide averages anyway. They can’t tell us whether the families actually hunting for the cheapest homes can manage the down payment and EMI.
Other things probably matter too. Is the project too far from work? Is it well built? Will it even be finished on time? These are real worries for buyers, but the data doesn’t measure them, so it’s hard to say how much they weigh.
What we can say is that simply building more cheap homes won’t fix this. Builders say they struggle to make them at those prices, and the ones already built are taking longer to sell. The real question is whether anyone can build homes people actually want, at a price they can actually pay.
So that’s what sits beneath the flat headline. Some premium brackets are booming, others are overbuilt, and the cheaper end is squeezed from both sides. Call it a boom or call it a slump, and you’d be missing the real story.

Hi everyone, I’m Kulsum , and welcome to the seventh edition of Weekly Tidbits. Mridula has been recovering from fever this week, so I’m filling in for her.
We spend a lot of time reading interesting stories that never make it into a full Daily Brief piece. So, once a week, we pick some of the best ones and add a little context.
We sort them into GEIC: Global, Economy, Industry and Company.
With that said, let’s get started!
If you prefer watching the video, here’s the link:
G — Global
[1] Asia’s factories get a boost from AI demand
Demand for chips and AI-related equipment helped manufacturing expand in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan in September. South Korea’s manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index rose to 53.9, while Taiwan’s reached 56.7. A reading above 50 signals expansion.
AI spending is showing up in factory orders across these economies. But the improvement was uneven: Malaysia and the Philippines recorded contractions, while higher energy costs continued to put pressure on manufacturers.
[2] Russia extends its diesel export ban
Russia has extended its ban on diesel exports by fuel producers until the end of October . It has repeatedly restricted exports to contain domestic fuel prices and address shortages following Ukrainian attacks on its refineries.
Russia is usually the world’s second-largest diesel exporter, so the restrictions matter beyond its borders. Keeping more fuel at home leaves less available for international buyers when supplies are already under pressure. Some shipments under government-to-government agreements have been allowed.
[3] Some Indian speciality drugs escape US tariffs
The US has exempted certain speciality medicines and their ingredients from pharmaceutical tariffs when imported from India and other eligible markets. The exemption covers categories such as rare-disease medicines, infertility treatments, and cell and gene therapies.
This is not a blanket exemption for every Indian drug. The 100% tariff applies to specified patented pharmaceuticals, while generic medicines and their ingredients are separately outside these pharmaceutical tariffs. For exporters, the treatment depends on the products they sell.
E — Economy
[4] India’s registered factory workforce crosses two crore
Employment in India’s registered manufacturing sector rose about 7.2% in FY25, adding roughly 14.1 lakh people and taking the total to around 2.1 crore. The figures come from the Annual Survey of Industries , released on September 30.
The survey covers the registered factory sector, so this is not a count of everyone working in Indian manufacturing. Small, unregistered businesses are outside its coverage. Within the surveyed sector, however, employment expanded alongside production, with industrial output rising about 7.8% during the year.
[5] Exporters get three more months of tax refunds
The government has extended the Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products, or RoDTEP, scheme until December 31, 2026. It was due to expire on September 30. The scheme refunds certain taxes and levies that exporters pay but cannot recover through other mechanisms.
These include electricity duties and taxes on fuel used to transport goods. Such costs get built into an exported product’s price, making it more expensive for overseas buyers. Refunding them helps Indian exporters compete, while the extension gives businesses more certainty about support for their upcoming shipments.
[6] India’s deep-tech funding push needs private money too
India could mobilise around $25 billion for deep-tech investment, according to a Mint report citing industry body IVCA. The estimate combines roughly $11 billion in government support with matching investment from private fund managers and additional capital. It is a potential combined funding pool, rather than a single newly announced government fund.
Deep-tech businesses work in areas such as semiconductors, space technology and advanced manufacturing. Turning their research into products can take years and substantial investment. The challenge is finding enough investors willing to finance that wait, particularly when a company needs to move from an early prototype to commercial production.
I — Industry
[7] Cheaper pump diesel attracts industrial buyers
Private fuel retailers Jio-bp and Nayara Energy have restricted diesel purchases at their outlets as industrial buyers turn to petrol pumps for cheaper fuel. According to Business Standard , Jio-bp outlets have capped purchases at 50 litres per customer per day, while limits at Nayara outlets range from 70 to 200 litres per transaction.
The reason is a gap between two prices for the same fuel. Retail prices have stayed unchanged since May, while prices charged to bulk buyers have moved more closely with international rates. That gives industrial customers a reason to buy at petrol pumps, putting pressure on supplies meant for regular retail customers.
[8] Airlines resist a forced shift to Navi Mumbai
Global airline body IATA has opposed a proposal to shift around one-third of each airline’s international passenger and cargo operations from Mumbai airport to Navi Mumbai. It says airlines were not adequately consulted and has raised questions about maintenance, catering, ground handling and other facilities.
Mumbai airport’s operator links the transition to Terminal 1’s redevelopment, scheduled to begin in January 2027. But moving flights requires airlines to reorganise schedules, aircraft, staff and supporting services months ahead. IATA supports the new airport, but wants airlines involved in deciding how and when their operations move.
[9] Government funding will support early-stage drug discovery
The Department of Pharmaceuticals is opening a new funding track for startups and smaller businesses developing new drugs. Under the ₹5,000 crore PRIP scheme, eligible companies or projects can receive assistance of up to ₹50 crore, provided institutional investors contribute at least 25% of the project cost.
The support targets early research, when a possible treatment is still far from clinical testing or commercial sales. By sharing some of that risk, the government hopes to attract private investment earlier and help more Indian discoveries progress towards clinical development.
C — Company
[10] Tata Trusts proposes a merger to keep Tata Sons unlisted
Tata Trusts has proposed merging Tata Electronics Systems Solutions and Tata Consulting Engineers into Tata Sons. The idea is to give the group’s holding company a larger operating business, with its own revenue, and change the financial ratios that determine its regulatory classification.
The Trusts argue that the combined business would no longer qualify as a non-banking financial company or a core investment company. That could provide a route to keeping Tata Sons privately held. The proposal still needs the necessary approvals, including from the RBI, before it can proceed.
[11] An Indian drugmaker borrows from private funds for a Japanese purchase
Gujarat Themis Biosyn has secured about $58 million from Orion Capital Asia to help finance its acquisition of MicroBiopharm Japan, according to Bloomberg . It also raised ₹585 crore through rupee debt securities to support the acquisition and other corporate needs.
Private credit involves borrowing directly from investment funds. Such lenders can offer quicker or more tailored financing for acquisitions, but the terms matter. Gujarat Themis’ rupee borrowing included five-year debentures carrying a 10% coupon and shorter 18-month notes paying 17.75%, showing how different parts of an acquisition can come with different financing costs.
[12] Radico takes Indian whisky to UK airport shelves
Radico Khaitan’s Rampur and Sangam whiskies are now available at duty-free shops in Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Birmingham airports. The company already has a presence across more than 65 duty-free locations globally and plans to expand to over 100.
Airport shops give Radico a way to introduce its brands to international travellers. The expansion also fits its growing focus on higher-priced spirits: its Prestige & Above portfolio contributed 70.3% of its Indian-made foreign liquor sales value in FY26. The UK listings give these brands another route to build recognition overseas.

Hi everyone, I’m Mridula , and welcome to the eighth edition of Weekly Tidbits.
We spend a lot of time reading interesting stories that never make it into a full Daily Brief piece. So, once a week, we pick some of the best ones and add a little context.
We sort them into GEIC: Global, Economy, Industry and Company.
Let’s get started!
If you prefer watching the video, here’s the link:
G — Global
[1] Europe’s gas winter could tighten supplies for Asia
Europe is heading into winter with less gas in storage than usual. The European Commission says the region can still meet demand, but it may have to rely more on liquefied natural gas, or LNG.
Storage works like a winter savings account. Countries fill it during summer, when demand is low, and use it when heating demand peaks. With less stored gas, Europe may have to buy more during winter itself.
India and other Asian countries compete for many of the same LNG cargoes. If a cold winter pushes Europe to buy more, Asian buyers may have to pay more or settle for less. Europe has more import terminals and suppliers than it did during the 2022 energy crisis, but the weather will still decide how tight the market gets.
[2] America’s farm debt may be bigger than it looks
American farm debt is at a record, and a Reuters investigation suggests official figures may still be missing some of it. More farmers are borrowing from fertiliser sellers, equipment companies and cooperatives instead of banks.
Source
Farmers are earning less while spending more. Crop prices have fallen, but fuel, fertilizer and machinery remain expensive. Suppliers often let farmers pay later because it helps them sell more, which effectively turns them into lenders.
That makes the debt harder to track. A bank knows what a farmer owes it, but not what the same farmer owes a tractor dealer or fertiliser seller. The total stress can stay hidden until repayments start getting missed.
[3] Finland halts work at two Google data-centre sites
Finnish authorities have ordered Google to stop major preparatory work at two planned data-centre sites until environmental assessments are complete. The sites are part of Google’s €13 billion investment plans in Finland.
An environmental assessment studies how a project will affect land, water and wildlife before major work begins. At these sites, trees had already been cut down, soil removed, and roads and drainage changed. Google has admitted that this fell short of its own standards.
We wrote recently about how India’s data-centre boom is already running into another physical constraint: water. The Finland episode shows the same broader problem. Building more computing capacity isn’t only about finding enough chips and electricity. Companies also need land, water and permission to build, and those can become bottlenecks too.
E — Economy
[4] The GST Council wants to make compliance easier
The GST Council recommended a broad set of reforms on October 8. Last year’s overhaul, which we wrote about here , was mainly about tax rates. This round is about how the system works day to day: registration, refunds, tax credits, exports and enforcement.
A big part of the changes concerns input tax credit, or ITC. Businesses pay GST on what they buy and subtract that from the GST they collect on sales. The Council wants to allow this credit on more expenses, including employee insurance, telecom towers and some pipelines. It also wants faster and more automated refunds, easier registration and cancellation, simpler rules for small online sellers, and fewer disputes over whether some services qualify as exports.
Enforcement is being eased too. The Council recommended removing GST officers’ arrest powers, raising the prosecution threshold from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore, cutting some penalties and reducing unnecessary checks on goods moving between states. Some changes can come through rules and notifications, while others still need changes to the GST law.
[5] India is aiming for $1 trillion in exports
India wants to export $1 trillion worth of goods and services this financial year, up from a record $863 billion last year. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said the government is also trying to get more companies to use India’s free trade agreements, which can lower the duties Indian goods face in overseas markets.
There is support on the cost side too. The government has extended the Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products scheme, or RoDTEP, until December 31. It refunds some taxes and charges that remain built into exported goods, such as costs linked to fuel, electricity and transport. It has also extended insurance support for some shipments to West Asia, where wars and shipping disruptions have made trade riskier.
These measures solve different problems. Trade agreements can make Indian goods cheaper abroad, RoDTEP cuts some of the costs exporters carry at home, and insurance reduces the risk of selling into disrupted markets. The $1 trillion target will still depend heavily on global demand, but these policies are meant to make it easier for Indian firms to compete for that demand.
[6] Rice prices could push up food inflation
Rice prices are rising in parts of India . Millers say paddy has become more expensive, and a weak monsoon has widened the gap between how much rice is available and how much people want to buy.
Paddy is rice before it has been milled. When millers have to pay more for it, they can’t keep selling rice at the old price. Part of that extra cost moves down the chain to wholesalers, then to shops, and finally to the households that buy it.
Farmers benefit, since they get a better price for their crop. But rice is a staple that most families buy every week or month, and it isn’t easy to cut back on. So even a small increase shows up quickly in food bills, and it can keep inflation high even if prices of other things start to cool.
I — Industry
[7] Gig platforms want a different social-security levy
IndiaTech , an industry group representing companies such as Ola, Swiggy, Zomato and Porter, wants the government to change how gig platforms pay towards worker social security.
Under the Social Security Code, platforms may have to contribute 1–2% of their annual turnover to a fund for gig workers, capped at 5% of what they pay those workers. We wrote about this system when the new labour codes came into force. A shared fund helps because gig workers can work across several apps instead of having one fixed employer.
IndiaTech’s objection is to using turnover. Platforms count revenue differently. One may record only its commission, while another records the full value of an order. That can make similar businesses pay very different amounts. IndiaTech wants the levy linked more closely to what platforms actually pay their workers.
[8] India wants to stockpile critical minerals
India is preparing a policy to stockpile critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt and rare earths. These are used in batteries, electronics and defence equipment, but India still depends heavily on imports for many of them.
We wrote recently about how concentrated these supply chains are, especially in China. A government reserve would give manufacturers some protection if imports are suddenly restricted or disrupted.
India is also planning four processing parks. The idea is to do more of the refining at home, instead of importing minerals that have already been processed elsewhere. The stockpile is the backup. The processing parks are the longer-term attempt to reduce that dependence.
[9] Textile output is rising while apparel output falls
India’s textile production rose 13.1% year-on-year in August, while apparel production fell 7.4% over the same period. Two parts of the same industry are moving in opposite directions.
Textile mills make yarn and fabric. Apparel companies turn that fabric into finished clothes and depend more directly on orders from retailers and global brands. Rising textile output alongside falling apparel output suggests the stronger growth is happening earlier in the value chain.
Source
We looked at this gap in our deep dive into India’s textile industry. India is strong at cotton, yarn and fabric, but has struggled more with the final step of making clothes and selling them globally. August’s numbers reflect that same imbalance.
C — Company
[10] GQG Partners cuts its stake in ITC
GQG Partners has sold about ₹9,395 crore worth of ITC shares in a large block deal. It sold 36.5 crore shares on October 8, almost all of the 38.99 crore shares it held at the end of June.
The sale comes after a rough year for ITC. From February 1, cigarettes moved to a 40% GST rate based on retail price, while excise duties were also increased after the compensation cess was phased out. Cigarettes remain ITC’s most profitable business, so higher taxes can either force the company to raise prices and risk weaker sales, or absorb some of the cost and take a hit to margins. ITC shares are down more than 30% since the tax changes were announced.
GQG has also been reducing stakes in other Indian companies, including several Adani Group firms. But it is not pulling out of India entirely: it has added to holdings such as JSW Energy and JSW Steel. The ITC sale looks more like a reshuffling of where GQG wants to put its money.
[11] SpaceX is buying spectrum for its mobile service
SpaceX has agreed to buy a portfolio of US mobile spectrum from investment firm Grain Management for Starlink Mobile, its service that connects ordinary phones directly to satellites.
Spectrum is the radio frequency phones use to send and receive signals. SpaceX is buying frequencies in the 800 MHz band, which travel relatively far and are useful for mobile coverage.
Starlink’s direct-to-phone service has mostly relied on partnerships with telecom companies and their spectrum. Owning frequencies gives SpaceX more control over the network it wants to build in the US and makes it slightly less dependent on those partners.
[12] Schneider Electric is buying PTC for $22.6 billion
Schneider Electric has agreed to buy US software company PTC for $22.6 billion, roughly ₹2.1 lakh crore.
Schneider mainly makes electrical equipment for factories, buildings and data centres. PTC makes software that companies use to design products, run factories and maintain equipment. Buying PTC would let Schneider sell customers both the equipment running a site and the software managing it.
Schneider is paying about 42% more than PTC’s share price before the deal was announced. It also plans to fund the purchase with a mix of debt and new shares. The bet is that combining hardware and software will bring in enough extra business to justify that premium.
That’s it for this week.
