Our goal with The Daily Brief is to simplify the biggest stories in the Indian markets and help you understand what they mean. We won’t just tell you what happened; we’ll tell you why and how too. We do this show in both formats: video and audio. This piece curates the stories that we talk about.
You can listen to the podcast on Spotify , Apple Podcasts , or wherever you get your podcasts and watch the videos on YouTube. You can also watch The Daily Brief in Hindi .
In today’s edition of The Daily Brief:
1. Where’s the last-mile of India’s LPG revolution?
Despite Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana expanding LPG coverage to over 10.5 crore women, many low-income households continue to rely on traditional firewood and “fuel stacking” due to high refill costs. CEEW studies highlight that while 80% of surveyed households expressed a willingness to transition fully to clean energy at ₹400 per cylinder, current subsidised prices remain significantly higher, leaving families caught between high fuel expenses and dangerous indoor air pollution.
2. Why are airlines opposing the move from Mumbai to Navi Mumbai?
Mumbai International Airport’s planned redevelopment of ageing Terminal 1 structures starting January 2027 requires moving displaced domestic flights into T2, forcing a 33% reduction in international flight capacity to Navi Mumbai. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) and global carriers strongly oppose this mandatory shift, citing operational inefficiencies, doubled ground setup costs, loss of connecting traffic, and concerns over historic slot allocations.
Where’s the last-mile of India’s LPG revolution?
Imagine the gas cylinder in your kitchen runs out tonight. For most households that use LPG, what happens next is almost automatic. You book a refill, pay when it arrives, and go back to cooking.
But that decision looks very different when you move down the income ladder. There is food to buy, rent to pay, medicines and school fees to cover. In fact, many would prefer to cook food using firewood, which is far cheaper than LPG. It can cook the night’s dinner without costing you anything right now.
That small decision, repeated across millions of kitchens, sits at the heart of India’s clean-cooking problem.
Over the last decade, India has worked hard to make LPG available to poorer households. Under the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana, more than 10.5 crore women have received gas connections. LPG coverage rose from 62% of households in 2016 to, on paper, more than 100% by 2024.
But owning a cylinder is not the same as cooking with it every day. An average Ujjwala household uses fewer than five cylinders a year , while a household cooking entirely on LPG would typically need 7-8. In many homes, the chulha comes back on for cooking.
In June, the government reduced the annual number of refills on which an Ujjwala household gets a ₹300 subsidy from 9 to 4 . As per the logic of the petroleum ministry, four refills are broadly what a typical household uses in a year. On those four, a 14.2 kg cylinder in Delhi costs ₹642 instead of ₹942. From the fifth refill onwards, the household pays full price.
There is a strange loop here. Poorer households use less LPG partly because refills are expensive. Now that low usage is also being used to decide how many refills should get support.
And the alternative is not harmless. Household air pollution from burning wood, dung and crop waste was linked to more than 9 lakh deaths in India in 2023.
Source
So why, after getting LPG into so many poorer homes, are so many families still lighting a chulha?
Three new studies from the Council on Energy, Environment and Water, or CEEW, help answer that question. Together, they surveyed more than 4,000 people across rural households , urban informal settlements and migrant workers . Our story is an amalgamation of their findings.
A cylinder isn’t a transition
The headline Ujjwala connection numbers can be misleading. Ujjwala made it easier to enter the LPG system, but after the first connection, gas becomes a purchase the family has to make again and again.
You can see this most clearly in rural India. Nearly 75% of the rural households CEEW surveyed across six states had used LPG in the previous three months. But fewer than a quarter cooked only with it. Half still relied mainly on firewood.
Source
These families hadn’t really substituted one fuel for another, but merely added LPG to a kitchen that continued burning wood and dung alongside it. Researchers call this fuel stacking .
From a rural household’s perspective, collecting firewood is far cheaper than the alternative. Think about when income arrives seasonally from a harvest, or unpredictably through daily-wage work. If the cylinder empties during a bad week , another LPG refill has to compete with groceries, medicines and other critical expenses.
That is also why 70% of the rural households surveyed that didn’t use LPG named refill cost as a major barrier. And these families stretch one cylinder for as long as possible. LPG might handle a quick meal while the chulha handles food that takes much longer.
Forget ordering another cylinder, even picking it up from a center adds to the cost. Only 47% of rural LPG users surveyed had cylinders delivered home. Everyone else had to travel to a distributor or pickup point , and that added to the bill beyond the cost of a refill.
Source
Close to the cylinder, outside the system
Now, how does the picture change when you move from a village to a city?
In a city, many poorer families live in what are called informal settlements . These are neighbourhoods that have grown outside the city’s formal housing system, where residents may not have recognised addresses, secure property rights or the same access to basic services as people in formal areas.
However, lighting a smoky chulha in a crowded neighbourhood is far less practical, and that is assuming the city is close to a forest area. LPG, meanwhile, is usually much easier to get.
CEEW surveyed households in these settlements across ten cities. Among them, 70% cooked only with LPG, compared with 23% in its rural sample. These are different groups, so this isn’t a clean urban-rural comparison, but a city does seemingly make access to gas easier.
Source
Even then, a connection doesn’t guarantee a full transition, and fuel stacking exists among poorer households here as well. Of the 10 cities, Ranchi had the highest rate of fuel stacking at around 50% despite also having the highest share of Ujjwala connections .
Source
Yet, affordability is only half the urban story.
About one in ten households got LPG without a formal connection through unauthorised dealers. Very simply, there is an additional cost to securing a cylinder connection informally. Formal users reported paying a median ₹850 for a standard 14.2 kg cylinder, while informal users paid ₹1,040.
Many of them had previously been refused a formal connection because they lacked required documents, including proof of current address. In fact, most of the formal users got their cylinders delivered home, but 79% of informal users did not enjoy the same privilege . Then, to serve the demand existing outside of the formal system, informal gas sellers stepped up. But they clearly will want extra for supplying a cylinder without the need of proper verification.
Half of the informal users also said they couldn’t afford the upfront cost. CEEW estimates that 13% of all households in its urban sample were eligible for Ujjwala but hadn’t enrolled.
What if your home keeps moving?
Every year sees millions of Indians move from their rural households to cities which house many of these jobs. So, many of these urban informal settlements are often inhabited by migrants, who primarily work in construction, sanitation and transport. CEEW surveyed them as well and found unique patterns in their fuel use.
Source
Around 79% of those who used gas relied on informal connections, while only around 4% were beneficiaries of the formal scheme. This tracks with the fact that migrants form a large chunk of informal workers in the Indian economy. There is no national data on how many migrants the scheme reaches, so that 4% isn’t a national figure. But perhaps, there is a reason for it.
You see, the LPG scheme was built around the idea of a settled household . Food subsidies faced a similar problem, which was tackled by the introduction of the “One Nation One Ration” Card . The newer version of the Ujjwala scheme similarly made LPG connections transferable, but getting into the formal system itself after moving still takes effort. And migrants without a proof of address are the most vulnerable to this reality.
There is also a marketing barrier, as migrants are often unaware that either such schemes exist, or that they’re eligible for it. This is not dissimilar to the finding of another CEEW study on stubble-burning, where farmers in Punjab were unaware of the state’s efforts to promote clean stubble disposal. We covered that report as well in the recent past.
Moreover, the opening hours of a gas distributor can overlap with the working day of a migrant. For a daily-wage worker, visiting a gas agency can mean losing income .
But even when migrants can get LPG, they often buy it differently. Informal buyers purchasing a full 14.2 kg cylinder paid around ₹71 per kilogram. But even among informal users, those buying smaller 5 kg cylinders paid around ₹100 per kilogram . The smaller purchase was the most expensive.
Source
But this is no irrational decision. A full cylinder may be better value, but that doesn’t help a daily-wage worker who doesn’t have a thousand rupees of cash on hand . It’s the same reason people buy shampoo in sachets instead of larger bottles, which are cheaper on a price-per-gram basis. That is why CEEW suggests testing pay-as-you-go “ LPG ATMs ”, where people could buy smaller amounts through formal channels instead of paying extra to informal sellers.
Who pays for the cleaner kitchen?
Across all three surveys, CEEW found the same broad affordability threshold: at ₹400 for a 14.2 kg cylinder, at least 80% of respondents said they would cook entirely with LPG.
It isn’t a magic number. The surveys were conducted between late 2024 and early 2025, before prices rose in April 2025 and again in 2026 . And ₹400 is what people said they would pay, not necessarily what they would spend when money gets tight.
Source
Still, it tells us something about the size of the affordability gap. An Ujjwala household today pays ₹642 for its first four refills and ₹942 after that. Getting anywhere close to ₹400 would mean somebody else absorbing much, much more of the cost.
India imports above 60% of the LPG it consumes, much of it from the Persian Gulf and through the Strait of Hormuz. When international prices rise sharply, the government doesn’t pass the entire increase on to households. State-owned oil marketing companies can instead sell domestic LPG below its market-linked cost, creating what is called an under-recovery .
This year’s West Asia crisis made under-recoveries unusually large. Saudi Aramco’s LPG benchmark rose about 46% between late February and early June. The petroleum ministry said the cost of supplying a domestic cylinder crossed ₹1,600 , while a regular consumer in Delhi pays ₹942. Cumulative under-recoveries on household LPG had reached ~₹60,000 crore by the end of FY26. Even the current price of ₹942 doesn’t cover the full market cost, and the difference eventually sits with the household, the government or the oil companies.
One may think of ₹1,600 as an exceptional figure in a strange time, which will revert to the mean once the crisis ends. But at this point, the situation in West Asia has itself become highly normalized, and so have the massive under-recoveries.
Conclusion
That brings us back to the loop we started with.
There is an understandable fiscal logic behind the four-cylinder rule. But the clean-cooking logic points the other way. The fifth, sixth and seventh cylinders are precisely the ones needed to move from occasionally using LPG to cooking with it all the time.
For one household, a cheaper cylinder might be enough. Another needs a smaller payment at one time. Another needs easier access to the formal system. There is an overlap between these household types — perhaps, the same person has experienced each issue that plagues each set of consumers. But it is clear that there is no single fix to all their problems anyway.
India’s first clean-cooking challenge was relatively easy to measure: get LPG connections into homes that had never had them. But now, you need to get them to refill more, and different sections of society have different (if not conflicting) constraints in that regard. This policy challenge only gets harder as the Strait of Hormuz crisis gets prolonged. And no policy solution is any less costly than the other.
Why are airlines opposing the move from Mumbai to Navi Mumbai?
If you’ve flown through Mumbai’s Terminal 1, you may have felt it could do with a makeover. Beside the city’s own T2 or Bengaluru’s newer terminal, it feels dated for an airport serving India’s financial capital.
The problems go beyond appearances. Mumbai International Airport Ltd, or MIAL, the airport’s operator, has cited structural distress in older buildings and difficulties separating arriving and departing passengers in its submissions to AERA , the airport tariff regulator. But rebuilding a busy terminal requires somewhere else to put its flights.
MIAL’s case to AREA on the issue
In January 2025, MIAL announced redevelopment starting that November , with T2 and Navi Mumbai absorbing the displaced traffic. That plan slipped because, according to the operator, Navi Mumbai wasn’t ready. By December, redevelopment was reportedly deferred to 2030 . The latest timetable brings the first phase forward to January 2027, with commissioning expected in 2029–30.
T1 won’t shut entirely at once . The first phase covers T1B’s north section, accounting for roughly one-third of T1’s capacity. Flights using the other sections can continue operating there for now.
The reported reshuffle would move the displaced domestic flights into T2, which already handles both domestic and international services. To make room, roughly one-third of international operations would move from T2 to Navi Mumbai. International airlines are therefore being asked to change airports because a largely domestic terminal is being rebuilt.
That is where the International Air Transport Association, or IATA, objects . Its complaint concerns the proposed relocation of international passenger and cargo operations to Navi Mumbai. It questions the consultation, whether the new airport is even ready and capable for those operations and what’s the basis of this share of flights to move there.
A flight comes with baggage
To understand those objections, consider what an airline actually has to move.
An international carrier with a modest Mumbai schedule could need separate ground teams, handling contracts, equipment and supervision if it splits operations between two airports. It hasn’t necessarily gained passengers, but it may have almost doubled its set of fixed costs.
Air France-KLM makes this point . It opposes splitting passenger operations, although it would consider moving them entirely if capacity at the existing airport became unworkable.
Air France-KLM’s General Manager for Middle East & India
Connections add another complication. If a feeder flight arrives at Mumbai and the onward international service departs from Navi Mumbai, the passenger now needs a transfer. An itinerary that previously worked may become unattractive or impractical.
There is also the aircraft itself. A widebody needs suitable parking, ground equipment and maintenance support authorised for its type. IATA is seeking clarity on those arrangements, alongside catering and crew logistics. These are questions about readiness for particular operations; they do not establish that Navi Mumbai is generally unsafe or incapable.
The impact will consequently vary by airline. A carrier with a large local operation may have more flexibility than one running a handful of tightly timed services. An equal percentage cut does not necessarily mean an equal burden.
Who owns the clock?
These operational concerns explain why airlines care so much about retaining their airport slots.
A slot is permission to use the airport infrastructure needed to arrive or depart at a particular time. Runways, gates, aircraft stands and terminal facilities all determine how many flights an airport can accommodate.
For airlines, the timing matters enormously. A commercially useful slot lets them coordinate connecting flights, aircraft rotations and crew schedules. Losing it can disrupt much more than a single departure.
What is a slot?
Under the Ministry of Civil Aviation’s slot guidelines , an airport-level committee comprising the operator, an Airports Authority of India air-navigation representative and DGCA assesses capacity. Airlines can comment before the findings and final capacity are published. The airport’s designated coordinator then allocates slots within those limits.
Airlines have conditional priority to retain slots from the previous equivalent season, known as historic precedence. Normally, this requires using a series of slots at least 80% of the time. The guidelines also require early consultation before capacity reductions. Reductions that cannot accommodate established historic slots should be avoided except in the most exceptional circumstances, and allocations must be neutral, transparent and non-discriminatory.
Historic slots must not be accommodate expect in most exceptional cases
Applied here, the question is how the demonstrated loss of T1 capacity translates into the proposed cuts to international operations.
MIAL says redevelopment is included in AERA’s tariff order. But AERA’s assessment of investment and airport charges does not settle which airline should give up which flight.
The extent of consultation remains disputed too. IATA’s own submission acknowledges attending a March 2024 meeting on MIAL’s capital plans. Discussing a terminal rebuild, however, is different from agreeing on the flights, facilities and timetable for relocation.
MIAL has promised to honour historic slots when T1 returns. That addresses longer-term access. Airlines still need clarity on how the smaller pool of capacity will be shared during construction.
Make room, with a plan
That temporary allocation could also shape how Mumbai’s two airports develop. Both share the same owner, so shifting flights helps build business at Navi Mumbai. Reports suggest a longer-term ambition to develop it as an international connecting hub , though that remains a reported strategy.
The immediate priority is making the transition workable. In our view, the operator needs to show how the proposed reshuffle limits avoidable disruption.
That means publishing the capacity lost at each construction stage and comparing alternatives. Could some airlines move their entire operation voluntarily? Could connected groups of flights move together? Would those options work better than dividing every carrier’s schedule?
Once the allocation is worked out, the move itself needs preparation. Nobody has to reinvent the wheel here. The industry already has a process for such transitions: Operational Readiness and Airport Transfer, or ORAT . It combines planning, staff training and operational trials to establish whether facilities and people can handle the intended services. IATA’s guidance calls for relocation arrangements developed with airlines and grounded in capacity analysis.
None of this guarantees every airline its preferred outcome. Some disruption may be unavoidable, and postponing necessary work carries costs too. There are no easy answers here, only compromises. Who compromises the most remains to be seen.

Markets lately have been unsettling.
If you track only Indian markets, you already know the story. The Nifty is down about 14% this year, and an SIP wouldn’t have helped the two-year negative return. Foreign investors keep selling, and the rupee keeps slipping.
Look beyond India, and it’s no calmer. The US stocks keep climbing, almost as if they haven’t noticed what’s going on around them. Bond yields are rising across the world, meaning governments and companies now pay more to borrow, with repercussions of their own. Even gold and silver, the stars of 2025, have come off their highs.
It’s natural to wonder whether a bigger fall is coming, if not in India then abroad, and what you should do with your money. Honestly, nobody can answer that with confidence. The only thing anyone can say is that if you are a long-term investor, this too shall pass. Beyond that, it’s guesswork.
But finance has a product for every anxiety. And for times like these, there is one with a very reassuring name: the All Weather portfolio, created by Ray Dalio and his team at Bridgewater. A simplified version for individual investors later became known as the All Seasons portfolio.
Let’s see what it is, how it has done, and whether it works for an Indian investor.
What is the All Weather portfolio?
Back in the late 1980s, Ray Dalio, founder of Bridgewater, began thinking about a simple question: Can I build a portfolio that does fine no matter what happens, without having to guess what happens next? In 1996, Bridgewater launched the All Weather strategy, initially for Dalio’s own trust assets.
His entire model rests on one idea: what surprise can the market throw at you next? And according to him, most surprises are about just two things: how fast the economy grows and how fast inflation in the country rises.
Each can turn out higher or lower than people expected. That gives you four kinds of weather.
From Bridgewater’s All Weather framework . These are tendencies, not rules.
Here’s what that means in plain words:
Economy booming: companies earn more, so stocks do well. Oil and metals do well, too, because demand goes up.
Economy slowing: interest rates usually come down; this creates demand for the existing higher interest bonds, which pushes up government bond prices. Stocks suffer.
Inflation rising fast : your money buys less every month, so gold and commodities shine.
Inflation cooling: generally helps bonds; stocks can benefit too, as long as economic growth doesn’t weaken sharply.
Every asset has a season it loves, and a season it hates. Not one of them does well in all four. This is a simplistic explanation, and things can be much more complex than what is shown here, but let’s sit with this idea for some time.
So Dalio thought, if I can’t know which season comes next, why not own something for every season?
The simplified portfolio he later shared with Tony Robbins (an American author) had 30% in stocks, 40% in long-term government bonds, 15% in medium-term government bonds (bonds, again), 7.5% in gold, and 7.5% in commodities (a broad basket such as oil, metals and agricultural commodities; the original literature does not clearly specify the exact basket).
Now, if you love equities, the moment you see 55% in bonds, you’d ask: Will this even make money? Fair question. Here’s how it did in the US.
Between 1984 and 2013, it gave about 9.7% a year, while the S&P 500 generated about 11%.
So no, it didn’t beat the stock market. But it got there with far less drama.
Volatility, as you know, is a measure of risk. The All Seasons portfolio's volatility was just 7.6% — roughly half the ~15% volatility typically associated with US equities. That’s the interesting part.
Remember, the current times are different. The portfolio data we saw was from an era when interest rates kept falling, and bond prices rose (remember, interest rates and bonds move in opposite directions?), which is the best possible weather for bonds. Today, it feels different.
Also, look at how this portfolio did when markets were crashing. I also compared with a 60:40 (equity:debt) portfolio, a popular investing strategy, for perspective.
2008 All Weather return as reported by Tony Robbins and reviewed by Ben Carlson. The 2022 All Weather figure is our estimate. The 60/40 is the Vanguard Balanced Index Fund. S&P 500 figures are calendar-year total returns.
See, in 2008, it did far better than even a balanced 60/40 portfolio, losing about 4% when the 60/40 lost 22%. Good enough.
But in 2022, when stocks and bonds fell together, it did about as badly as an all-equity portfolio. Which brings us to the two catches of Dalio’s mix of assets.
First, things can be different. In 2022, stocks and bonds fell together, which usually doesn't happen. Check this chart from Morningstar . The ‘All Weather’ portfolio can fail in these situations.
The second catch is you. When markets are in a bull market, this portfolio will feel painfully slow, and your friend who has higher equity will look like a genius. That’s exactly when most people give up on it. A portfolio works only if you can sit through it.
How would it have done in India?
So we tried the same recipe with Indian ingredients. Here’s what our Indian All Weather portfolio looks like.
We moved the 7.5% in commodities into gold, since broad commodity funds aren’t really available to Indian retail investors.
And here’s how it did against Indian stocks and a regular 60:40 portfolio.
In India, too, over the last 15 years, All Weather earned almost as much as a regular 60:40 portfolio, with about half the swings and much smaller falls. It lags when markets are booming, but holds up far better when they crash.
Take this year: the 60:40 is in the red, while All Weather is still up, mostly thanks to gold.
What do you do with all this?
So, does the All Weather portfolio actually work? Historically, mostly yes - if by “working” you mean making the bad years less painful, not beating equities every year. Historically, that is largely what it did.
But don’t treat Dalio’s 30/40/15/7.5/7.5 as some proven formula. Dalio shared it, and Tony Robbins, an American author, made it famous. There is no formal academic study on this portfolio. Besides, there’s no reason to assume the next 15 years will look like the last 15.
So what’s the real lesson here? Diversification. Dalio’s mix is just one way of doing it. The point is to own different things that don’t all fall at the same time, and that matters most in times like these.
And for an Indian investor, there’s one big thing missing from Dalio’s mix: global stocks. When India is under stress, the rupee often weakens. That helps global investments when their returns are converted back to rupees. And global doesn’t just mean just the US.
Now, if you really don’t know where to invest in the current markets, the outlook looks bleak, and you’re tired of people telling you this is the best time to start a equity SIP, one practical option is a multi-asset allocation fund.
These funds spread your money across equity, debt, and gold, and some also invest abroad. They rebalance for you, too, so you don’t have to do a thing.
There are two kinds:
Some multi-asset funds actively change the mix between equity, debt, gold and other assets. Examples include ICICI Prudential Multi-Asset Fund, DSP Multi Asset Allocation Fund, SBI Multi Asset Allocation Fund and Nippon India Multi Asset Allocation Fund.
Others follow a more predefined, rule-based mix and largely use index funds or ETFs. Examples include Zerodha Multi Asset Passive FoF and ICICI Prudential Passive Multi-Asset FoF.
Before picking one, just check the mix. Two multi-asset funds can behave very differently.
An all-weather portfolio is simply a diversified portfolio built so you don’t have to bet on what happens next. No portfolio works in every kind of weather. The goal is to own one you can stick with when the weather changes.

Nearly two decades ago, two researchers at Duke University, a well-known university in the US, tried an unusual experiment. They used software to study emotions in executives’ voices across 1,647 earnings calls from 691 companies in 2007. An earnings call is a discussion where a company’s leaders explain its latest results and answer questions from analysts and investors.
The researchers wanted to see whether the way a CEO or CFO sounded could tell us something about the company. They found links between these voice signals, how the business performed later and how its shares performed.
Since then, some investors have explored using voice analysis to help make decisions. Imagine looking for clues even in a slight hesitation in someone’s voice. Researchers are still studying how reliable these signals are, but it shows how closely investors follow management when results come out.
Today, we can explore management commentary with AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. Give them the latest earnings-call transcript alongside a few earlier ones, and we can start checking what management promised, what it delivered and what it expects next. We will come back to this later.
With results season getting underway, there is a good opportunity to learn fundamental analysis by actually doing it. Fundamental analysis means studying a company’s business, finances and prospects. Once results are published, the same public filing is available to large institutions and individual investors.
Reading the results, forming a view and observing the market’s response brings that learning together. A rising or falling share price does not automatically make an analysis right or wrong, but the difference between business performance and market reaction gives us something more to investigate. Before exploring management’s explanation, it helps to understand the numbers being discussed. Let us begin with TCS.
Making sense of TCS’s quarter
TCS is one of India’s biggest IT companies and usually announces its results early in the season. On October 8, it published its results for the three months from July to September.
Above are TCS’s quarterly results on Tijori . Each column covers three months, and the figures are in ₹ crore. These are consolidated results, which include TCS and the companies it controls, called subsidiaries.
Before comparing the quarters, let us understand what each row means.
Net sales: The money TCS earned from selling its services and products. No expenses have been deducted yet.
Operating expenses: The everyday costs of running the business, such as salaries.
Operating profit: What remains after subtracting these everyday costs from sales. In this table, depreciation is subtracted further down.
Other income: Money earned outside the main business, such as interest on investments.
Interest: What TCS pays for borrowing money.
PBDT: Profit before depreciation and tax. It includes other income and deducts interest and any other applicable charges.
Depreciation and amortization: Computers and software last several years, so their cost is spread across those years instead of being counted all at once.
Profit before tax: The profit left before subtracting income tax.
Tax: The income-tax expense recorded for the quarter.
Profit after tax: The profit left after subtracting tax.
Exceptional items: Unusual gains or costs shown separately, such as a gain from selling a building or a charge for closing a business unit. These can temporarily lift or reduce profit, so it helps to understand what caused them and whether they could happen again. They may already be included in the profit figures above.
Net profit: Some subsidiaries have other owners too. Their share of the profit is removed, leaving the profit belonging to TCS shareholders.
EPS: Earnings per share. It shows how much profit belongs to each share, not how much cash shareholders receive.
Operating profit margin: How much operating profit remains from every ₹100 of sales.
Net profit margin: How much finally remains as net profit from every ₹100 of sales.
Now let us read the numbers together. TCS earned ₹73,188 crore in sales, also called revenue or the “top line” because it appears at the top of the statement. Look one column to the left: sales were ₹72,275 crore in June. That means they grew about 1.3% quarter-on-quarter, or QoQ, which compares the latest quarter with the previous one.
Next, look at September last year, when sales were ₹65,799 crore. Against that, sales grew about 11.2% year-on-year, or YoY. Together, these comparisons tell us that TCS is earning considerably more than a year ago, while its increase over the previous quarter is smaller.
Both comparisons matter, especially when a business has seasonal patterns. An air-conditioner company may sell more during summer than during the monsoon. A QoQ fall would not necessarily mean it was struggling. YoY compares similar seasons, while QoQ helps us follow more recent changes.
For TCS, currency adds another layer. Much of its revenue comes from clients outside India. When that revenue is converted into rupees, exchange-rate changes can make it look bigger or smaller. After removing currency effects, sales grew 0.5% over the previous quarter, compared with 1.3% in rupees. So a sizable part of the reported growth came from currency movements, rather than growth in the business itself.
But earning more does not automatically mean keeping more. Operating expenses also increased, though slightly slower than sales. Tijori’s operating profit margin was about 26%, almost unchanged from June, but below the 27% of a year earlier. About ₹26 remained from every ₹100 of sales before depreciation, interest and tax.
TCS calculates its own operating margin after also subtracting depreciation and amortization, which is why it is lower, at 24%. We should use the same measure when comparing quarters.
Finally, net profit was ₹13,884 crore, up about 4% QoQ and 15% YoY. Notice the exceptional items in earlier quarters, though. These can make comparisons look stronger or weaker, so their explanation matters before we attribute all the profit growth to better business performance.
We now have a first impression: sales and net profit increased, while margins were broadly steady compared with June and lower than a year ago. The numbers give us a first impression of how the business is doing. But how has that performance been reflected in its share price? Putting quarterly results alongside a chart showing the stock price helps us see where the two move together and where they differ. Let us look at TCS over several quarters.
Putting the results next to the share price
The chart below brings those two pieces together: how TCS’s quarterly numbers changed and how its stock moved over the same period.
Each candle shows one week of trading. Green candles show weeks when the stock closed higher than it opened, while red candles show weeks when it closed lower. The dotted lines mark results announcements, and the boxes show revenue and profit growth compared with the previous quarter and the same quarter last year.
Look at January 2026. Revenue increased, but profit fell both QoQ and YoY. The stock declined sharply in the weeks that followed. In April, the numbers improved, but the recovery in the share price did not last. Stronger results alone were not enough to reverse the falling price trend.
Was this weakness specific to TCS, or were other IT companies showing a similar pattern? HCLTech, which announced its latest results on October 12, gives us another business to compare.
This chart follows the same format: HCLTech’s weekly price movement below, quarterly revenue and profit growth in the text boxes, and dotted lines marking the announcement dates. Reading both charts together helps us spot where the companies’ performance was similar and where it differed.
In January 2026, HCL Tech also reported higher revenue but lower profit, both QoQ and YoY. Its stock subsequently fell too. Around the October 2025 announcements, both stocks showed some stability followed by a recovery, although their profit growth differed.
Comparing companies from the same sector helps us explore whether a change is specific to one business or more widespread. If several companies report similar improvements or difficulties, there may be an industry trend worth investigating. Two companies give us a starting point, but we need more peers to build that picture.
More recently, both companies reported higher revenue and profit, both QoQ and YoY, in their April and October 2026 results. These are encouraging numbers, but we still need to understand what drove them. Was the improvement coming from more business, lower costs or the absence of a charge that had reduced an earlier quarter’s profit? And can it continue?
The charts give us patterns to investigate, rather than proof that a particular result caused a price move. To understand the explanation behind the numbers, let us turn to management’s discussion of the quarter.
Listening to the people running the business
Many listed companies hold an earnings conference call, often called a “concall”, around the time they announce their results. TCS and HCL Tech did so for their latest Q2 results too. On these calls, management explains the quarter and takes questions from analysts and investors. Analysts study companies for a living, and they may ask about the same things we noticed: rising costs, slower growth or whether an improvement can last.
Above is the management commentary section on TCS’s results page , where the archived earnings call is available to listen to.
HCL Tech’s earnings-call recordings, transcripts and investor presentations are available through its Investor Relations page . A transcript is simply a written record of the discussion, which can be downloaded and read.
These calls can be long and full of unfamiliar terms. To make them easier to follow, we uploaded both companies’ July–September 2026 transcripts to ChatGPT and asked:
“Can you go through both HCL Tech and TCS earnings-call transcripts and let me know what the commentary is around revenue, profits, issues and future outlook?”
Above are the attached transcripts, our prompt and the beginning of the response. Both cover Q2 FY27, or July–September 2026, so we are comparing what management said about the same three months.
The response brings out a difference worth exploring. It describes HCL Tech as seeing stronger revenue growth and improving margins, while TCS is seeing a gradual recovery in demand and spending more to prepare for future growth. It also notes that both are optimistic about AI, without suggesting that overall IT spending has fully recovered.
This adds context to the quarterly numbers. We can start understanding what helped profits, what held them back and what management believes could improve next. A useful follow-up is: “Based on this discussion, what should I check in the next quarterly results?” That gives us specific developments to follow over time.
If finding transcripts and uploading them sounds like homework, our Markets team at Zerodha has you covered. The Chatter breaks down company results and management commentary in simple language.
The same exercise can be done with Claude, Gemini or another AI tool that accepts documents. Adding earlier calls from the same company can also help compare previous targets with actual delivery.
We have now read the numbers, studied the charts and explored the explanation behind them. Let us put those pieces together and follow the exercise through with an initial view.
Putting the learning into practice
At the start, we said results season is a good time to practice fundamental analysis. With two IT giants having announced their results, it is only fair to take that practice a step further and explain what I make of the information. Below is how IT has performed YTD.
My reading is that TCS and HCL Tech are worth a closer look. Both stocks have been weak, and their valuations have come down. TCS’s P/E is around 15, compared with roughly 27 at the end of FY25. HCL Tech’s is around 18.5, compared with about 25 then. P/E tells us how much investors pay for every ₹1 of annual earnings per share.
Their September-quarter results add to the interest. TCS’s revenue grew 11.2% YoY and net profit rose 15%. HCL Tech’s revenue grew 11.5% and net profit increased 21.2%. Both earned more revenue and profit than in the same quarter last year.
AI threatens some existing services, but it is also creating new business. HCL Tech’s advanced AI revenue reached $219 million for the quarter, up 78% YoY in constant currency. TCS reported annualized AI revenue of $3.1 billion. These numbers show that both companies are finding business opportunities in AI.
TCS has also proposed acquiring MHP, Porsche’s Germany-based technology and management consulting business. This would expand its presence among European automotive and manufacturing clients. The move suggests a willingness to take long-term bets and build client relationships despite current uncertainty.
New contracts are another encouraging sign. TCS reported total contract value of $9.6 billion, while HCL Tech reported $3.3 billion in new deal bookings. These represent work signed that can generate revenue as it is delivered. From here, the important things to follow are whether these contracts translate into sales growth, whether margins improve and whether other IT companies report similar progress.
Different readers may reach different conclusions from the same information. Forming a view gives us something to revisit when the next results arrive. If the business develops as expected, we can examine what we understood correctly. If it does not, we can investigate what we missed or what changed. Following that process over several quarters is how we get better at reading a business.
Closing Bell
Results season brings a fresh set of numbers and explanations from businesses every quarter. Reading them together, comparing companies and following changes over time helps turn financial terms into an understanding of how businesses work.
One quarter may look strong because of a temporary benefit. Another may look weak because the company is spending on future growth. The learning comes from looking beyond the headline and following whether those explanations hold up in later quarters.

Whether it is the EMI on your home loan or the interest on your fixed deposit, most interest rates in the country trace back to one number: the repo rate. It is one of the biggest forces influencing interest rates across the country, and the RBI sets this rate based on the state of the economy.
When it moves, everything else follows. When the RBI raises it, loans get expensive and you earn more on your fixed deposits. When the repo rate is cut, both loan rates and fixed deposit rates fall.
In the last year and a half, the repo rate has been falling. It was at 6.5% at the start of 2025. By December 2025, it had come down to 5.25%, and it has stayed there through 2026. Accordingly, banks have been lowering FD rates. If you recently renewed an FD, you have probably felt it.
But you know what? The rates on Post Office schemes did not budge. Returns from schemes such as Time Deposits and National Savings Certificates have remained unchanged since January 2024.
Time Deposit rates (6.9%, 7.0%, 7.1%, 7.5% for the 1, 2, 3, and 5-year tenures, respectively) have been the same since 1 January 2024. NSC has been at 7.7% since April 2023.
If you think about it, this is actually a bit odd. Post Office schemes carry a full government guarantee. On the other hand, banks give you only ₹5 lakh of deposit insurance through DICGC (Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation).
Going by the basic rule of risk and reward, the riskier option should pay more. Banks should be offering higher rates than the Post Office, not the other way around. And yet, look at the numbers.
Small finance banks would offer higher rates, but among the large banks compared to PO schemes, the latter wins. Clearly.
So the decision looks easy. Higher rate & government guarantee; just go to the Post Office, fill out the form, done.
Except, it’s not.
There are three things you need to look at before you compare any two fixed-income products: how the interest compounds, how the interest is paid out to you, and how much of it the government takes as tax. Each one of these can change who wins.
Factor one: how the interest compounds
When a bank says your FD earns 7.5%, it is natural to think your ₹1 lakh would earn about ₹7,500 in the first year.
But bank deposits are usually quarterly compounded. That means the interest on your FD is calculated every three months at the rate of 7.5% per annum. Each quarter, that interest gets added to your principal, and the next quarter you earn interest on a slightly bigger amount. So you end up earning a little more than ₹7,500 in the year 1 (about ₹7,714).
Most Post Office schemes also work on quarterly compounding. But NSC, one of the most popular and highest-return Post Office schemes, compounds only once a year.
Say a small finance bank is offering an FD at 7.6% (quarterly compounding) and NSC at 7.7% (annual compounding). At the end of five years, what you earn on the FD at 7.6% would actually be slightly more than what you get from NSC at 7.7%.
The difference may not be significant, but the point is that a lower rate that compounds more often can match or beat a higher rate that compounds less often. Do not just go by the headline rate.
Factor two: how the interest is paid
This one gets almost no attention.
When you put money in a cumulative bank FD, the interest stays inside the deposit until it matures. And the interest already earned keeps earning more interest
A Post Office Time Deposit works differently. It calculates interest the same way. But once a year, it takes that interest out and credits it into your savings account.
Why does this matter? Because that interest sitting in a savings account earns just 4%, instead of 7.5% if it had stayed in the deposit.
So when you are comparing Post Office Time Deposits and FDs, keep this point in mind.
Factor three: tax
This is the biggest one. It can flip the winner entirely.
Interest from bank FDs, Post Office Time Deposits, and NSC is added to your income and taxed at your slab rate every year.
If you are in the 30% bracket (plus 4% cess), out of every ₹100 of interest you earn, about ₹31 goes to the government.
The section 80C tax benefit extended for Post Office schemes, as per the old tax regime, is not available here.
See the table below for what post-tax returns actually look like at the 30% slab.
The interest you earn becomes so low that it hardly beats the country's inflation rate.
This is where arbitrage funds come in. I have explained what arbitrage funds are here . They do have exposure to equity markets and do not come with a guaranteed return, but they are one of the less risky mutual fund categories out there.
It behaves like a debt product, but is taxed like an equity product.
If you hold for more than 12 months, your gains are taxed at just 12.5% (plus cess), and the first ₹1.25 lakh of such gains per year is completely tax-free. Compare that to the 30% you pay on FD interest. That is the difference.
For example, if an arbitrage fund gives you about 6% after tax, a fixed deposit or term deposit would need to offer you about 8.7% before tax to match that at the 30% slab. That’s a big difference in the fixed income space.
We also went back to 2013 and checked how arbitrage funds actually did against the Post Office TD rates available at the same time.
The interesting bit was that before tax, Post Office Time Deposits often looked better. But after tax, arbitrage funds came out ahead in most 1, 2, and 3-year periods for someone in the 30% tax bracket.
For a five-year tenure, arbitrage funds remained competitive with NSC scheme. NSC had one big advantage: you knew your return from day one, which is not the case with mutual funds.
A big reason was the tax. Time Deposit interest gets taxed at your slab rate every year, while arbitrage funds get equity taxation if you hold them for more than 12 months.
So, what to choose?
While Post Office schemes, especially the Time Deposits across different tenures, look superior on the face of it compared to bank FDs, the quarterly compounding and cumulative nature of bank fixed deposits can narrow the gap considerably.
On top of that, Post Office schemes come with less ease of access and stricter withdrawal restrictions, so when you factor those in, bank FDs may actually edge out.
If you are in a higher tax bracket and can lock your money away for five years, NSC still looks like a good option. Higher rate, interest stays invested until maturity, return locked on day one. Arbitrage funds are not a bad choice either. Going by the past, arbitrage funds have roughly matched NSC after tax at the 30% slab, but NSC gives you certainty.
For tenures of 1-3 years, for investors in the highest tax bracket, our historical comparison shows that arbitrage funds become particularly competitive; beyond 12 months, their tax treatment becomes especially favorable.
And if you are looking at debt mutual funds, the same rule applies: always check the post-tax expected return, not just the headline number. Since April 2023, all debt fund gains are taxed at your slab rate, so the tax advantage that debt funds once had is gone.
The headline rate is what you see. But the rate that matters is the one that lands in your pocket after compounding, payout structure, and tax have had their say. Those three things are never printed on the brochure upfront, and they can completely change the answer.
Why are Post Office rates still high when FD rates are falling?
The government is supposed to follow a formula while setting small savings rates. It looks at government bond yields and generally adds a small extra return on top. That extra return could partly be to compensate for the lower flexibility of these post office schemes.
That said, several small-savings schemes are paying more than this formula would suggest because the government decided to keep the rates unchanged for reasons we may not fully understand.
Of all schemes, NSC currently has the highest premium relative to the formula's suggested rate. PPF, on the other hand, is roughly in line with the formula.

Technical versus fundamental analysis is one of the longest-running debates in the stock market. Spend enough time around investors and traders, and you will hear someone explain why their approach works and why the other one is a waste of time. :)
Rakesh Jhunjhunwala had a more practical way of looking at it. In a 2009 interview, he explained that trading helped him generate money to invest. When studying a business, he looked at its growth opportunities, competitive strengths and the quality of its profits. When trading, he studied price movements.
But the two were connected. He explained that a favourable view of the business became more convincing when the price began moving in line with it. That could give him greater confidence to hold or add to an investment. At the same time, a rising price alone was not enough for him to build a portfolio.
This is where the debate becomes interesting. A stock can break above an earlier high and still reverse. A company can earn more each year without its share price rising much. Sometimes, improving business numbers and price movements point in the same direction. Let us look at three Indian companies to understand these situations better.
Adani Total Gas: When a technical breakout fails
A stock struggles to cross an earlier high. Then, when it finally breaks through, it does so with a large green candle and a sharp increase in trading volume. For someone using technical analysis, this can look like a promising setup.
Adani Total Gas offered such a setup in September 2025. After remaining below its June high of ₹720 for roughly three months, the stock crossed that level and closed around ₹780 on September 22.
The image above shows the price candles and trading volume beneath them. The dotted line marks the previous ₹720 high. On the right, two unusually tall volume bars accompany the sharp rise in price, with the large green candle breaking through the earlier high. On the breakout day, volume was nearly 27 times its average over the preceding 20 trading sessions.
The price had crossed its previous high, and strong trading activity supported the move. But it failed to sustain the breakout. The stock quickly slipped below ₹720 and continued falling over the following months.
The chart above shows the aftermath. From around ₹780 on the breakout day, the stock fell towards ₹520 by February 2026, a decline of roughly 33%. Someone who invested ₹1 lakh at ₹780 and held through that fall would have seen it shrink to around ₹67,000, excluding costs.
Without a stop-loss or another exit rule, this would have been a painful trade. A stop-loss is a pre-decided price at which a trader exits if the trade moves against them. It could have limited the loss here, although a sudden price gap can mean selling below the intended exit price.
The setup had an upward breakout and unusually strong volume. Yet the expected rise did not follow. Technical analysis can give us reasons to enter a trade, but even a convincing signal can sometimes fail. Deciding what to do when that happens is part of the approach too.
That said, looking at the business comes with its own challenges too. You can have good reasons to own a company and still wait years for its share price to reward you. Hindustan Unilever offers an example.
Hindustan Unilever: When growing earnings do not lift the stock
Surf Excel, Dove, Lifebuoy and several other HUL brands are familiar names in Indian households. People buy these products regularly, and the company has an established business serving that demand. For a fundamental investor studying its brands, profits and growth opportunities, there is plenty to look at.
Its earnings also made progress. Between FY2020 and FY2024, earnings per share rose from around ₹31 to ₹43, an increase of roughly 38%. Earnings per share, or EPS, is the company’s profit attributable to each share. A rising EPS means the business is earning more for each share an investor owns.
The chart above shows the share price in the upper panel, with each candle representing one month. The green column bars below show annual earnings per share. Notice how earnings increased over the years, while the share price went through several rallies and falls without delivering a similar sustained rise. The business was earning more, but owning its shares did not reward investors in the same proportion.
This can be frustrating. You follow the company, see its earnings improve and feel that your understanding of the business is being proved right. Yet your investment does not move as you expected. HUL paid dividends too, which added to returns and are not shown in the price candles.
Part of the explanation lies in the price investors are willing to pay for those earnings. Imagine a company earning ₹10 per share, with its stock trading at ₹500. Investors are paying ₹50 for every ₹1 of annual earnings. Later, earnings rise to ₹14 per share, but investors are willing to pay only ₹35 for every ₹1 of earnings. The share price would then be ₹490. Earnings have grown by 40%, but the stock is slightly lower.
These numbers are illustrative, but they show why growing profits do not automatically produce growing share prices. The price paid at the beginning matters, as do the expectations built into it. Valuation is therefore part of fundamental analysis, alongside understanding the business.
HUL’s example shows the limitation of relying on earnings growth alone. You can correctly identify a business making progress and still face years of disappointing share-price performance.
Growing earnings gave HUL’s investors something positive to follow, but the share price did not keep pace. MTAR Technologies offers a different situation, where a sharp improvement in earnings appeared alongside a price breakout.
MTAR Technologies: When technical and fundamental analysis come together
Earlier, we saw a breakout that failed despite strong trading volume. We also saw growing earnings that did not translate into similar share-price gains. The chart below brings MTAR’s price movements and quarterly earnings together.
The image above shows weekly price candles at the top, trading volume in the middle and quarterly EPS (thick green bars) below. The purple dotted line marks MTAR’s September 2023 high of around ₹2,920. After remaining below that level for more than two years, the stock closed around ₹3,086 in the week beginning January 26, 2026, breaking above its earlier high.
Now look at the EPS bars. Earnings jumped from ₹1.38 per share in September 2025 to ₹11.28 in December, roughly an eightfold increase over the preceding quarter. Compared with December 2024, EPS had more than doubled. The December results were announced on January 29, during the same week as the closing breakout.
The price suggested that the market was becoming more optimistic about MTAR’s prospects. The earnings jump gave that optimism something concrete to rest on. To understand what might be changing, an investor could also examine the company’s customers and orders.
MTAR manufactures precision components and assemblies. One of its important customers is Bloom Energy, a US company that makes fuel-cell systems to generate electricity. In July 2025, Bloom announced that it would supply power systems to selected Oracle data centres in the US, supporting demand for AI and cloud computing. For MTAR, growing demand for its customer’s equipment offered a possible source of additional business.
That possibility came with actual orders. In September 2025, MTAR disclosed orders worth around ₹386 crore from Bloom, scheduled for execution by March and June 2026. These developments were public before the January breakout and gave investors a business reason to follow the stock.
But one strong quarter does not establish a lasting improvement. The next thing to watch was whether earnings would remain high and whether the price would sustain its breakout.
The chart above shows what followed. EPS increased further to ₹14.40 in March 2026 and ₹16.33 in June. The December jump was followed by two quarters of even higher earnings, adding evidence that the improvement was continuing as those results became public.
The share price also rose substantially. By October 5, 2026, it was around ₹7,649, approximately 162% above the weekly breakout close of ₹3,086. A ₹1 lakh investment at that closing price would have grown to around ₹2.62 lakh, excluding costs. But the candles show sharp falls along the way too. Holding through the rally would have been harder than the final return makes it look.
In this case, the two approaches complemented each other. The breakout showed strength in the price, while customer developments, fresh orders and stronger earnings helped explain what might be driving it. Later results gave investors more information to judge whether that improvement was continuing.
Closing Bell
A technical analyst could show us plenty of breakouts that worked beautifully. A fundamental investor could point to businesses that became multibaggers. Both would have good reasons to believe in their approach. :)
These examples do not settle that debate. One failed breakout does not make technical analysis useless, just as a period of weak share-price returns does not make studying a business pointless. And MTAR’s rally alone does not prove that combining the two will always work.
But it does show how a practical approach to picking stocks could draw on both. Improving business numbers can give us a reason to pay attention, while price movements can show whether the market is beginning to share that interest. A stock gathering momentum can also send us back to the business to understand what might be changing.
That brings us back to Rakesh Jhunjhunwala’s approach . Understanding the business gave him a reason to invest. When price movements supported his assessment, they added confidence to hold or buy more.
Perhaps we can leave the debate open. Using both approaches can help us understand a stock better, make a more informed decision and recognise when our view needs to change. We can do that without being certain which side “wins”.

Last week, I went on a roadtrip across Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. Every hour or so, I’d come to a stop at a toll plaza; and a few seconds later get a little text saying ₹x was debited from my FASTag account.
By the time I reached my destination, I’d spent over ₹1,000 on tolls alone.
Sidenote: Put all the FASTtags in India together and the annual collection is a whopping ₹82,000 crores !
But somewhere along the way, I started thinking about this “fee” that I’m forced to pay. Haven’t I already paid for this road? I pay road tax when I buy a car. I pay tax on every litre of fuel. And my income is taxed and a part of it goes towards the roadways and highways budget too.
So what exactly is the toll for?
Also, why does it feel like toll plazas never actually close, even on roads that were built decades ago?
Okay, so let’s take the three things I thought I’d paid, one at a time.
Road tax. That’s the one-time tax you pay when you register a car. But here’s the thing. It’s a state tax. It goes to the state government, not to the people who build national highways. So when I pay road tax in Karnataka, it’s not earmarked for the NH-44 I drove down. Instead, that money is allocated to the road outside your apartment and state highways,.
Fuel tax . Every litre of petrol and diesel carries a Road and Infrastructure Development Cess which flows into a pot called the Central Road and Infrastructure Fund (CRIF). This year, that cess is expected to bring in about ₹47,000 crore .
But the pot isn’t just for highways anymore. It also funds energy, water and sanitation projects. And in 2026-27, the amount going from it to NHAI (National Highways Authority of India), the body that builds our national highways, is exactly zero.
There’s another wrinkle: responsibility for CRIF was transferred from the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) to the Ministry of Finance in 2018. So the control over the funds has shifted ministries and priorities.
Then there’s the highways budget which is the big one.
In Budget 2026-27, MoRTH got ₹3.1 lakh crore out of which NHAI alone got about ₹1.87 lakh crore. So if the government is already spending that much on roads — financed through taxes we pay on income, GST, investments etc — why do I still pay at the booth?
Well, the one thing that you don’t know is that the “budget” is partly made of tolls.
Yup, when the government allots a certain amount for roads, it also factors in the earnings from tolls. There’s something called the Permanent Bridge Fees Fund which is filled with toll money. And this budgeted allocation is released to NHAI for developing & maintaining National Highways. This year, it’s sending about ₹35,000 crore to NHAI.
So your toll is already part of the budget.
And the reason why tolls exist is that building these roads doesn’t come cheap.
For example, an audit report by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India on the Bharatmala project (a highway and infrastructure programme) said that the approved cost per km of road was ₹15.37. If you do the maths, it means, the nearly 35,000 km of road that was due for construction under this project alone would total a massive ₹5.35 lakh crore.
And that’s just the approved cost, mind you. The audit found that the sanctioned cost had more than doubled to ₹32.17 crore per kilometer.
In other words, the cost per kilometre of the awarded works was substantially higher than the original Bharatmala estimate.
This could be partly because of leakages and inefficiencies in the road building process and also because costs have shot up. Take land acquisition alone for instance. After the land acquisition law changed in 2013, the cost of land for highways jumped from about ₹80 lakh a hectare to about ₹3.6 crore a hectare. That’s more than four times.
That adds up.
And if you look at the government target of roughly 10,000km of roadways every year and assume the ₹32 crore per km figure is what stays, then we’re dealing with ~₹3.2 lakh crore of expenditure on roads annually.
That’s about the same as the ministry’s entire ₹3.1 lakh crore budget for the year.
So if you’re thinking “if there’s a highways budget, why tolls?”, well, now you know the budget alone barely covers building the new roads. That’s before a single rupee goes to maintenance or debt.
Hence, tolls.
And if you think about it from an economic perspective, a toll converts a highway from a public good into a priced infrastructure asset.
If the government built every national highway corridor using general tax dollars, a non-vehicle owner living in a rural village would be subsidizing a family driving a private SUV from Bengaluru to Kochi. So, the logic is straightforward: high-speed corridors reduce transit time, cut fuel consumption, and lower vehicle wear and tear. The toll is theoretically a fee that captures a fraction of the value you save by using a superior road, rather than forcing the general taxpayer to foot the bill.
It’s the “user-pays” principle in practice.
Now just to tie this all in together, we do have to talk about all the different ways in which these roads are built and tolls are collected. And the big difference among the models is who takes the risk. Who pays to build it? Who loses money if not enough cars show up? Who fixes the potholes?
BOT (Build Operate Transfer - Toll ) is the classic. A company builds the road with its own money, then collects tolls for 25 to 30 years to earn it back. If traffic is thin, that’s their problem. If traffic is strong, the project can generate substantial revenue. Eventually, the road is transferred back to the government.
HAM (Hybrid Annuity Model) splits the bill. The government pays 40% of the cost upfront. The company raises the other 60% and gets paid back by the government in installments over 15 years or so. The government generally bears the traffic risk. And the government collects the tolls.
EPC (Engineering, Procurement, Construction) is the simplest. The government pays a contractor to build the road, and collects the tolls itself.
And then there’s a fourth one.
TOT (Toll-Operate-Transfer) lets the government take a road that’s already built and open, and lease out the right to collect its tolls. Simply put, instead of waiting decades to collect those tolls itself, the government can monetise the asset. A private investor pays a big lump sum today. In return, they get to keep your tolls for years.
This is called asset monetisation. And it’s big. As of mid-2025, the ministry had raised about ₹1.52 lakh crore this way. And the money from monetised highways goes toward repaying NHAI’s massive debt that it has racked up over the years.
For a country that has expanded highway construction dramatically — India went from building 12 km of highway a day in 2014-15 to 29 km a day in 2024-25 — all these mechanisms come into play. And governments don’t have to choose between “taxes” or “tolls.” They can use both.
But here’s something else that bugged me during the road trip and the subsequent rabbit holes.
Some of those roads have been around for well over a decade. Surely they’ve been paid off by now?
Many have. The toll stays anyway.
That’s because of a 2008 change to the rules. It allows tolls to continue forever , even after the private company’s concession period ends. Once the road goes back to NHAI, the toll money goes into the Consolidated Fund of India, the government’s main account.
Perpetual tolling. That’s the actual term.
Take two plazas in Tamil Nadu, Boothakudi and Chittampatti. Since tolling started in 2010, the two together have collected ₹1,202 crore.
The Tamil Nadu government has demanded that 32 toll plazas be shut down, because the cost of building those roads has already been recovered. NHAI hasn’t budged.
Parliament has pushed back too. In August 2025, its Public Accounts Committee, chaired by K.C. Venugopal, took on the “perpetual tolling regime” directly. It recommended that tolls end, or drop sharply, once a road’s construction and maintenance costs are recovered. It also suggested an independent regulator to decide toll rates
Hopefully that will change things for the better.
Until then, for a country building highways at a fast clip, these are questions we’ll argue about.’

Imagine you run a pension fund in Toronto. You have $100 million to park somewhere safe for a few years.
Option 1 is to lend it to the US government. A 10-year Treasury (that’s what US government bonds are called) pays about 5.3% now. It’s a good option because your money stays in dollars. You don’t lose sleep over it.
Option 2 is to lend it to the Indian government. The yields are higher; a 10-year G-sec (the moniker for Indian government securities) pays about 7.3%. You’ll make a little more money and that’s always an enticing proposition.
That 2 percentage points is the US-India bond yield spread. It’s the spread that investors look at when they’re weighing their options.
But there’s a catch.
It’s not just that spread which matters. Because to buy that Indian government bond, you first have to convert your dollars into rupees. And when you want the investment back, you have to convert those rupees back to dollars.
So the question you’re really asking isn’t “which one pays more?” It’s “is 2 extra percentage points enough to make me sit through the rupee’s ride?”
Because if the rupee weakens by a little under 2% over the year, that extra interest is wiped out*. You would have been better off investing in US Treasuries. And the rupee has a habit of sliding against the dollar — in just the past 5 years, it has fallen by nearly 25%.
Now all of this sounds like one of those esoteric numbers that only lives on an investment manager’s or trader’s screen. But it feeds into our lives too — it shows up in the price of petrol; in the home loan EMI; and in whether the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) can raise rates when inflation is high and the economy needs it.
And since it matters to us, we need to take it from the top.
On 7th October, the RBI raised the policy rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%. It was the first interest rate hike since February 2023.
It also changed its stance to “calibrated tightening.” That’s India’s central bank saying: don’t expect us to cut rates anytime soon, rather, there may be more of these hikes coming in an orderly manner.
The reason for this hike isn’t hard to fathom. It was quite expected, actually.
Crude has been above $100 a barrel. Monsoons have been deficient and that always leads to higher food prices. Inflation is creeping up and is expected to touch 5.8% over the next few quarters. That’s close to the higher end of India’s comfort zone.
And hiking rates, theoretically, is a way to temper spending and growth. To control inflation.
So rate hikes it is.
Now hold that thought.
Because here’s where we get into the spread or the yield gap between India and the US. The two percentage points spread we spoke about at the start? That’s a result of the gap narrowing. And it’s at the narrowest it has been in nearly two decades. Look at the chart.
The gap has been getting compressed because the US yields have been on the rise. And it may not end here.
If you check the minutes from the last meeting of the US Federal Reserve, the central bank, you’ll realise that more rate hikes are on the cards.
Which means, the gap between US and Indian yields could narrow even further pretty soon.
But why should we care about this gap?
Think back to being the fund manager in charge of a pension fund again. You’re deciding where to invest the “safe” money. Higher yields in the US is definitely going to be your choice over India. Your new investments will be directed to the US and you might even pull out money you had invested already into India
And that is a problem.
Because India needs this foreign money. Quite literally.
I’ll explain.
See, India buys more from the world than it sells to it. And the single biggest item on that bill is oil. We import more than 85% of the crude we use, so every time Brent crosses $100, the hole gets deeper.
That hole has to be filled with dollars coming in from somewhere. Factories that foreign companies build here. Foreigners buying Indian stocks and bonds. NRIs parking money in Indian banks (which the RBI promoted recently with the FCNR swap window ).
But here is what is happening: money is leaving.
In just one week in mid-September, as US yields crossed 5%, foreign investors pulled about ₹5,100 crore out of the Indian bonds that are open to them. It’s not a humongous amount but given that India is part of some emerging market bond indices and that passive inflows are a given because of that, any money leaving is something to definitely pay attention to.
And as US yields rise and Indian equities underperform, even US bonds seem more attractive than Indian stocks. Over the whole of September, foreign investors took out roughly $3.7 billion from Indian stocks.
Nothing dramatic had changed inside India. In fact, everyone’s revising the economic growth outlook for the better. It’s just that the Treasury just started paying more. And the gap stopped being worth the trouble.
And that feeds into the rest of the economy.
Here’s how the chain works.
When foreign investors leave, they sell rupees and buy dollars. More people selling rupees means the rupee falls. A weaker rupee means everything India buys in dollars costs more in rupees. Even if the global price of commodities such as oil doesn’t budge.
So petrol and diesel get pricier. Then freight and logistics too. Then everything trucks carry — fertilizer, edible oil, phones and laptops.
That’s imported inflation.
And it’s the very thing the RBI just hiked rates to fight.
See the loop?
A thin spread pushes money out. The rupee weakens. Inflation rises. The RBI has to tighten rates.
But here’s where it gets interesting.
Let’s fast forward a year. Say inflation has cooled, but growth is slowing. Businesses aren’t borrowing and investing in new capacity; people have cut back on consumption. The RBI wants to cut rates to give the economy a push.
When the India-US bond yield is at a 5% spread, it’s easy. The RBI can cut rates and still have enough wiggle room to keep attracting foreign investors.
When the spread is only 2%, that room disappears. Cut interest rates by 0.50% and the gap is just 1.50% (ceteris paribus, as they say)
You (the fund manager in Toronto) will do the math again. The rupee only has to slip about 1.5% before you lose money. So you leave. The rupee falls. Imported inflation comes back. And the cut loses its potency. .
Which means while the decision regarding interest rates is made in Mumbai, you can’t ignore the role Washington plays. It complicates things.
But is a wider spread always better?
It depends.
If the gap widens because Indian rates go up, and the RBI is trying to keep attracting foreign investors, the cost of getting those dollars gets passed on. Home loans get pricier. EMIs go up. Businesses think twice before borrowing to build that new plant. And the government’s own interest bill grows, which leaves less money for everything else.
Why the gap widens matters more than how much as well. If the RBI is credibly fighting inflation and on the other side of the shore the US yields fall because America’s economy cools, then it’s a good thing. The bad way is when investors demand higher yields because they’re nervous about runaway inflation or profligate government borrowing. That’s never a good thing.
And you also have to remember that money that comes for the spread will also leave for the spread. Japan’s famous carry trad e is proof of that. And even India has experienced this before. In 2013 , the US Fed just hinted it would slow down its bond-buying. Money rushed out of emerging markets and by September that year, the rupee had lost almost 15% since April. The RBI ended up hiking the repo rate to 7.5% to steady things.
So yeah, put all this together and you’ll see why Indian policymakers will be closely watching what happens in the US too. Sometimes, it’s about minding the gap just so that the other moving parts of the economy stay in check.
These are interesting times for sure.
*Foreign funds do hedge the rupee risk but currency hedging isn’t free. The cost of hedging typically counteracts the ~2% yield advantage and reduces the additional returns.

💡 KEY EPISODE TAKEAWAYS

- No-Cost EMI Reality: Lenders and retailers do not give interest-free money. Processing fees, GST on interest, lost cash discounts, and delayed-payment penalties ensure the lender profits.

- The "30-Second Rule": Ask yourself if you will still enjoy what you bought while you are still paying back the monthly installments.   

- Real Estate Misconception: Historical real estate appreciation was tied to land parcels. Taking a 30-year loan for a high-density apartment in city outskirts carries very different economics.

How do we understand innovation in India? And why has India been much better at some forms of innovation than others?
Rakesh Basant has spent nearly 30 years as a professor of economics at IIM Ahmedabad, where he is now the JSW Chair Professor of Innovation & Public Policy. He was also one of the founding members and eventually chairperson of the Centre for Innovation, Incubation and Entrepreneurship, now known as IIMA Ventures.

He joins Subtext for a wide-ranging conversation on how knowledge moves between firms, the three forms of innovation: process, product and practice, and why moving from process innovation to product innovation can be so difficult.

The conversation also covers competition and innovation, intellectual property and the incentives it creates, why Indian pharma has historically excelled at process innovation, and what it would take for India to take on higher-risk product innovation.

We also discuss why R&D needs to be de-risked, the role of public-private partnerships, how complementary assets determine whether new technologies can actually reach the market, and why temporary protection can help firms build capabilities without becoming a permanent substitute for competition.

The conversation then moves to the less visible ways companies protect knowledge, from lead times and speed to market to tacit knowledge and learning by doing, before turning to India's universities and research institutions, their links with industry, incubation, and the role of institutions like IIM Ahmedabad and IITs in building an entrepreneurial ecosystem.

Finally, we discuss what India can learn from the development experiences of East Asian economies, why mass education and human capital matter for industrialisation, and what it actually takes to build an innovation ecosystem from the ground up.

We trace how traders learned to reverse-engineer the formula to extract the market's own expectations, what the volatility smile revealed about a central assumption, and how one terrible day in 1987 changed options pricing forever.
