No Cost EMI is not actually free.

Let’s say, you bought a phone worth ₹1 lakh phone.
In a regular EMI, the bank charges you interest. So the ₹1 lakh gets converted into a loan, interest is added say 10% and you repay the amount over a number of months.
But in a No-Cost EMI, you still buy the ₹1 lakh phone and divide the payment across the EMI tenure but there is no interest!
So where did the interest go?
It’s still there. The retailer paid it on your behalf! 
Why?
Because the retailer wants to sell more phones and  saying “₹1 lakh today” feels very different from saying “just ₹8,153 per month.”
The smaller monthly payment can make the purchase feel more affordable, which can help the retailer sell more phones.
But here's the catch. :👇:

Even though you aren't paying the interest directly, the transaction still has to account for the interest component.
In our example, the ₹1 lakh purchase is categorised into a principal component of around ₹91,000 and an interest component for the rest.
Your monthly EMI comes to around ₹8,153, and over the tenure you repay ₹1 lakh.
But you can still end up paying GST on the classified interest component.
Then there can be a processing fee + GST on the processing fee.
So, in this example, you end up paying around ₹1,072 extra.
And
there's another hidden cost.
What happens if you want to close the EMI before the tenure ends?
You could have to pay:
:1️⃣: Foreclosure charges
:2️⃣: GST on the foreclosure charges
:3️⃣: The remaining interest
:4️⃣: GST on that interest
But honestly, there's an even bigger cost that people completely forget about.
The EMI itself.
A few thousand rupees a month can feel so small that you don't realise how much you're committing to.
And when you have a credit card and the ability to buy something even when you don't actually have the savings for it, that's where things can start getting dangerous.
One EMI becomes two.
Two becomes three.
And suddenly, a large part of your income is already committed before the month even starts.
That's how you can slowly enter a debt spiral.
The problem isn't necessarily buying the phone.
The problem is buying things you can't actually afford just because the EMI makes them feel affordable.
Before taking an EMI, ask yourself:
Can I actually afford this purchase — or can I only afford the EMI?
We've also made an entire video on how you can spend better and still buy the things you actually want.

How much you earn doesn’t tell you if you’re good with money. Your habits do.

Here are 4 simple checks you can do today:

1. EMI-to-Income Ratio
Add up all your monthly EMIs and divide them by your monthly in-hand income. Ideally, this number should be below 30%. The higher your EMIs, the less room you have to save, invest, or deal with unexpected expenses.

2. What are you buying on credit?
Think about everything you’ve purchased on EMIs or with your credit card. Is it helping you earn more or build your future (an asset)? Or is it simply something that loses value the moment you buy it (a liability)? If most of your debt is funding liabilities, it may be time to rethink your spending habits.

3. Credit Card Utilisation
If your credit limit is ₹2 lakh and you’re regularly spending ₹1.6–1.8 lakh every month, you’re using 80–90% of your available credit. While doing this occasionally isn’t a problem, making it a habit can hurt your credit profile and may also indicate that you’re relying too much on borrowed money.

4. Emergency Fund
If your income stopped tomorrow, could you pay your bills for the next six months? That’s what an emergency fund is for. Keep around 6 months’ worth of expenses in a safe, easily accessible place that isn’t linked to the stock market. It’s one of the strongest financial safety nets you can build.

These aren’t hard rules. They’re simple checkpoints that can tell you whether you’re building a strong financial foundation.
How many out of 4 do you already have? Let me know in the comments. 👇

What happens after a stock makes a new 52-week high? Is it a sign that the stock has already run too far, or could it actually tell us something about where the stock goes next?

The 52-week high is one of the most visible numbers in any stock screener. But despite being so widely available, many investors instinctively avoid stocks making new highs.

We start with William O'Neil's observation that 98% of investors he surveyed said they did not buy stocks making new highs, even though buying stocks showing strength was central to his own approach.

We then look at what exactly a 52-week high means, the different ways of measuring it, and why weekly closing highs and distance from the high can be useful ways of looking at the data.

The episode also goes back to the history of the idea, from Nicolas Darvas and his famous "boxes" to William O'Neil, CAN SLIM, and Investor's Business Daily.

We then look at the academic research behind the 52-week high effect, including the 2004 study by George and Hwang and more recent research on Indian stocks, before exploring the behavioural explanation for why the effect might exist.

Finally, we run our own backtest on the NIFTY 750, looking at stocks that make a new 52-week closing high, applying a 52-week cooldown between signals, and tracking what happens over different holding periods.

The aim isn't to suggest that you should simply buy every stock that makes a new high. Instead, we look at whether the 52-week high can be useful as a first filter for stock selection.

Can a method built around reading charts be turned into a set of rules that we can test? And what happens when we apply Stan Weinstein’s Stage Analysis to Indian stocks?

Stan Weinstein’s approach to the stock market is largely discretionary. It involves reading charts, identifying trends, and making judgements about where a stock stands in its cycle. Weinstein himself questioned whether every breakout could be treated equally by a computer.

In this episode, we take a rules-based approach to Stage Analysis, to the extent possible, and explore how it works in our markets.

We start with Stan Weinstein’s background and how he developed his approach to trading. We then look at how he analysed markets, why he preferred weekly charts, and how his top-down approach moved from the overall market to sectors and then individual stocks.

We break down the four stages of his method: the base, the advance, the top, and the decline. We also look at the conditions Weinstein wanted to see before buying a breakout, including volume and relative strength, and how he approached exits and position sizing.

Next, we explain how we translated this largely visual method into rules that could be tested using weekly data. The test looks for stocks moving from a prior downtrend into a breakout, with additional conditions around moving averages, volume, and relative strength.

Finally, we test this rules-based version of Stage 2 on Nifty 500 stocks from October 2013 to September 2026, examining the trades, winners and losers, and how the strategy performed across the period.

The aim isn't to suggest that this test captures everything Weinstein intended, or that the approach will necessarily work the same way in the future. Instead, we explore what a rules-based version of Stage Analysis can tell us, and what would still need to be tested before using it as a stock-selection approach.

3 SIP myths you should know before you start investing :👇:

1. Any SIP will give similar results if you stay invested long enough
Not true. A SIP in large caps, mid caps and small caps can have completely different outcomes. In a specific period, small and mid caps may offer higher returns, but they also come with deeper drawdowns and a higher chance of negative returns over shorter periods. What you invest in matters just as much as how long you stay invested.

2. The best-performing fund will keep giving the best returns
One year’s No. 1 fund can drop far down the rankings the very next year. Instead of chasing last year’s winner, choose funds based on your goals, time horizon and overall portfolio.

3. Stopping your SIP is the best move when markets fall
When markets fall, your fixed investment buys more units at lower prices. During COVID, long-term SIP returns temporarily fell to just 2–4% for some investors. But those who stayed invested through the recovery later saw returns climb back to around 13.5% CAGR.

What you invest in, how long you stay invested and whether you can stay disciplined during bad markets matter just as much.

Today, RBI increased the repo rate by 25 basis points, from 5.25% to 5.50%, for the first time since February 2023.

But why does RBI increase rates?

One major reason is inflation. India’s CPI inflation rose to around 4.8% in August 2026, while higher crude prices, geopolitical risks and rupee weakness have also added to inflationary pressure.

But does that mean your home loan EMI will automatically become more expensive?
Not always.
Broadly, home loans can have two types of interest rates: fixed and floating.
If you have a fixed-rate home loan, your interest rate usually stays the same during the fixed period.
But if you have a floating-rate home loan, your rate can change when the benchmark linked to your loan changes.

For example, on a ₹50 lakh home loan for 20 years, if your interest rate increases from 7.75% to 8%, your EMI can go from around ₹41,047 to ₹41,822.
That is about ₹775 more every month.

Now, when interest rates rise, banks have commonly kept the EMI unchanged and extended the loan tenure instead. So your monthly payment may look the same, but you could end up paying EMIs for longer and paying more interest overall.

However, RBI rules require lenders to give borrowers options when a floating rate resets. You may be able to increase your EMI, extend the tenure, use a combination of both, and in applicable cases switch to a fixed rate or make a prepayment.
And if you want to reduce the overall interest burden, one option is to pay one extra EMI a year. This can help reduce the interest you pay and close the loan earlier.

You can use this calculator and input your numbers to see how a change in interest rate can impact your EMI, tenure and total interest.

Growpital: How the ₹193 Crore Investment Scheme Worked
Growpital, a Jaipur-based agri-tech platform, promised investors assured, tax-free returns of 10–15% a year, with some plans offering returns as high as 18.5%. SEBI’s investigation found that the farming operations and revenues used to support these claims were largely fictitious. The platform raised over ₹193 crore from more than 5,200 investors between 2020 and early 2024, while routing nearly ₹96 crore through layers of intermediary entities to companies controlled by its promoters.
SEBI also found that Growpital’s legal structure made investors appear to be LLP partners, even though they had little to no control over the supposed farming businesses. The investigation uncovered questionable land records, inflated revenue claims and transactions backed by fabricated invoices. SEBI subsequently ordered refunds with interest, market bans and monetary penalties against the entities and individuals involved.

We’ll cover:
●Growpital’s investment pitch: How it promised high, assured returns through farming projects.
●SEBI’s investigation: How a simple calculation exposed the gap between claimed and possible farm revenue.
●Where the money went: How investor funds were routed through multiple entities and what action SEBI took.

Many of us use Credit Cards in our day to day life to get the points and rewards! But using the credit card the wrong way can cause great harm to your financial health!

Here are the 3 things you should take care when you use your credit card next:

Credit Card Limit:
Credit beaures have never said anything about the 30% threshold, but it’s a good personal finance practice to keep your credit limit below this number. Don’t use more than 30% of your available credit card limit. If all your credit cards combined give you a limit of 5 lakhs, the best practice is to utilise less than 30% (1.5Lakhs) of the limit at any given point of time. Generally exceeding more than 30% very frequently might negatively impacts your credit rating or your CIBIL score.

Closing Credit Cards ?
Don’t close your old credit cards, your credit limit or the interest rate on your loans depends a lot on your credit history. Your oldest credit card plays a big role in strengthening your available credit history, so if the card doesn’t have a significantly high fees or a security concern it is generally not recommended to close your oldest card.

Credit Card = Debit Card
Credit Cards can be a good way to benefit from the reward and the cash backs but considering it as the primary and ease source to take loans can turn out to be fatal. The best practise is to use your credit cards to make only those purchases which you can make with cash outright!

In today’s episode of The Daily Brief, we take a deep dive into one key story and cover another story shaping Indian and global markets:

1. Can ₹84,000 Crore Help India Find More Oil?
India imports nearly 89% of its crude oil requirements, while domestic production continues to decline. The government’s ₹84,084-crore Samudra Manthan scheme aims to encourage offshore oil and gas exploration by sharing drilling costs, improving geological data and funding common infrastructure. But will these incentives attract enough investment to reduce India’s dependence on imported energy?

We’ll cover:
- Why India’s domestic oil production is falling and what untapped reserves could mean.
- How the Samudra Manthan scheme plans to reduce exploration risks for companies.
- The challenges of offshore drilling, investment returns and the timeline for new oil production.

2. Why Is Rice Getting Expensive Despite Record Stocks?
Rice prices in India are rising even as government warehouses hold nearly four times the required buffer stock. A weak monsoon could reduce this year’s harvest, while government rice stocks haven’t necessarily translated into lower market prices. Meanwhile, surplus rice continues to be allocated for ethanol production, raising questions about food security and price management.

We’ll cover:
- How the weak monsoon could affect India’s rice production and food inflation.
- Why government buffer stocks aren’t effectively bringing down retail rice prices.
- How ethanol production and lower reservoir levels could affect future rice supplies.

In today’s episode of The Daily Brief, we take a deep dive into one key story and cover another story shaping Indian and global markets:

1. Why LPG Connections Aren’t Enough
India has dramatically expanded LPG access through the Ujjwala scheme, but getting a gas connection hasn’t meant giving up firewood and traditional chulhas. High refill costs, documentation hurdles and last-mile access mean many poorer households still struggle to use LPG as their primary cooking fuel.

We’ll cover:
- Why many Ujjwala households still rely on firewood despite having LPG connections
- How refill costs, informal LPG access and migrant challenges affect usage
- Why making clean cooking affordable is becoming an increasingly expensive policy challenge
 
2. Why Airlines Resist Navi Mumbai
Mumbai Airport’s Terminal 1 redevelopment could require shifting some international flights from T2 to Navi Mumbai International Airport. Airlines are pushing back because splitting operations across two airports could increase costs, complicate passenger connections and disrupt valuable airport slots.

We’ll cover:
- Why Mumbai’s T1 redevelopment could push international flights to Navi Mumbai
- Why airlines are worried about costs, connections and operational readiness
- How airport slots and capacity allocation complicate the proposed shift

- How India regulates the prices of scheduled and non-scheduled medicines.
